method: Built from work/recommendations.jsonl (2,779 mentions): mentions were first grouped by a normalised title key, with Everything is Everything and Seen and the Unseen episodes keyed by show and episode number (matched to episodes.jsonl titles where the number was missing), then every group was reviewed by hand to merge variant titles and split different works that share a name (book vs film or TV series, originals vs covers). A mention naming several works is filed under the first-named one; 'why' is a hand-written synthesis of the cited reasons for works mentioned in two or more episodes, and the verbatim reason otherwise.

items.title: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
items.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' framework for Indian economic policy: when the state should step in, why its failures cut across every domain (HR, contracting, budgeting, checks on coercive power), and why the fix is checks and balances and small, reversible steps. Amit calls it a masterpiece and the rare public-policy primer set in India; in the second edition each of its 45 chapters comes with a reading list.

items.title: Why Freedom Matters (Everything is Everything, Ep 10)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Despite the title, an economic history of India told through the lens of freedom: the boom after 1869, Nehru's Fabian socialism, the lost years from the 1962 war to the Emergency, and the opening-up that lifted millions out of poverty. The hosts point to it whenever an episode needs the big story of why the closed, top-down economy failed.

items.title: Life Lessons
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Amit and Ajay's course on what they wish they had been taught at twenty: learning how to learn, frameworks for thinking, writing, probabilistic intuition, economics, the history of thought, personal finance (Ajay's module is 'legendary') and health. It comes with a community of curious people, with meetups and book clubs.

items.title: The Art of Clear Writing
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's writing course, which treats clear writing as a test of clear thinking. It teaches concrete rules (put the verb soon after the subject, make every sentence go forward or deeper), simplicity, steel-manning and reading like a writer, through exercises and deliberate constraints.

items.title: Understanding the State (Everything is Everything, Ep 25)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The foundation of the show's thinking on government: the state is a monopoly on violence that acts through coercion, so every intervention, paid for by taxes, must be justified. It opens a series (with When Should the State Act? and the public choice episode) that the hosts call a complete toolkit for deciding when and how the state should act.

items.title: The Long Road to Change (Everything is Everything, Ep 36)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' theory of change: policy improves through a decades-long pipeline of data, research, rival proposals, public debate, committee reports and draft laws, not by whispering in a joint secretary's ear. It explains why reforms such as inflation targeting took years, and why reforms nobody looks after fade away.

items.title: The Reformers (Everything is Everything, Ep 28)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The human story of the people who worked behind the scenes, often for decades and without reward, to open India up in 1991. Amit counts it among their best episodes, and the hosts point to it whenever a later reform story needs its backstory.

items.title: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 335)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
items.why: A five-and-a-half-hour masterclass from Ajay on the war and the deep histories of Russia and Ukraine, built on a lifetime of reading and a counter to Russian propaganda. It is the source of ideas the hosts keep returning to, from Ukraine's 'Uber for artillery' and cheap drones at mass scale to clear definitions of strategy, operations and tactics.

items.title: The Beauty of Finance (Everything is Everything, Ep 21)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's masterclass on why finance exists and why it matters to the real economy: finance as 'the brain of the economy', not a casino for the rich, traced back to medieval trading voyages. The hosts treat it as the foundation for all their finance talk, from the cost of capital for manufacturing to fixing Indian finance at the root.

items.title: Ajay Shah Brings the Dreams of the 20th Century (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 402)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
items.why: A ten-and-a-half-hour conversation with Ajay about his life and ideas, including the inside story of how India built a good equity market through SEBI, NSE and NSDL. The hosts point to it as the long-form source for Ajay's views, and as proof that audiences will go deep and long.

items.title: Four Papers That Changed the World (Everything is Everything, Ep 41)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts explain landmark papers in plain language, notably Coase on why firms exist and Hayek on how prices coordinate a society no planner can grasp. Ajay calls it a cleaned-up masterpiece because Amit kept stopping him whenever he slipped into jargon.

items.title: How to Do Development (Everything is Everything, Ep 57)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The case, built on Lant Pritchett's evidence, that every human welfare indicator tracks per capita GDP, so sustained growth, not redistribution or small solvable projects, is the way out of poverty. It also argues that development is learning by doing and goes wrong when pride and emotion creep into policy.

items.title: The Use of Knowledge in Society
items.creator: Friedrich Hayek
items.why: Hayek's argument that the knowledge needed to run an economy is dispersed among millions of people, and that prices, not planners, carry it: a language through which strangers tell each other what they want and lack. Amit calls it perhaps the most important essay of the twentieth century and still rereads it; it makes the folly of legislating prices impossible to unsee.

items.title: How Family Firms Evolve (Everything is Everything, Ep 34)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Original thinking from Ajay on how Indian firms evolved over 30 years and how they should mature: from family control to dispersed shareholding, a powerful board and a management team accountable to it. With its companion episode on imperial firms, it is the core of the show's argument that firms are central to growth.

items.title: Public Choice Theory Explains SO MUCH (Everything is Everything, Ep 33)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Explains that politicians and bureaucrats respond to incentives like everyone else, so the state is no benevolent beast and government failure is far more common than market failure. Amit says every Indian must watch it; the hosts use it to explain everything from captured subsidies to why central banks need checks on their power.

items.title: Seeing Like a State
items.creator: James C. Scott
items.why: Scott's account of how state schemes to improve the human condition fail when bureaucracies cannot 'see' the society they rule, with a toolkit (state legibility, high modernism, metis) you can apply almost anywhere. It chipped away at Ajay's faith in technological high modernism, and its line that 'the greatest fertilizer of all is the tender gaze of an owner' is his favourite case for ownership.

items.title: The Life and Times of KP Krishnan (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 355)
items.creator: Amit Varma with KP Krishnan
items.why: An eight-hour oral history from a reformer inside the Indian state: how India handled the 2008 crisis, fought for inflation targeting and built the bankruptcy code. People have told Ajay it is the single best product for understanding the Indian state; Amit calls it an absolute masterpiece.

items.title: Fixing the Knowledge Society (Everything is Everything, Ep 24)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Why academia has drifted away from real-world problems: journal-based promotion and departmental incentives narrow every discipline, filter out creative mavericks and leave academics writing for each other. It also argues that since universities no longer give you the humanities, you have to educate yourself through books, films and art.

items.title: Graduating to Globalisation (Everything is Everything, Ep 48)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's case that internationalisation is the engine of growth: competing with the world forces firms to import best practices and raise their game, and the gains spread through the economy. The hosts use it to argue against tariffs and currency controls and for welcoming FDI.

items.title: The Importance of the 1991 Reforms (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 237)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay Shah
items.why: Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay on what 1991 achieved and left undone (factor markets, agriculture), and how freeing parts of the economy set off the discovery and trade behind India's growth spurt. It brings the bizarre pre-1991 world alive and corrects the belief that the reforms were simply a response to the crisis.

items.title: When Should the State Act? (Everything is Everything, Ep 26)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's masterclass on market failure in its precise technical sense (public goods, externalities and the rest) and on the narrow conditions under which the state may intervene, conditions that are necessary but not sufficient. The second part of the state series, it supplies the method the hosts then apply to vaccines and other policy questions.

items.title: How I Reversed My Type 2 Diabetes (Everything is Everything, Ep 9)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Amit's account of reversing his diabetes through diet: eat less cereal, avoid processed food, and treat ghee as a superfood and sugar as poison. It also tells how the sugar lobby funded flawed research, how the 1977 US dietary guidelines fed the obesity epidemic, and how India's cereal subsidies worsen its diabetes.

items.title: Our Population Is Our Greatest Asset (Everything is Everything, Ep 20)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The argument that people are brains, not stomachs: humans are innovators whose creativity beats scarcity, so India's problem is too few children and too little training of minds, not too many people. It also covers migration offsetting low birth rates in some states, and Ajay's point that fertility tracks a nation's mood.

items.title: What's Wrong With Indian Agriculture? (Everything is Everything, Ep 18)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Why Indian farming, which employs 40 to 60% of Indians against about 5% in rich countries, is held back by the lack of a working price system: MSPs that favour cereals over pulses, loan waivers instead of structural reform, gluts and collapsing prices. The fix the hosts propose is to get prices working and the government out of the way, so entrepreneurs can find new markets.

items.title: A Deep Dive Into Education (Everything is Everything, Ep 54)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Decades of both hosts' thinking on education packed into about an hour, an episode Amit is proud of. It questions the assumed link between schooling and development (rich countries end up with universal schooling, but schooling isn't what made them rich) and asks how to raise people who challenge conventions.

items.title: From Imperial to Adaptive Firms (Everything is Everything, Ep 37)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: How Indian firms moved from regional satraps in the 1980s to top-down 'imperial' firms with uniform best practices, and then to 'adaptive' firms that pair rules with local flexibility. It argues that a country as diverse as India needs firms like starfish, with thinking people spread around rather than one central brain; Ajay calls it 'metis in firms'.

items.title: Stay Away From Luxury Beliefs (Everything is Everything, Ep 46)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: On beliefs imported from rich-world discourse that make their holders feel virtuous while hurting the people they claim to help, such as the minimum wage, or opposing sweatshops that beat every other option workers have. A counterintuitive frame for spotting the fallacies in fashionable opinion.

items.title: The Brave New Future of Electricity (Everything is Everything, Ep 40)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's masterclass on the power sector: solar, wind, storage and time-of-day pricing, why electricity prices must be allowed to move, and why fixing Indian power is a 25-year journey that Indian manufacturing depends on. Amit calls it one of the show's best episodes.

items.title: The Globalisation Episode (Everything is Everything, Ep 95)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' foundational thinking on globalisation: first principles, a potted intellectual history up to the Second World War, and why tariffs harm a country's own people and shift wealth from the poor to the rich. It argues that human flourishing has come through trade and peaceful cooperation, and that India could seize this moment.

items.title: The Problem With Digital Public Goods (Everything is Everything, Ep 56)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: A critique of 'digital public infrastructure' such as Aadhaar and UPI: state-backed monopolies created by coercive power, without checks and balances, that crowd out competing private systems. It also argues that deleting data should be the default, and that more computers in a poor country's government are not progress in themselves.

items.title: Beware of These Five Fallacies! (Everything is Everything, Ep 45)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: How instincts evolved in small hunter-gatherer tribes mislead us in large, complex societies: zero-sum thinking, top-down thinking, blindness to spontaneous order and the pull of strong leaders. It explains why economics' deepest truths feel counterintuitive, which helps when judging any economic debate.

items.title: Economics in One Lesson
items.creator: Henry Hazlitt
items.why: Hazlitt's 1946 'collection of light bulbs' that uses the basics of scarcity and incentives to clear up fallacies about price controls, tariffs, inflation and government spending, teaching you to ask what the money would have done if left with consumers. It carries Bastiat's thinking forward; Lant Pritchett told Amit it turned him onto economics.

items.title: I, Pencil
items.creator: Leonard Read
items.why: A pencil narrates its own making from materials and know-how scattered across many countries, coordinated by prices with no one in charge. It joins Adam Smith's invisible hand to Hayek's insight about knowledge, and the hosts treat it as the best first intuition for spontaneous order and the myth of self-sufficiency.

items.title: Lant Pritchett Is on Team Prosperity (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 379)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Lant Pritchett
items.why: A deep conversation with Lant Pritchett on why growth, not redistribution, drives human welfare, why causality runs from development to education, and why many RCTs solve small measurable problems instead of moving the needle on poverty. Amit says it changed how he sees development, but urges listeners to read Pritchett's work too.

items.title: Poker and Life (Everything is Everything, Ep 38)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: What Amit's five years as a professional poker player taught him about life: most of what happens is luck, so don't let success go to your head or failure crush you, and focus on doing the right things. It also covers game-theory-optimal versus exploitative play, and why there is nothing immoral in gambling.

items.title: Seven Stories That Should Be Films (Everything is Everything, Ep 23)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The first of the show's series of true stories the hosts would turn into films, and Amit's favourite episode at the time. It is the show's lighter side, built on Amit's view that stories illuminate the world; the tales follow the same archetypal arcs as great films.

items.title: The Double 'Thank You' Moment
items.creator: John Stossel
items.why: Stossel's simplest picture of positive-sum exchange: when you buy a coffee, you thank the barista and the barista thanks you, because both are better off. Amit says he has never written a piece that explains the magic of markets as fundamentally; Ajay uses it to show why voluntary trades, even with speculators, leave both sides better off.

items.title: The Four Quadrants of Conformism
items.creator: Paul Graham
items.why: Paul Graham's two-axis map of thinkers (conventional or independent, passive or aggressive) that singles out the aggressively conventional-minded as the loudest voices and the real obstacle to new ideas. The hosts use it to explain who attacks every disruptor and turns intellectual fashion into enforced orthodoxy.

items.title: The Great Redistribution
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's argument that market interventions such as tariffs or bans on FDI in retail quietly move money from many dispersed, poor consumers to a few organised, rich interest groups, the opposite of their stated intention.

items.title: The Loneliness of the Indian Woman (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 259)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Shrayana Bhattacharya
items.why: Amit's most popular Seen and the Unseen episode, a conversation with Shrayana Bhattacharya (who gave him the 'anti-uncle' label) on the economic and social lives of Indian women. It documents what conventional marriage and everyday norms do to women's agency, and the gulf between the genders.

items.title: The State of the Ukraine War (Everything is Everything, Ep 14)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's military-strategy analysis of the war: how it is changing the way wars are fought, Ukrainian innovation, and its demographic toll on Russia, from deaths to the flight of a million of its best and brightest. The hosts' later episode on hybrid warfare builds on it.

items.title: Going Bankrupt in India (Everything is Everything, Ep 80)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Why bankruptcy is a healthy, normal part of economic life, and how the politics of India's bankruptcy reform gave big companies outsized influence, left operational creditors weak and squeezed small manufacturers' working capital. It also covers financial resolution, which Ajay sees as essential to controlling moral hazard.

items.title: Inflation Targeting Rocks! (Everything is Everything, Ep 68)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The full story of inflation targeting, which Ajay pushed for from the 1990s and which took more than fifteen years to become law: a lesson in how slowly good policy arrives. It also makes the case that reliable 4% inflation is the foundation of long-term financial planning.

items.title: Price Controls Lead to Shortages and Harm the Poor
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's case that you cannot legislate scarcity away: price caps discourage producers and innovators, so goods don't get cheaper but vanish into shortages and black markets, hurting the poor they claim to protect.

items.title: Rethinking Innovation Policy (Everything is Everything, Ep 59)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Why research funding in India is 'a truly bad space', and the alternative: an industry-neutral approach that contracts R&D out through grants to universities and private firms rather than having bureaucrats pick sectors. It treats innovation as a 20-year positive-externality problem, not a regulation problem.

items.title: That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen
items.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
items.why: Bastiat's broken-window parable, which teaches you to look past a policy's visible effect to its unseen costs and introduced opportunity cost decades before the term existed. It gave Amit's podcast its name and was the basis of Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson; its lesson applies to taxes, state funding of the arts and how you spend your own hour.

items.title: The Art of Podcasting (Everything is Everything, Ep 49)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Amit's fullest thinking on the craft of podcasting, which Ajay says also explains how the modern media and creative economies work. It covers conversation and listening, and why the conventional wisdom about short attention spans is wrong.

items.title: The Hiking Episode (Everything is Everything, Ep 35)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay on his passion for hiking, from the Goecha La trek beneath Kanchenjunga to why the worst accidents happen when you think you're almost home. Non-hikers get lessons too, on avoiding competitiveness and treating life as a performance; it moved Amit, a non-hiker, to go on a hike.

items.title: The Journey of Indian Finance (Everything is Everything, Ep 71)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: An insider's account of how Indian finance was built: 25 years in which the finance ministry, SEBI, NSE and academics worked together, and how reform petered out once that group scattered. Ajay argues there is no hard political reason not to finish the job, and that cheaper capital would transform manufacturing.

items.title: The Life and Times of Montek Singh Ahluwalia (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 285)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Montek Singh Ahluwalia
items.why: Montek Singh Ahluwalia's first-hand account of his decades in the reform engine room and the 'silent revolution' that built up from the late 1970s. It shows that people quietly preparing reform ideas for years are what made 1991 possible.

items.title: The UNIX Episode (Everything is Everything, Ep 32)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's deep dive into the bottom-up story of Unix and free software, built by people working for decades with no promised reward. He uses it to frame why the Soviet Union never got to CPUs, Unix and the internet, and as a model that designers of digital public infrastructure should study.

items.title: We Should Celebrate Rising Divorce Rates
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's provocative argument that rising divorce rates, often lamented as 'becoming like the West', show more women gaining the agency and means to leave bad marriages. The hosts use it as an example of a creative proxy metric for women's empowerment.

items.title: Why Talent Comes in Clusters (Everything is Everything, Ep 8)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Why the brightest people concentrate in places like Silicon Valley and Bell Labs, and how a cluster becomes a magnet for more talent, helped by friendly regulation and a culture where it is okay to fail. Ajay calls it the essence of how to think about making Indian cities work.

items.title: Abby Philips Fights for Science and Medicine (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 310)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Abby Philips
items.why: A long defence of scientific medicine from liver doctor Abby Philips, on the tension between doing right by patients and giving them what they want. Philips's argument that even an occasional drink does the liver more harm than it does the heart good changed Amit's behaviour.

items.title: Consumer Pyramids Household Survey (CPHS)
items.creator: CMIE
items.why: CMIE's household survey (about 190,000 households, three times a year, across some 100 homogeneous regions) makes India's diversity measurable, from fivefold income gaps between regions to how many households really live off farming. Ajay uses it to see India region by region rather than as one monolith, and even to check the government's CPI weights.

items.title: Demystifying GDP (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 130)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Rajeswari Sengupta
items.why: Rajeswari Sengupta on what GDP can and cannot measure and how the number is built, including how government make-work and roads to nowhere inflate it. The hosts still conclude that, flaws and all, national income is a great indicator of welfare.

items.title: Don't Mess With the Exchange Rate (Everything is Everything, Ep 67)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Why the exchange rate is the most important price in the economy and should be set by the market: rigging it to make exporters look competitive is a transfer from the poor, and managing it invites currency crises. It also explains why monetary policy is only easy with a floating rate and inflation targeting.

items.title: Fixing Indian Education (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 185)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Karthik Muralidharan
items.why: A deep dive with Karthik Muralidharan into what's broken in Indian education and how to fix it, including his point that the system is optimised for sorting, not teaching. Amit cites its 45,000-word transcript as proof that audio is the most efficient way to go deep with an expert.

items.title: India Needs Decentralization (Everything is Everything, Ep 47)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The case for subsidiarity in a country as large and varied as India: do as little as possible at the Union level and push power down to cities, where people can see and talk to the officials responsible for their sidewalks. A companion to the episode on separation of powers.

items.title: India's Massive Pensions Crisis (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 347)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah and Renuka Sane
items.why: Ajay and Renuka Sane on the old versus new pension scheme: a bipartisan reform built by a small intellectual community, and how institutional memory vanished once that community dispersed. It also explains the pension bill eating India's defence budget.

items.title: Paul Graham's essays
items.creator: Paul Graham
items.why: Free essays that Amit calls 'a treasure given to mankind': models of simple, clear writing, each workshopped for months, by someone who also builds things. They teach that great companies come from iterating and learning by doing, and offer frameworks for life, not just business.

items.title: The Blank Slate
items.creator: Steven Pinker
items.why: Amit's gateway into natural selection and evolutionary psychology: Pinker examines human nature and society through our evolutionary hardwiring. Amit says, with admitted hyperbole, that he divides his life into before and after reading it.

items.title: The China Model is Broken (Everything is Everything, Ep 16)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Why Chinese state control and industrial policy caused deep problems behind the cherry-picked EV and solar successes: Xi's centralisation and nationalism, capital controls, real-estate overbuilding, the exit of foreigners and a failed equity market. It is the hosts' background for China's slowdown and the collapse of FDI into China.

items.title: The End of History?
items.creator: Francis Fukuyama
items.why: Fukuyama's essay captures the post-1989 belief that liberal democracy had won the argument for good. Amit uses it to show how authoritarianism, the China model and nationalism have since shaken that belief, and to question whether progress is inevitable (note the question mark in the title).

items.title: The Evolution of Everything
items.creator: Matt Ridley
items.why: Ridley finds the same bottom-up process, with no planner or designer, behind natural selection, language, prices, cultural norms and common law. For Amit it bridges his two intellectual awakenings, natural selection and spontaneous order; he suggests reading it and then using an AI to dig into each example.

items.title: The Evolution of Everything (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 96)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Matt Ridley
items.why: Amit's long conversation with Matt Ridley, a companion to his book, on how order emerges bottom-up without central design, across biology, culture and markets.

items.title: The Fatal Conceit
items.creator: Friedrich Hayek
items.why: Hayek names the core error behind central planning and price controls: the belief that anyone can know enough to run a complex society from the top down, when the knowledge it needs is spread across everyone. Ajay notes that the computer revolution keeps reviving that conceit.

items.title: The Journey of Indian Finance
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's economic history of Indian finance from 1947 to today, which Amit calls close to magisterial and the definitive work on the subject. It doubles as the roadmap of the unfinished reform agenda; Ajay points readers to Table 2, a one-page chronology of milestones.

items.title: The Nature of the Firm
items.creator: Ronald Coase
items.why: Coase's answer to why firms exist when markets can coordinate through prices: contracting is costly. It treats the firm as something to understand rather than a profit-maximising black box, and the hosts use it to ask how centralised firms need to be and how gig work and startups are redrawing their boundaries.

items.title: The Populist Playbook (Everything is Everything, Ep 42)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Populism is not 'what is popular' but a dangerous package of beliefs and methods, rising worldwide alongside nationalism, that works by inventing enemies and selling insular slogans like import substitution. Amit loves it; the hosts use it to explain hostility to FDI and how populists exploit crises.

items.title: The Power Broker
items.creator: Robert Caro
items.why: Caro's masterpiece works on three levels: a biography of Robert Moses, a biography of New York reshaped by top-down planning, and a study of how power corrupts an idealistic man. Ajay calls it a fundamental input for Indians thinking about urban planning.

items.title: The Power of Moore's Laws (Everything is Everything, Ep 87)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Built around Wright's Law: productivity rises about 20% with each doubling of cumulative output, so volume drives down costs and tiny factories can't compete, in services as well as manufacturing. Ajay tells anyone who thinks of themselves as a business or economics person to watch it.

items.title: The Practice of Medicine (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 229)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Lancelot Pinto
items.why: Dr Lancelot Pinto, one of the rare doctors who reads papers daily, on medical practice and how overtreatment driven by patient demand cost lives during COVID. His don't-overmedicate approach saw Amit through COVID twice on paracetamol.

items.title: The Selfish Gene
items.creator: Richard Dawkins
items.why: Dawkins's metaphor of the selfish gene which, read carefully rather than literally, explains why humans are capable of love and altruism. It gave Amit a frame for looking at himself and the world and solidified his atheism; Ajay draws from it why top-down control keeps failing.

items.title: Understanding India's Pensions Disaster (Everything is Everything, Ep 65)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: A first-principles account of pension reform: how a small community with a shared philosophy built the NPS, and how guarantees and the old mess returned once that community dispersed and its knowledge faded. Amit calls it a masterclass; Ajay calls the reversal generational amnesia.

items.title: What Ails Indian Manufacturing? (Everything is Everything, Ep 104)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's diagnosis of why Indian manufacturing is weak: eight ways it differs from services, twelve things that hobble it in India (from duties on imported inputs to labour laws) and seven items for every state's growth strategy. Later episodes on manufacturing, FDI and trade build on it.

items.title: A Meditation on Form
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's essay on how form dictates content: long-form podcasting is a different activity from short-form, not a longer version of it, and its patience, listening and curiosity changed him as a host and perhaps as a person.

items.title: Against the Grain
items.creator: James C. Scott
items.why: Scott's account of how agriculture and grain-based early states made life worse for ordinary people, overturning the story of steady progress. Amit calls it a masterpiece; Ajay calls it one of the most perfect executions of a book and a model for anyone learning the craft.

items.title: Are You Just One Version of Yourself? (Everything is Everything, Ep 3)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: On whether character is contingent and whether we can ever know ourselves: a small change in brain chemistry, as with Phineas Gage, can make you a different person. The hosts return to it when asking how much circumstances shape who someone becomes.

items.title: Caste, Capitalism and Chandra Bhan Prasad (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 296)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Chandra Bhan Prasad
items.why: The Dalit thinker whose two heroes are Ambedkar and Adam Smith, a pairing central to Amit's hope for ending caste. A 'great TIL' conversation that reframes things like diabetes and the ghunghat as markers of Dalit mobility and choice.

items.title: Early Indians
items.creator: Tony Joseph
items.why: Tony Joseph uses the genes of living people to reconstruct thousands of years of Indian history: the first Indians, the Harappans, the Aryan migration, and how caste endogamy set in about 2,000 years ago after millennia of intermingling. Amit calls its findings stunning.

items.title: Essays
items.creator: George Orwell
items.why: Orwell's nonfiction, which Amit prefers to the novels: a chronological look at Orwell the thinker, who banged out three or four brilliant columns a week. Amit reads two or three as a cure for writer's block, because the clarity and rhythm of the prose 'would free something within me'.

items.title: How to Think About Cricket (and Life) (Everything is Everything, Ep 19)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Amit's contrarian ideas on cricket strategy and tactics, first developed in 2008 and still not well understood, which he says hold truly novel insights. Ajay applies its idea of a player's marginal contribution to winning to academic hiring and funding.

items.title: India's Problem is Poverty, Not Inequality
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit separates two problems people routinely confuse and that need opposite solutions: in a positive-sum world inequality can rise while poverty falls, as in India after 1991, so ending poverty through growth is the real moral imperative. It turns on whether you would rather be poor in the US or in Bangladesh.

items.title: It is immoral to have children. Here's why
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's deliberately provocative column: we agree not to act on people without consent, cause pain or kill, yet a child is born without consent and will suffer and die. He says it isn't the standard antinatalist argument, and uses it to stress that having children is a responsibility far beyond material comfort.

items.title: Life Lessons From Chess in 2024 (Everything is Everything, Ep 81)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Lessons from chess on why renewal matters more than mastery (experts in narrow fields stop learning), why young players peak in a finite game, and why a great firm recruits from all over the world. Amit loves it and thinks it is underrated.

items.title: Marginal Revolution
items.creator: Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok
items.why: The blog Amit thinks has been the best in the world for 15 years: two economists thinking aloud in clear prose every day, a model for academics and better sense-making than a newspaper's economics pages. Amit has found great music and novels through Tyler Cowen's annual best-books lists.

items.title: Metrics of Empowerment (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 88)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Devika Kher, Nidhi Gupta and Hamsini Hariharan
items.why: Three scholars invent unconventional, intuitive measures of women's empowerment, from who orders the groceries to women in prisons and solo travel, alongside Amit's own: rising divorce rates. It seeded a later episode on the same theme.

items.title: Milton Friedman on the minimum wage
items.creator: Milton Friedman
items.why: Friedman's short video argument that a minimum wage doesn't lift a low-productivity worker's pay to the legal floor: it makes the job illegal, so the wage drops to zero. It sent Amit, who once believed in minimum wages, down a rabbit hole that changed his worldview.

items.title: On Exactitude in Science
items.creator: Jorge Luis Borges
items.why: Borges's one-paragraph parable of cartographers whose perfectly accurate map is as large as the empire and out of date the next moment: no representation can fully capture reality. The hosts reach for it whenever they discuss maps, thoroughness or the limits of models.

items.title: Our Parliament and Our Democracy (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 253)
items.creator: Amit Varma with MR Madhavan
items.why: A long conversation with MR Madhavan on how India's parliamentary rules, especially the anti-defection law, weaken its democracy. It is also the source of Amit's framework separating electoral politics, legislative politics and governance, games that need different skills.

items.title: Perfect Days
items.creator: Wim Wenders
items.why: Wenders's film pairs the striving of simply being at your work with moments of silence and solitude we rarely get; Amit calls it 'a film that could only be made by an old man'. Nomsita Haritashya says it changed her view of life, filmmaking and work, and Amit picked it to educate Ajay about cinema.

items.title: Population Is Not a Problem, but Our Greatest Strength
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's challenge to the school lesson that population is India's biggest problem: people are brains, not stomachs, population density drives prosperity, and the ills blamed on population are failures of governance.

items.title: Private Truths, Public Lies
items.creator: Timur Kuran
items.why: Kuran's theory of preference falsification and preference cascades: regimes look unanimously supported until people discover that others secretly disagree too. Amit uses it to explain the collapse of Soviet communism, the Modi wave and the open bigotry that social media unlocked.

items.title: Public Choice – A Primer
items.creator: Eamonn Butler
items.why: A short, masterful introduction to public choice theory, readable in under an hour, that explains why state failure is practically everywhere though everyone talks only of market failure. It was Amit's 'gateway drug' into the field, and easier going than Buchanan and Tullock's own books.

items.title: Pushpesh Pant Feasts on the Buffet of Life (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 326)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Pushpesh Pant
items.why: A remarkable conversation in which Pushpesh Pant urges Indians to explore their own country's food diversity, sharing the imagined maps in his head (regions mapped by their souring agent) and how 'classically Indian' ingredients came from outside.

items.title: Rahul Matthan Seeks the Protocol (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 360)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Rahul Matthan
items.why: Rahul Matthan makes the strongest case that Aadhaar has privacy built into its design, the view Ajay challenges. It also covers lenders judging creditworthiness from behavioural data, and is the source of Amit's argument that privacy is a historical achievement made possible by thicker walls and separate rooms.

items.title: The 1991 Project
items.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan (Mercatus Center)
items.why: Shruti Rajagopalan's treasure trove of chronicles and oral histories of the 1991 reforms, including the legendary 'M document'. Amit says it fills him with awe because it shows the reformers had worked for a decade and a half before 1991.

items.title: The Blind Watchmaker
items.creator: Richard Dawkins
items.why: Dawkins shows how intricate design, like the eye, arises without a designer: the biological counterpart of Hayek's point about economies. It is one of the books that made natural selection Amit's first framework.

items.title: The Clash of Economic Ideas
items.creator: Lawrence H. White
items.why: Lawrence White's history of the big economic debates of the last century, from Keynes and Friedman to Fabian socialism and central planning, showing that each school was right in some ways and wrong in others. A good starting point; Amit also likes its picture of how ideas travel from research to policy to the public.

items.title: The Collected Works of Frédéric Bastiat
items.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
items.why: The writings of 'the man who really turned me on to freedom', as Amit puts it: Bastiat put complex economic ideas into simple language without dumbing them down, and gives you a framework for seeing the world. Amit ranks him with Sowell and Hazlitt as essential first-principles reading.

items.title: The Greatest Productivity Mantra: Kaator Re Bhaaji! (Everything is Everything, Ep 11)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The show's productivity mantra: between a great idea and its realisation lies drudgery, and the remedy is to keep doing the work until magic happens. It also covers the growth mindset and Dweck's study, and shows how Amit researches a Seen and the Unseen episode.

items.title: The LEAP Blog
items.creator: Ajay Shah (co-editor)
items.why: The peer-reviewed research blog Ajay co-edits, where his ideas are available to anyone at any time. Its hundreds of articles helped build India's literature on regulatory theory, the slow, upstream policy writing the hosts say India needs.

items.title: The Life and Times of Jerry Pinto (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 314)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Jerry Pinto
items.why: An eight-and-a-half-hour oral history that Amit calls perhaps his most memorable, and the episode through which many listeners find the show. Its Faria story inspired him, and tearing up with Pinto over their mothers is his example of how a host's vulnerability draws guests past rehearsed sound bites.

items.title: The Life and Times of the Indian Economy (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 387)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Rajeswari Sengupta
items.why: A nearly ten-hour tour with Rajeswari Sengupta of India's growth episodes and failures and the costs of its post-independence economic choices. It was the year's most popular episode; listeners watch it more than once and take notes.

items.title: The Logic of Collective Action
items.creator: Mancur Olson
items.why: Olson's account of 'concentrated benefits and diffuse costs': why small, organised interest groups beat the large, unorganised public. The hosts also use his thinking to explain what a state is, and why even a self-interested ruler gains from letting people prosper.

items.title: The Moral Animal
items.creator: Robert Wright
items.why: Amit's pick among books on natural selection because it deals with morality: how evolution produced our better instincts (it taught him 'reciprocal altruism') and how marriage evolved, with monogamy and polygamy as adaptations to different circumstances.

items.title: The Mystery of Capital
items.creator: Hernando de Soto
items.why: De Soto's idea of 'dead capital': without property rights, untitled slum homes and restricted land are worth something but can't be borrowed against or invested, so the poor can't turn what they own into capital. Amit calls it one of the greatest books he has read, full of 'today I learned' moments.

items.title: The Seen and the Unseen
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's long-form podcast of three-to-eight-hour deep dives, conversations no gatekeeper would have commissioned, which have become an oral history of India; its show notes list every book mentioned. Ajay suggests parents play it as 'a soundtrack of the child's life', because children gain from overhearing rich conversations about ideas.

items.title: The Tamilian Gentleman Who Took on the World
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's piece on Viswanathan Anand rising without the Soviet school's systematic training, like taking a Maruti 800 into a Formula One race, which shows how extraordinary his world-championship career was.

items.title: The World in 2050 (Everything is Everything, Ep 106)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: A playful but serious attempt to imagine the world 25 years out, from swarms of cheap drones in war to how relationships might be organised once love, sex, companionship and parenting come apart. Ajay uses it to argue that fifty-year retirement spreadsheets are an illusion.

items.title: Wanderers, Kings, Merchants
items.creator: Peggy Mohan
items.why: Peggy Mohan reads India's past through its living languages, doing with language what Reich and Joseph did with genes: migrating men married local women, so children spoke their mothers' tongue first, and Sanskrit absorbed local sounds such as retroflexes. Amit says its insights blew his mind.

items.title: Where Has All the Infrastructure Gone? (Everything is Everything, Ep 55)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: A first-principles challenge to India's optimism about every new road and airport: infrastructure has diminishing returns, and big recent gains brought no comparable rise in FDI, manufacturing exports or jobs. Ajay concludes that infrastructure is no longer India's binding constraint.

items.title: Who We Are and How We Got Here
items.creator: David Reich
items.why: Reich explains how full-genome studies reconstruct human history and overturned received wisdom from archaeology. It is the source of Amit's favourite line: India is not one large population like the Han Chinese but thousands of small ones.

items.title: You're Missing
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: The Springsteen song that gave the show its name and worldview: its line 'everything is everything' points at all the world's wonders while marking someone's absence. Amit uses it with writing students as a model of plain words carrying deep emotion.

items.title: 'Wet Streets Cause Rain': Michael Crichton on Gell-Mann Amnesia
items.creator: Michael Crichton
items.why: Crichton's explanation of Gell-Mann Amnesia: we catch the media getting our own field wrong, then trust it on everything else. The hosts use it to explain the crisis of trust in generalist newspapers, and its title phrase as a memorable label for reverse causation.

items.title: 1000 True Fans
items.creator: Kevin Kelly
items.why: Kevin Kelly's argument that creators don't need scale: a thousand true fans paying $100 a year is a living, wherever in the world they are. It sounded theoretical when written, and Amit says subscription models like Substack have made it real.

items.title: A Scientist in the Kitchen (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 204)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Krish Ashok
items.why: Krish Ashok on the science and origins of Indian food, with the story of a blind colleague who listens to audio at 6x speed, Amit's favourite example of how much the brain can adapt.

items.title: A trade deficit with a babysitter
items.creator: Tim Harford
items.why: Harford always pays his babysitter and she buys nothing from him, yet both are better off: a neat demolition of panic about bilateral trade deficits and of the misleading word 'deficit'.

items.title: Atomic Habits
items.creator: James Clear
items.why: The best book on productivity Amit has read, and the one to start with if you read only one: turn your mind from goals to habits and processes, the compound interest of self-improvement, and use small rewards to make habits stick.

items.title: Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah Will Not Wear a Blue Tie to Work (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 389)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah
items.why: Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah on financial privacy and the inside story of how analysts and wonks came together to draft India's bankruptcy code, which Amit calls absolutely inspiring.

items.title: Blade Runner 2049
items.creator: Denis Villeneuve
items.why: One of Amit's favourite films, which he loves even more than Ridley Scott's original masterpiece: a magnificent meditation on the shaping of the self and the nature of memory.

items.title: Blue
items.creator: Joni Mitchell
items.why: Amit's favourite Joni Mitchell album, by a singer-songwriter and guitarist ahead of her time whose polio-shaped guitar playing fits no single genre. Listen on headphones on a quiet day, alone, starting with 'All I Want', 'Little Green', 'River' and 'A Case of You'.

items.title: Bootleggers and Baptists: The Education of a Regulatory Economist
items.creator: Bruce Yandle
items.why: Yandle's 'beautiful way of thinking about how regulation works': the moral crusader (the Baptist) and the black-market supplier (the bootlegger) both want the ban, so they lobby for the same end, sometimes with the bootlegger funding the Baptist. It explains why prohibitions persist.

items.title: But Clouds Got In My Way: Bias and Bias Correction of VIIRS Nighttime Lights Data in the Presence of Clouds
items.creator: Ayush Patnaik, Ajay Shah, Anshul Tayal and Susan Thomas
items.why: Ajay's group's paper documenting a cloud-related bias in NASA/NOAA nighttime-lights data, with a conservative correction; the data measures prosperity monthly at half-kilometre resolution without depending on the government. Ajay also holds up its witty title as a model.

items.title: Climate Change and Our Power Sector (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 278)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Akshay Jaitly and Ajay Shah
items.why: Akshay Jaitly and Ajay on climate change and India's power sector, centred on the electricity grid: the conversational version of their case for reforming electricity.

items.title: Coomi Kapoor Has the Inside Track (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 305)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Coomi Kapoor
items.why: A long conversation with Coomi Kapoor, whose first-hand account of the Emergency Amit relies on; a companion to her book The Emergency: A Personal History.

items.title: Declutter (Everything is Everything, Ep 30)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Much of the hosts' personal philosophy of life: recognise your constraints, especially time, prioritise accordingly, and prefer processes to grand goals. Ajay later added a counterpoint: some clutter, like an unused computer, can become the next breakthrough.

items.title: Determinants of Trade Misinvoicing
items.creator: Ila Patnaik, Abhijit Sen Gupta and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's co-authored paper measuring how Indian businesses misinvoiced trade on a staggering scale to get around exchange controls and achieve de facto convertibility, which shows that capital controls fail.

items.title: Devangshu Datta Traded His Corduroy Pants (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 348)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Devangshu Datta
items.why: A life-and-times conversation with the hosts' friend Devangshu Datta, from chess and his Brahmo Samaj background to a family tree with three great-grandfathers who had institutions named after them and a fourth who was a river pirate in Bengal.

items.title: Doing better than a competitive exam
items.creator: Nitin Pai and Ajay Shah
items.why: Nitin Pai and Ajay's case against organising Indian education around single exams like UPSC, IIT-JEE and the boards, with a proposal: a conceptual exam to qualify the top one lakh students, then a lottery for IIT seats.

items.title: Don't Mess With the Price System (Everything is Everything, Ep 66)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Why the price system should be treated as sacred: price controls almost always lead to shortages, and free prices let a shock work itself out through many small adjustments rather than one big collapse. It pairs with the episode on the exchange rate.

items.title: Don't Run a Country Like a Company (Everything is Everything, Ep 60)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Why business intuitions don't carry over to public policy: policymaking is a completely different and hard-won body of knowledge, and forgetting that is the trap behind many calls for industrial policy. Ajay recommends it to rich people with 'great man syndrome', Elon Musk included.

items.title: Dunkirk
items.creator: Christopher Nolan
items.why: Amit, no Nolan fanboy, calls it the best war film ever made; Ajay, who knows the period deeply, sees it as the model for letting real events carry the drama.

items.title: Early Indians (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 112)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Tony Joseph
items.why: Amit's long conversation with Tony Joseph on the genetic history of the subcontinent, the audio companion to Early Indians, including how India's migrant groups mixed for thousands of years before endogamy locked in.

items.title: Economic Facts and Fallacies
items.creator: Thomas Sowell
items.why: Sowell names foundational economic fallacies from which many other errors grow; Amit says he finished it a much clearer thinker about economics. It also argues that the economy began recovering within months of the 1929 crash and government intervention made things worse.

items.title: Economic Growth Is Enough and Only Economic Growth Is Enough
items.creator: Lant Pritchett and Addison Lewis
items.why: Pritchett's paper, which Amit calls a masterpiece of data and clear language, finds that human welfare indicators from health onwards correlate at around 99% with per capita GDP, leaving redistribution and welfarism a sliver of the story.

items.title: Education in India (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 77)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Amit Chandra
items.why: An earlier long-form conversation with Amit Chandra on the state of Indian education, another field the hosts say suffers from keeping prices out.

items.title: Emacs
items.creator: Richard Stallman
items.why: Ajay's editor of choice: a fifty-year-old, fully programmable tool whose age has produced elegant design and bulletproof code. A few hundred lines of Lisp let you build your own productivity world on top of it, and org mode keeps outlines in plain text files on your own machine.

items.title: Fear the Boom and Bust (Keynes vs. Hayek rap battle)
items.creator: Russ Roberts (lyrics)
items.why: A rap battle between actors playing Keynes and Hayek, with lyrics by EconTalk's Russ Roberts, which the hosts recommend together with its sequel, Fight of the Century: a delightful way into the clash between the two dominant economic schools of the 20th century.

items.title: Freedom House democracy scores
items.creator: Freedom House
items.why: Freedom House's democracy rankings, from Norway at the top to North Korea at the bottom: a decent, easy-to-use measure. Ajay uses it to judge how much state legibility a country can safely adopt, and for a simple investing rule: buy index funds of the top 20 democracies, about 5% in each.

items.title: Gita Press and the Making of Hindu India
items.creator: Akshaya Mukul
items.why: Mukul's masterpiece shows how deeply Hindu nationalist ideas ran through Indian society over the decades: the communal strain was there all along, secular liberals were the fringe, and politics simply caught up with society.

items.title: Glimpses of World History
items.creator: Jawaharlal Nehru
items.why: Nehru's letters to his daughter Indira, a history of the world written from prison largely from memory. Ajay ranks it among the great intellectual creations, proof of what careful, sustained letter-writing can produce.

items.title: Gods, Guns and Missionaries: The Making of the Modern Hindu Identity
items.creator: Manu Pillai
items.why: Manu Pillai shows how fluid Hinduism was for centuries and how a shared Hindu identity formed gradually, first against Islam and then against the British and their missionaries. Its opening essay, 'A Brief History of Hinduism', is reason enough to buy it, Amit says.

items.title: Government's End: Why Washington Stopped Working
items.creator: Jonathan Rauch
items.why: Rauch's account of how special interests captured the American state, coining 'demosclerosis': interest groups and regulations multiply until they are nearly impossible to reverse and crowd out other policymaking. Written in the 1990s and still true, it is Amit's warning that India could easily get there.

items.title: Hardcore History
items.creator: Dan Carlin
items.why: One man reads around forty books per episode and then simply talks, with no script, co-host or sound effects, and it is riveting. Amit credits it with teaching him about history, humanity and the power of audio storytelling.

items.title: History of European Morals
items.creator: W.E.H. Lecky
items.why: The source of the 'expanding circle': through history we extend moral consideration from family to tribe to nation and beyond. Amit uses it to explain past horrors like slavery, and to worry that today's circles are shrinking.

items.title: How Many Friends Does One Person Need?
items.creator: Robin Dunbar
items.why: Dunbar's finding that we can sustain only about 150 meaningful relationships, in tiers of roughly 5, 15, 50 and 150, with most of our emotional energy going to the closest few. Ajay takes it as a reason to put deliberate effort into the few close bonds that make or break a life.

items.title: India Moving
items.creator: Chinmay Tumbe
items.why: Amit calls it one of the great books of the last ten years. Its eye-opening insight is that marriage is India's largest source of internal migration, which shows how much of their lives and identity women give up when they marry.

items.title: India's Greatest Civil Servant (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 167)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Narayani Basu
items.why: Narayani Basu on V.P. Menon and the integration of the princely states, a 'fast-track colonisation' achieved in a couple of years through coercion and broken promises. Amit treats it as his own unresolved case of ends and means.

items.title: Instant cross-border payments vs. current account inconvertibility
items.creator: Ajay Shah and Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah
items.why: Ajay and Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah show that India's official claim of current account convertibility is not true once you read the actual rules and laws, part of Ajay's case that the Indian state treats cross-border activity as suspect.

items.title: Is Globalization Doomed? (Everything is Everything, Ep 96)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The second part of the globalisation two-parter: how the open international order broke down, mainly because China, and to a lesser extent India, didn't play by the rules, and why trade barriers cripple manufacturing.

items.title: Is the Singularity Near? (Everything is Everything, Ep 2)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' early episode on AI, with Amit's argument that AGI is about five years away and easier to reach than people assume. They return to it on AI's role in modern war and when planning a follow-up.

items.title: Kashi Ka Assi
items.creator: Kashinath Singh
items.why: A line from Kashinath Singh's book, about playing your harmonium while the world goes to hell, gives Amit his stance on social media: block the toxic accounts and build a feed of the finest minds. The hosts also push back on the temptation to withdraw it captures: if you care about the world, you have to understand it.

items.title: Larry White and the First Principles of Money (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 397)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Lawrence H. White
items.why: Lawrence White's masterclass on free banking: banks issuing their own competing currencies ran for decades in parts of the world without chaos. It made Amit rethink his instinctive objections and question the assumption that only the state can issue money.

items.title: Lessons from an Ankhon Dekhi Prime Minister
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's case for reading: experience gives us only a few dots, slowly, while books let us collect many dots fast, live many lives and reach deep, complex truths about the world that experience alone can't.

items.title: Luck is All Around
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: A short, vivid case for how much luck lies behind your existence and everything else, and the life lesson that follows: don't let good luck make you arrogant or bad luck make you defeatist.

items.title: Malini Goyal is the Curious One (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 377)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Malini Goyal
items.why: Journalist Malini Goyal on Bangalore: her diagnosis of a city with 5G software and 2G hardware, and her research on its dating culture, which found that when everyone has ten choices, people who want a partner to grow with struggle to find one.

items.title: Narendra Modi takes a Great Leap Backwards
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit links Mao's grand designs to demonetisation through one shared delusion, that a leader can redesign society to a master plan, and calls demonetisation the largest assault on property rights in human history. He uses it as a case study of leaders without skin in the game making huge mistakes.

items.title: Newton the Alchemist. Gandhi the Black Swan (Everything is Everything, Ep 7)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts go under the hood on how Newton and Gandhi emerged, tracing their intellectual influences rather than judging them by their highlight reels. It set the template for a later episode that does the same for Nehru.

items.title: Om Namah Volume
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: One of Amit's poker columns, on his life lesson to 'put in volume': a small edge pays off only over a large sample. He also uses it to explain why youth now dominates chess.

items.title: Order Without Design
items.creator: Alain Bertaud
items.why: Amit's desert-island book on cities: Bertaud brings economics and many other disciplines to urban planning, exposes the follies of high modernism and respects the local knowledge behind why streets and cities work as they do.

items.title: Our Unlucky Children
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's argument that markets give us forty flavours of potato chips and a thousand shampoos while education stays one-size-fits-all, built in the 19th century to produce workers, because markets aren't allowed to work there.

items.title: Praise for intelligence can undermine children's motivation and performance
items.creator: Claudia Mueller and Carol Dweck
items.why: The study behind Amit's advice to 'focus on verbs, not adjectives': children praised for being smart later tried less and even cheated, while children praised for effort kept improving. Useful for parents, and for how you talk to yourself.

items.title: Profit = Philanthropy
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's argument that in a world of voluntary exchange the only way to profit is by making someone else better off, which makes profit an incentive to do good and the highest form of philanthropy.

items.title: Public Finance research at XKDR Forum
items.creator: XKDR Forum
items.why: XKDR Forum's research programme on public finance and government contracting, studied field by field to draw general lessons. Ajay sees building the state's contracting capability, from defence procurement to science funding, as a high priority.

items.title: Raees: An Empty Shell of a Gangster Film
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's review arguing that the film gets prohibition economics backwards: a real bootlegger would fund the anti-alcohol politician, not fight him, because their incentives are aligned.

items.title: Range Rover (Amit's poker column for the Economic Times)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: The archive of the poker column Amit wrote for the Economic Times, in which he applied poker's probabilistic thinking beyond the table: the full body of his poker writing for readers who want to go deeper.

items.title: Roam Research
items.why: Amit's note-taking tool, which he calls a game changer: nested entries and two-way links turn any term into a hub of related notes, replacing his scroll-and-search Word files and making up for a memory he says isn't great.

items.title: Shruti Rajagopalan's talk on India's constitutional amendments
items.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan
items.why: Shruti Rajagopalan's talk tracing how India's Constitution has been amended from Nehru onwards whenever governments wanted to do something unconstitutional, until amendment became the routine way to make the unconstitutional constitutional. Amit says everyone should watch it.

items.title: Stage.in
items.creator: Vinay Singhal
items.why: Vinay Singhal's 'Netflix for Bharat', streaming content in dialects like Haryanvi and Bhojpuri: Amit's live example of technology and long-tail markets reversing the homogenisation of dialects. He believes in it enough to have tried to invest.

items.title: State Building
items.creator: Francis Fukuyama
items.why: A slim book that replaces the vague 'big state versus small state' debate with two dimensions: how much a state tries to do and how well it does it. India, Amit argues, is a weak state that does too much, the worst of both worlds, when it should do a few things, starting with the rule of law, well.

items.title: Superforecasting
items.creator: Philip Tetlock and Dan Gardner
items.why: A masterful primer on probabilistic thinking: TV experts, rewarded for exuding certainty, are often wrong, while good forecasters keep updating their priors. It covered so much that Amit dropped his plan to write his own book on what poker taught him about probability.

items.title: SVB, Banking and the State of the Economy (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 323)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah and Mohit Satyanand
items.why: Ajay and Mohit Satyanand on the SVB collapse and banking fundamentals, including the counterintuitive case that bank failures are part of a healthy system, and how electronic payments let a bank's money flee over a weekend.

items.title: Swapna Liddle and the Many Shades of Delhi (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 367)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Swapna Liddle
items.why: Historian Swapna Liddle on Delhi: Delhi College, poetry in the city's newspapers and mushaira newsletters, and how the British used education to push their narratives about Indian history.

items.title: The Adda at the End of the Universe (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 309)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Vikram Sathaye and Roshan Abbas
items.why: Amit's adda with friends Vikram Sathaye and Roshan Abbas, the source of stories he keeps returning to: the friend who changed his mind about living long, healthy lives, and talented small-town kids losing their depth in Bombay, a reminder that clusters can corrupt as well as uplift.

items.title: The Bankable Wisdom of Harsh Vardhan (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 352)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Harsh Vardhan
items.why: Harsh Vardhan, whom Ajay calls a deep thinker on banks, argues that banking, magical and fundamentally fragile, is essential to a successful capitalism. It also has the anecdote that even well-connected banking insiders struggle with KYC.

items.title: The Book Club: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (Storytel audio episode)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's short audio introduction, made for Storytel, to Mary Wollstonecraft's A Vindication of the Rights of Woman: how one of his great heroes extended Locke's rights to women and so began modern feminism.

items.title: The Broken Script
items.creator: Swapna Liddle
items.why: One of Amit's favourite history books: Delhi from 1803 to 1857, when Persian collapsed, print and newspapers boomed and poetry was popular culture, until it all ended in 1857.

items.title: The Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi
items.creator: Mahatma Gandhi
items.why: Ninety-nine volumes, free to read, in which you can watch a man engage with the world in writing every day, with unvarnished honesty, like a blogger of his time. Amit uses them to show how prolific writing kept Gandhi evolving and made India's founders great thinkers.

items.title: The Death and Life of Great American Cities
items.creator: Jane Jacobs
items.why: Jane Jacobs's argument that cities are about people, not buildings and highways, and grow organically from the bottom up: spontaneous order and metis against Robert Moses's high modernism. Amit counts her among the great thinkers of the 20th century and says everyone has to read her.

items.title: The Discovery of India
items.creator: Jawaharlal Nehru
items.why: The book Ajay calls 'literally the book that invents the idea of India': an idea grounded in history and free of hatred, in a modern synthesis comfortable with science and liberal democracy. Ajay read it at 12 and urges adults who read it as children to go back to it.

items.title: The Economics and Politics of Vaccines (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 223)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay on the economics and politics of vaccines, which Amit calls a potted masterclass on healthcare: why prevention beats cure, and why public health and healthcare are different things.

items.title: The Emergency: A Personal History
items.creator: Coomi Kapoor
items.why: A journalist's first-hand account of the Emergency, when half the opposition and hordes of journalists were jailed and a sterilisation drive spun out of control. Amit adores it as a lesson in what the Indian state's power can do and why democracy must not be taken for granted.

items.title: The Expanding Circle
items.creator: Peter Singer
items.why: Singer's argument that our moral circle keeps widening and will one day include animals. Amit thinks people two centuries from now may judge us for eating animals as we judge Jefferson for keeping slaves, though he notes wryly that the circle hasn't yet expanded to include all humans.

items.title: The First Assault on Our Constitution (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 194)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Tripurdaman Singh
items.why: Tripurdaman Singh on the First Amendment to India's Constitution, which Amit says badly harmed free speech in India: a conversational way into the story Singh tells in Sixteen Stormy Days.

items.title: The Forgotten Greatness of PV Narasimha Rao (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 283)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Vinay Sitapati
items.why: Vinay Sitapati on why Narasimha Rao deserves much of the credit for the 1991 reforms, and on the reformers around him. One of Amit's most popular episodes, best paired with Sitapati's book Half-Lion.

items.title: The Forgotten Man: A New History of the Great Depression
items.creator: Amity Shlaes
items.why: A contrary history of the Great Depression that Amit has a lot of sympathy for: government interventions, not the stock-market crash, turned a downturn into a depression.

items.title: The Gita Press and Hindu Nationalism (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 139)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Akshaya Mukul
items.why: The conversational companion to Akshaya Mukul's book on how the Gita Press, through culture and religion, fed modern political Hinduism. Amit also draws from it his argument that foreign powers can only deepen divisions that already exist.

items.title: The Heart of Disruption (Everything is Everything, Ep 86)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Why big companies crumble when they can't adapt and how some escape that fate, told through Netflix's 2007 streaming bet and the first half of Amit's own startup saga.

items.title: The Horrors of KYC (Everything is Everything, Ep 74)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The case that India's KYC regime has mainly built mass surveillance of citizens' finances while never stopping a terrorist plot, and that the real danger is a state watching citizens and turning its coercive power on them. Ajay sees it as the privacy battle India has to fight first.

items.title: The Incredible Curiosities of Mukulika Banerjee (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 276)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Mukulika Banerjee
items.why: Mukulika Banerjee's research stories: her fight for funding and her fieldwork in the North-West Frontier Province hunting for surviving Khudai Khidmatgars, which Amit calls a classic quest narrative.

items.title: The Incredible Insights of Timur Kuran (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 349)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Timur Kuran
items.why: The long version of Timur Kuran's ideas, from preference falsification and the Soviet collapse to the long divergence. It is also the source of the analogy that universities, like obsolete waqfs, sit on capital that no longer serves its original purpose.

items.title: The Law
items.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
items.why: Bastiat's mid-19th-century masterpiece on the relationship between the state and society, which Amit says carries wisdom in every paragraph and is a strikingly modern lens on India. It is free to read.

items.title: The Life and Times of Chess (Everything is Everything, Ep 52)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: A synthesis of Amit's knowledge of and enthusiasm for chess, walking through every world champion up to Ding and the role of computers in the game.

items.title: The Lost Decade
items.creator: Puja Mehra
items.why: Puja Mehra's account of how India's growth stalled after 2008, through decisions like retrospective taxation and the reshuffle that made Pranab Mukherjee finance minister. Amit uses it to show that the slide came from India's own policy choices, not any foreign plot.

items.title: The Lowest Hanging Fruit On The Coconut Tree: India's Climate Transition Through The Price System In The Power Sector
items.creator: Akshay Jaitly and Ajay Shah
items.why: Akshay Jaitly and Ajay's case for a market-based electricity sector that drives India's climate transition through the price system, rather than the state picking favoured technologies. Ajay counts it among his favourite papers and sees the reform as necessary for manufacturing.

items.title: The Outlaws (Everything is Everything, Ep 61)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Stories of mavericks such as Semmelweis, Mendel and Darwin who were ignored by the establishment and vindicated late, sometimes at the cost of lives. The hosts use them to argue that path-breaking work would not get through peer review, and that authoritarian societies crush exactly these people.

items.title: The Pathan Unarmed
items.creator: Mukulika Banerjee
items.why: Ten years of fieldwork on how Pathan peasants, stereotyped as violent, built the subcontinent's greatest nonviolent movement, the Khudai Khidmatgar: Bacha Khan rooted it in the inner jihad and the Pashtun codes of courage, hospitality and refuge. Amit calls the finding profound and says the book deserved far more readers.

items.title: The Refreshing Audacity of Vinay Singhal (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 291)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Vinay Singhal
items.why: Entrepreneur Vinay Singhal on building Stage, a dialect-first streaming business that proved sceptical VCs wrong and is pushing back against Hindi's pressure on India's dialects, including a 'reverse migration from Bollywood'.

items.title: The Soul of a New Machine
items.creator: Tracy Kidder
items.why: A journalist embedded with a Data General team building a CPU takes you into the minds of the engineers and their leader, Tom West, including the emptiness once the quest was over. It was young Ajay's first glimpse of engineering done with all your heart and soul.

items.title: The Three Globalizations (Everything is Everything, Ep 17)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's framework of three globalisations, from the first era without capital controls, when London bond issues built Indian railways, to today's, where access to the advanced-economy core depends on good behaviour in military and foreign affairs. It explains how supply chains now follow foreign-policy alignment.

items.title: The Tragedy of Our Farm Bills (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 211)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay and Amit on India's farm bills, which would have kept APMCs but given farmers the choice to sell elsewhere, and on why farm reform keeps stalling. A companion to the EIE agriculture episode.

items.title: The Wealth of Nations
items.creator: Adam Smith
items.why: The founding text on how nations become prosperous: Ajay says Smith is to economics what Darwin is to biology, and it is 'eerie' how much he got right. It is also the source of the standard view of cartels as an ever-present threat.

items.title: Understanding Gandhi, Parts 1 and 2 (The Seen and the Unseen, Eps 104–105)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Ramachandra Guha
items.why: Amit's first two episodes with Ramachandra Guha, on Gandhi, for which Amit read some thirty books, so they distil a whole shelf of biographies. They include Guha's answer that Gandhi was right about what he had personally experienced, and show Guha himself behind the caricatures.

items.title: Understanding India Through Its Languages (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 232)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Peggy Mohan
items.why: Peggy Mohan's linguistic history of India in conversation, the companion to her book Wanderers, Kings, Merchants.

items.title: Unlikely is Inevitable
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's column on the law of truly large numbers: with a big enough sample, unlikely runs are bound to happen, so losing several hands in a row as an 80% favourite is neither a rigged game nor proof of a bad decision, and bad luck shouldn't be read as fate.

items.title: Vitalik Buterin Fights the Dragon-Tyrant (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 342)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah with Vitalik Buterin
items.why: A three-way conversation with Vitalik Buterin on politics and identity, the source of his insight that the core weakness of voting systems is how easily people can be bribed, and of Ajay's argument that cash's anonymity protects us from a surveillance society.

items.title: Wanting
items.creator: Luke Burgis
items.why: Burgis brings René Girard's mimetic desire into everyday life: we want things because others want them. It helps you tell borrowed desires (the Mercedes, the prize, the label) from intrinsic ones, which alone make you put in the hard yards; Amit thinks mimetic desire drives choices like marriage and children more than people realise.

items.title: What Bruce Springsteen Means to Us (Everything is Everything, Ep 13)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: A labour of love about the musician who matters to both hosts, which Amit calls the show's least-watched episode. Ajay draws from it Springsteen's idea of a child as 'another shot', the anchor of his case that having a child is an act of optimism.

items.title: What Just Happened Between India & Pakistan? (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 418)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Pranay Kotasthane and Aditya Ramanathan
items.why: A conversation recorded as events unfolded, with Pranay Kotasthane and Aditya Ramanathan, on the latest India-Pakistan clash, which showed both sides using fairly advanced equipment. It is where Amit asked his most worrying question: how long before drone swarms are used for terror attacks on Indian cities, a risk he sees for 2026, not 2050.
