items.title: Why We Sleep
items.creator: Matthew Walker
items.why: The book that taught Amit how underrated sleep is: without it you can't be your best self, sleep-deprived drivers are more dangerous than drunk ones, and night owls, roughly 30% of people, simply run on a different rhythm.

items.title: FSLRC Report (Vol 1) and draft Indian Financial Code (Vol 2)
items.creator: Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission
items.why: The FSLRC report, a crisp summary of 20 years of Indian research on regulation written as compact chapters ending in drafting instructions, and the draft Indian Financial Code it produced. Ajay calls the code the best-drafted modern law in Indian history, a worked example of checks and balances on regulators that also incubated inflation targeting.

items.title: 100 True Fans
items.creator: Li Jin
items.why: Li Jin's more concentrated version of Kevin Kelly's idea: a hundred fans paying $1,000 a year give a creator the same income from a smaller, more committed audience.

items.title: A Billion Wicked Thoughts
items.creator: Ogi Ogas and Sai Gaddam
items.why: Uses hard data on anonymised internet behaviour, revealed rather than stated preferences, to show what men and women want, and explains why through natural selection. Amit calls it a masterpiece that made what he knew intuitively 'high definition'.

items.title: A Deep Dive Into the Indian Military (Everything is Everything, Ep 31)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay, who speaks to rooms full of generals, on reforming India's military, starting with pensions: without fixing them there is no money for a modern military. Amit says Ajay's involvement is why the episode is popular and credible.

items.title: A new dawn for nuclear energy?
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's writing on nuclear energy, behind his optimism and his argument for separating nuclear weapons from nuclear power and treating reactors as a business.

items.title: A Passion for Cycling (Everything is Everything, Ep 53)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Amit's passion for professional cycling, which he says will remain 'the greatest sport on earth' even when autonomous cars take over, because human endeavour, character and difficulty don't go away.

items.title: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
items.creator: Mary Wollstonecraft
items.why: The founding protofeminist text, written with no role models: it applies Locke's natural rights to women, argues that a false education makes women slaves of the male gaze and grounds virtue in reason. It may read tame today, so read it against its time.

items.title: Accelerating India's Development
items.creator: Karthik Muralidharan
items.why: Karthik Muralidharan's book is the source of striking facts the hosts use: the average district is bigger than 85 countries, only 3% of India's budget is spent locally against 50% in China, and more spending on buildings, school bags or 'better' teachers does nothing for learning outcomes.

items.title: Administrative Procedure Act (US, 1946)
items.why: The 1946 US law that binds every federal agency to a single rulebook, which Ajay calls a brilliant blueprint for checks and balances on regulators and the same idea as India's draft Indian Financial Code. Read it together with the court rulings that built a jurisprudence constraining regulators.

items.title: Adolescence
items.creator: Jack Thorne and Stephen Graham
items.why: A TV series whose one-take format lets the action unfold organically, which Amit calls a new pinnacle in filmmaking and a story about the human condition, not either side's politics. It also depicts a corner of the manosphere that grows out of real resentment on dating apps.

items.title: Age of Pandemics
items.creator: Chinmay Tumbe
items.why: Chinmay Tumbe's history of pandemics: how cholera's link to water was found and then resisted for decades, especially in India, and how past pandemics ended as strains evolved towards less virulent forms, which is why Amit expected COVID to become something we live with.

items.title: Ajay Shah on the Dangers of Digital Public Infrastructure (Brave New World, Ep 72)
items.creator: Vasant Dhar with Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay on Vasant Dhar's podcast, laying out his fundamental objection to India's so-called 'digital public goods': by the strict definition they are generally rival and excludable, so they are not public goods at all.

items.title: Anatomy of a Fall
items.creator: Justine Triet
items.why: A masterpiece, Amit says, about the tension between telling a simple, explainable story and respecting how complex the world is, and proof that we are in a golden age of cinema.

items.title: Answering Machine
items.creator: The Replacements
items.why: A great song with an immortal line, 'How do you say goodnight to an answering machine?', whose sadness is lost on people who never used one.

items.title: Astral Weeks
items.creator: Van Morrison
items.why: Van Morrison's masterpiece of deeply moving songs, born when the producer replaced his musicians with jazz players, including bassist Richard Davis, who improvised around him.

items.title: Atomic State: Big Science in Twentieth-Century India
items.creator: Jahnavi Phalkey
items.why: Jahnavi Phalkey's history of the early pioneers of nuclear science in India, including the 1940s struggle among three scientists in which one won out and the other two didn't.

items.title: Avoid hydroponics (Ajay's anti-recommendation)
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's anti-recommendation: hydroponic leaves look clean, but growing plants in water starves their root microbiome and leaves them nutritionally inferior, so prefer plants grown in healthy soil. He later uses the same pattern to explain what simple carbs do to the human gut.

items.title: Backstage
items.creator: Montek Singh Ahluwalia
items.why: Montek Singh Ahluwalia's memoir of the reform years, full of human detail about working inside the system and concrete examples of how licensing strangled Indian enterprise.

items.title: Basic Economics
items.creator: Thomas Sowell
items.why: Sowell's book for learning the basic concepts of economics in simple language, one of Amit's go-to answers when asked for a single fundamental book; he says to read all of Sowell's books.

items.title: Being Muslim in India (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 216)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Ghazala Wahab
items.why: Amit's conversation with Ghazala Wahab, which he holds up as a showcase of what his chapter-by-chapter note-taking produces; her book also supplies a beautiful example of 'show, don't tell'.

items.title: Beware of Industrial Policy (Everything is Everything, Ep 89)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The case against the state picking winners: industrial policy in developing countries has to start from state capability and public choice theory.

items.title: Biju Rao Won't Bow to Conventional Wisdom (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 392)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Biju Rao
items.why: One of Amit's favourite episodes: Biju Rao argues that you can't make policy from data on a desk in Washington but have to get your hands dirty on the ground, and that India has its own deep tradition of village-level deliberative democracy.

items.title: Biophilia
items.creator: E.O. Wilson
items.why: E.O. Wilson's idea of biophilia, a sense of wonder at and presence with every form of life: where Ajay's reverence for 'statistically improbable' arrangements of atoms begins, and what hiking gives him.

items.title: Blueprint for Armageddon
items.creator: Dan Carlin
items.why: The Hardcore History series that kept Amit outside his building after runs, weeping in the rain: the letters soldiers wrote to their wives and girlfriends the night before a reckless mission in which they all died taught him the power of audio storytelling, along with lessons on resilience, tragedy and the folly of nation states.

items.title: Both Sides Now
items.creator: Joni Mitchell
items.why: 'The great song', as Amit calls it, which gave Ajay's paper But Clouds Got In My Way its title.

items.title: Brave New World
items.creator: Vasant Dhar
items.why: Vasant Dhar's podcast, which Amit calls great and backs as the show of a very dear friend.

items.title: Caged Tiger: How Too Much Government Is Holding Indians Back
items.creator: Subhashish Bhadra
items.why: Bhadra's frame that constitutions are products of their circumstances: America's was built to protect people from the state, while India's, drafted amid turmoil and fragmentation, centralised power to protect the state from the people and paid only lip service to freedom.

items.title: Can Economics Become More Reflexive?
items.creator: Vijayendra Rao
items.why: Vijayendra Rao's argument, which is the show's own thesis that everything is everything, that economics has drifted into a silo away from anthropology and sociology, with four things economists can learn from ethnographers: cognitive empathy, taking words seriously, studying process and making people participants.

items.title: Capital Account Openness in India and a Comparison with China: Then Versus Now
items.creator: Nidhi Aggarwal, Sanchit Arora and Rajeswari Sengupta
items.why: Shows India's de facto openness to foreign capital rising over the years until India is more open than China: capital controls don't close the economy, they just make the rich pay lawyers and accountants.

items.title: Capital Ideas
items.creator: Peter L. Bernstein
items.why: A lovely, if slightly dated, story of how the ideas of modern finance emerged once models and computers came in; Ajay calls it 'just great fun'.

items.title: Capitalism and Freedom
items.creator: Milton Friedman
items.why: Not an introductory book, but Ajay says each chapter is 'like an earthquake' that shakes you into thinking about the world; part of the foundational reading behind Amit's understanding of markets and freedom.

items.title: Caste and the Census (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 417)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: A timely debate on what counting caste in the census could do to Indian society.

items.title: Centrally Sponsored Government Schemes (The Seen and the Unseen)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Pranay Kotasthane
items.why: Pranay Kotasthane on how schemes designed in Delhi fail to fit the very different needs of India's states and work as a backdoor for central control over state subjects.

items.title: ChatGPT Deep Research
items.creator: OpenAI
items.why: Amit calls it 'off the charts good': it asks clarifying questions, cites sources and writes deep custom reports, and has replaced Google for him, down to building an art-history guide to each museum he visited. Your curiosity has to drive it, and you still verify the sources.

items.title: ChessBase India
items.creator: Sagar Shah and Amruta Mokal
items.why: Sagar Shah and Amruta Mokal's chess platform, which began as a labour of love (covering obscure tournaments, interviewing players, analysing games) and pioneered using computers to illuminate the game. Amit would give its founders a 'Bharat Ratna for chess'.

items.title: Conversation and Society (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 182)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Russ Roberts
items.why: Russ Roberts on the art of conversation and Adam Smith's moral philosophy, an episode Amit remembers for its 'magical chemistry'.

items.title: Cross-border activities in India need more freedom, not less
items.creator: Pratik Datta and Ajay Shah
items.why: Pratik Datta and Ajay's argument that the Indian state's fine-grained control of cross-border capital curbs the natural freedoms of people and firms, and that its anti-internationalisation stance needs to go.

items.title: Dawn of the third globalisation?
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's 'novel insight' that globalisation isn't dead: it now runs inside a club of well-behaved countries, enforced through economic statecraft, and excludes rogue players.

items.title: Deepak VS and the Man Behind His Face (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 373)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Deepak VS
items.why: Deepak VS, an entrepreneur in his mid-twenties whom Amit calls an incredibly fine thinker, is always throwing out thought experiments that denormalise things; he pointed out that any new entrance test would be gamed within a year.

items.title: Dekalog
items.creator: Krzysztof Kieślowski
items.why: Ten films made for Polish television, 'a web series before the web', which Amit calls the pinnacle of cinematic storytelling, above even Kieślowski's Three Colours trilogy. They aren't directly about the commandments but are beautiful human stories everyone should see.

items.title: Designing the Monetary Policy Committee
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's design for a monetary policy committee as a commitment device: the government-appointed governor sits with four independent economists, so only one of five votes is exposed to political pressure. It traces the idea from FSLRC's proposal to the 2016 amendment of the RBI Act that created the committee.

items.title: Desperately Seeking Shah Rukh
items.creator: Shrayana Bhattacharya
items.why: Shrayana Bhattacharya uses Indian women's adoration of Shah Rukh Khan as a lens on Indian society and how lonely its women are; Amit says it 'contains multitudes', from economics and sociology to beautiful writing.

items.title: Don't Get Fooled by Success
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's column on survivorship bias: a fund's track record can be pure luck, so don't read success stories as proof of genius when many similar attempts may have failed unseen.

items.title: Don't Insult Pasta
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: A playful satire on demands not to offend religious sentiment (if you don't want me to offend your god, don't offend mine), part of Amit's two decades of columns on free speech in India.

items.title: Early Seen and the Unseen episode on demonetisation with Suyash Rai
items.creator: Amit Varma with Suyash Rai
items.why: An early episode with Suyash Rai, the source of his point that cost-benefit analysis hides an immorality when the costs fall on one group and the benefits on another.

items.title: Economic Learnings of India for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Bihar (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 345)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's guests on Bihar describe both the inventive things happening there, evidence of India's untapped potential, and young people without jobs who have lost hope: the human face of a demographic dividend turning into a disaster.

items.title: Economical Writing
items.creator: Deirdre McCloskey
items.why: McCloskey shows how to write about economics, or any complex subject, so that lay readers find it clear and interesting: exactly what Amit's students from jargon-rewarding fields like sociology and anthropology need.

items.title: Economics in One Lesson (Everything is Everything, Ep 109)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' episode on Hazlitt's seen-versus-unseen lens, applied to tariffs and government spending: you have to count what would have happened without the intervention.

items.title: EconTalk
items.creator: Russ Roberts
items.why: Russ Roberts's podcast, a long-time favourite of Amit's and the closest to his own approach: relaxed, conversational and deep, focused on ideas rather than the guest's life.

items.title: Elite Imitation in Public Policy (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 180)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan and Alex Tabarrok
items.why: Shruti Rajagopalan and Alex Tabarrok on why policies that Indian elites copy from abroad fail in India: a long conversation about their premature-imitation thesis.

items.title: Emergent Ventures
items.creator: Tyler Cowen
items.why: Tyler Cowen's grant programme, the original model for funding unconventional individuals; Amit finds it wonderful that it backs mad ideas from people with no credentials.

items.title: Emerging Markets Conference
items.why: A conference Ajay values because knowledge and ideas matter there rather than a 'great lineup of famous people'; a recent edition had a whole session on the red-hot field of the US administrative state.

items.title: Essays on Nationalism
items.creator: Rabindranath Tagore
items.why: A slim, beautiful book of deep and timeless ideas: Tagore supported Indian independence yet saw nationalism as toxic whoever wielded it. Ajay calls Tagore one of the most beautiful writers of English; Amit applauds his prescience a century on.

items.title: Even Cowgirls Get the Blues
items.creator: Tom Robbins
items.why: Ajay quotes two lines from Tom Robbins's novel: one reminds him that people who seem prickly are usually fine once you get going, the other that stagnation is a mindset, since only those who think they are on routine flights are on them.

items.title: Every Act of Government Is an Act of Violence
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's core claim that the state runs on coercion, starting with taxes, so every state action carries a moral cost that has to be justified; it is why he ranks spending on innovation below the rule of law and basic infrastructure.

items.title: Every Grain of Sand
items.creator: Bob Dylan
items.why: A beautiful Dylan lyric about our place in the natural order, 'like every sparrow falling, like every grain of sand', which Amit uses for the idea that the answers are distributed all around us.

items.title: Ex Machina
items.creator: Alex Garland
items.why: A film that asks whether something we create that approaches consciousness has rights: if an AGI is conscious by every definition we use, why should being made of bits rather than organic matter deny it moral standing?

items.title: Exit, Voice, and Loyalty
items.creator: Albert O. Hirschman
items.why: Hirschman's framework of exit, voice and loyalty shows what India underuses: Indians rely on loyalty or a little voice, while Americans exit, moving if they dislike their city or state. Ajay's enthusiasm sent Amit to read Hirschman's other work, and he urges listeners to do the same.

items.title: Export Versus FDI in Services
items.creator: Rudrani Bhattacharya, Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's co-authored paper taking the export-versus-FDI question to services: in Indian software, firms that invest abroad are less productive than pure exporters, which turns the standard internationalisation ladder upside down.

items.title: Father Returning Home
items.creator: Dilip Chitre
items.why: One of Amit's favourite poems, whose phrase 'man's estrangement from a man-made world' and closing image of 'nomads entering a subcontinent through a narrow pass' have stayed with him.

items.title: Five Epic Stories That Must Be Films (Everything is Everything, Ep 29)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: More true stories pitched as films, in the format of the Stories That Should Be Films series.

items.title: Frankenstein
items.creator: Mary Shelley
items.why: Written with no genre or craft models to follow, a pioneering work of proto-science fiction with an innovative nested structure of three narrators. Its question, whether the beings we create have rights, is live again with AI.

items.title: Free to Choose
items.creator: Milton Friedman and Rose Friedman
items.why: The Friedmans' case for voluntary exchange, which Amit uses to argue that capitalism means consent and is the opposite of cronyism; a core text on his 'recommend everything by Friedman' list.

items.title: Free to Choose (TV series)
items.creator: Milton Friedman
items.why: An accessible, watchable version of Friedman's case for freedom, and Amit's example of lasting work that becomes a body of knowledge others build on, unlike the daily flow of tweets and columns.

items.title: Friedrich Hayek: The Ideas and Influence of the Libertarian Economist
items.creator: Eamonn Butler
items.why: Butler's short primer on Hayek, a friendly way into a thinker whose own books can be heavy going ('though what a great writer', Amit adds).

items.title: Google Earth
items.creator: Google
items.why: Ajay's 'paradise' on a big screen: terrain mode, 3D views and aerial flybys, plus a practical use for hikers, checking the elevations of summit, base and campsite before you go. He prefers the desktop version.

items.title: Graduating to Globalisation: A Study of Southern Multinationals
items.creator: Dilek Demirbas, Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's co-authored study of outbound FDI by Indian firms that now build factories and companies abroad: a glorious and often overlooked mode of internationalisation that was unimaginable when he was young.

items.title: Great Books of the Western World
items.creator: Mortimer Adler (editor)
items.why: Mortimer Adler's set, whose thematic essays on death, love, desire, purpose and agency draw on the entire canon, fill Amit with awe and send him to the original authors. It is also the one sentimental artefact he kept while decluttering.

items.title: Half-Lion
items.creator: Vinay Sitapati
items.why: Sitapati's biography of Narasimha Rao, which shows him as a great man of learning and constant reinvention who staked his political capital on the 1991 reforms, not just a politician who happened to be there.

items.title: His Dark Materials
items.creator: Philip Pullman
items.why: Books Amit calls masterpieces, asking you to trust him blindly; years later they still make him smile or tear up. They also gave him a picture of the AI companions he expects: one spirit animal all empathy, another all wisdom.

items.title: How China Escaped the Poverty Trap
items.creator: Yuen Yuen Ang
items.why: Yuen Yuen Ang's account of what actually happened in China, which backs Amit's refusal to take a caricatured, good-versus-evil view of a deeply complex country. He finds it provocative and even quarrels with its framing of the poverty trap.

items.title: How Cormac McCarthy Became a Copy-Editor for Scientific Books and One of the Most Influential Articles in Economics
items.creator: Josh Jones
items.why: The story of novelist Cormac McCarthy cleaning up a scientific paper, which Ajay says everyone in academia should study as a lesson in how research should be written.

items.title: How I Gained 1 MILLION Subscribers
items.creator: Ali Abdaal
items.why: Ali Abdaal's growth graph shows exponential growth in practice: almost nothing for a long time (about 1,000 subscribers after 50 videos and half a year), then a near-vertical line. Concrete proof that growth takes a long time to compound.

items.title: How Laissez-Faire Made Sweden Rich
items.creator: Johan Norberg
items.why: Norberg shows in detail that the Nordic countries got rich as free-market economies first and built their welfare states afterwards: Amit's answer to people who cite Scandinavia against the case for freedom.

items.title: How Music Works
items.creator: David Byrne
items.why: The best book Amit has read about music, which he gives to everyone: it shows how venues and technology, from cathedrals to CBGB's, shaped the music played in them, feeding his obsession with how form shapes the world. Read it even if you don't care about music.

items.title: I Play to Play
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's essay on the philosophy that guides his life and that he gives every young person he advises: the game itself, not winning, is the reward.

items.title: If You Are a Creator, This Is Your Time
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's five reasons this is a good time for creators: they own the means of production, need no gatekeepers, face no constraint of form, reach audiences directly and can monetise directly.

items.title: In a Silent Way (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 316)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Gaurav Chintamani
items.why: Musician Gaurav Chintamani on how a big hit can become a curse (you keep changing, but audiences keep shouting for a three-minute song from twenty years ago) and on whether originality even exists.

items.title: In Defense of Globalization
items.creator: Jagdish Bhagwati
items.why: Ajay's single go-to book on globalisation, which Amit calls magnificent and the natural companion to Ajay's case for it; Bhagwati's work also underlies the hosts' arguments on rent-seeking.

items.title: In Praise of Floods
items.creator: James C. Scott
items.why: James C Scott on the diversity that existed before the agricultural age, and on how suppressing every small disaster builds up a much bigger one, which Amit applies to bailouts and moral hazard. He has misgivings but calls parts of it a masterpiece.

items.title: India Awakes
items.creator: Johan Norberg
items.why: Johan Norberg's film tells Barun Mitra's story of using satellite imagery as court evidence to win land rights for tribals, an inspiring case of property rights changing incentives on the ground.

items.title: India's Agriculture Crisis (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 140)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Barun Mitra and Kumar Anand
items.why: Barun Mitra and Kumar Anand on agriculture as a field where the state controls everything and farmers suffer, including the year MSPs were promised for 24 commodities but paid for only six.

items.title: India's Lost Decade (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 116)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Puja Mehra
items.why: Puja Mehra on what went wrong after 2008 and how the reform era unravelled, a companion to her book The Lost Decade.

items.title: India's Supply Chain Vulnerability with Chinese APIs
items.creator: Gautam Bambawale, Vijay Kelkar, Raghunath Mashelkar, Ganesh Natarajan, Ajit Ranade and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay and co-authors on the genuine national-security worry about Chinese supply chains, and how to address it narrowly, cleanly and with minimal state intervention, rather than by distorting the whole economy or handing one company at a time a big contract.

items.title: India: An agricultural trade powerhouse
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's case for India's stake in agricultural trade: the global market is the biggest stabiliser of food prices, which India's on-off import and export bans undermine.

items.title: Indian Colours
items.why: The source of many of Ajay's art shirts: it prints contemporary Indian art on shirts, cups and stoles and pays artists royalties, so ordinary people can surround themselves with beauty without spending lakhs on originals.

items.title: Is India a Flailing State?
items.creator: Lant Pritchett
items.why: Pritchett's image of the Indian state as a world-class brain of senior officials whose nerves to the limbs are cut, so nothing changes on the ground. Ajay uses it to explain both the state and pre-1990s Indian firms.

items.title: Is Manufacturing the Answer? (Everything is Everything, Ep 105)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The sequel to What Ails Indian Manufacturing?, which dismantles the myth of manufacturing as unskilled assembly-line labour.

items.title: Jahnavi and the Cyclotron (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 319)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Jahnavi Phalkey
items.why: Jahnavi Phalkey on a 1940s tussle among three scientists over building India's physics institutions, which shows normal politics returning once extraordinary times end. Amit asks everyone to listen; it ranges far beyond nuclear science, even to Patti Smith and Robert Mapplethorpe.

items.title: James Heckman's work on early childhood (The Heckman Equation)
items.creator: James Heckman
items.why: Hard-nosed return-on-investment evidence that the biggest payoffs come from interventions at ages 0 to 5, especially for disadvantaged children: hearing complex 'ten-letter words' early builds a layer of intelligence that can't be made up later.

items.title: Jhumpa Lahiri on Conversations with Tyler (Ep 17)
items.creator: Tyler Cowen with Jhumpa Lahiri
items.why: A great interview in which Jhumpa Lahiri discusses learning Italian from scratch as an adult and writing a book in it, and names Agota Kristof as a model.

items.title: Josh Felman Tries to Make Sense of the World (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 321)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Josh Felman
items.why: A conversation with Josh Felman, whom Amit calls a great thinker, that revealed things about him even Ajay, a friend of fifteen years, had never heard. Felman also coined the central idea of the hosts' exchange-rate episode.

items.title: Knowingless
items.creator: Aella
items.why: Aella's Substack, one of the few newsletters Amit pays for: strong data work on young people's sexual lives from a former sex worker who is also a very good data scientist, 'so packed with insight' about gender relations.

items.title: Laws Against Victimless Crimes Should Be Scrapped
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's case that banning prostitution, betting and alcohol only hands these activities to the underworld.

items.title: Madame George
items.creator: Van Morrison
items.why: One of Amit's favourite songs of all time, 'an absolutely epic' song and the centrepiece of Astral Weeks, an album he considers a masterpiece.

items.title: Madame George (Luka Bloom cover)
items.creator: Luka Bloom
items.why: Another fantastic version of Van Morrison's Madame George, by the Irish singer-songwriter Luka Bloom.

items.title: Madame George (Marianne Faithfull cover)
items.creator: Marianne Faithfull
items.why: 'A glorious ethereal cover' of Van Morrison's Madame George, one of the two great versions Amit recommends alongside the original.

items.title: Magic Fruit: A Poetic Trip
items.creator: Vaishnav Vyas
items.why: A musical play and poetry by Vaishnav Vyas, one of the show's young crew, which 'absolutely blew [Amit] away' with its creativity and ambition; he says it proves the young can have both youth and wisdom.

items.title: Making Sense
items.creator: Sam Harris
items.why: Sam Harris's conversation podcast, which Amit recommends for the art of conversation: he learned a lot about podcasting from its flow and rhythm in the early days, though it is now mostly paywalled and Harris has moved in different directions.

items.title: Maps Are Magic (Everything is Everything, Ep 44)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' fuller discussion of maps, which also gives Ajay's example of a genuine digital public good, in contrast to UPI and Aadhaar.

items.title: Marching For Salt
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's surprising point that independent India taxed salt far more than the British did, evidence that the freedom struggle is incomplete, and more of his take on Gandhi.

items.title: Math Is Better Than the Brigadier's Girlfriend (Everything is Everything, Ep 15)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: An early episode that the hosts cite as in-person collaboration at its best, and as background for the Data General connection Ajay draws later.

items.title: Memories and Things (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 195)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Aanchal Malhotra
items.why: Aanchal Malhotra on memories and the things that carry them: the conversation where Amit began thinking seriously about abstract categories versus concrete human connection, and that gave him his 'Chinese whispers all the way down' view of memory.

items.title: Metrics for Intervention (Everything is Everything, Ep 101)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Four metrics (discretion, number of transactions, stakes and transparency) for judging how hard a job is for the state, which explain why bureaucracies struggle to see the world accurately and why finance is among the hardest areas to regulate well.

items.title: Midnight in Chernobyl
items.creator: Adam Higginbotham
items.why: Gripping reportage on what happened behind the scenes at Chernobyl, showing the disaster as a failure of the Soviet state, rooted in its structure and incentives so that it seems bound to happen. Amit prefers it to the TV series.

items.title: Moondance
items.creator: Van Morrison
items.why: The counterpoint to Astral Weeks: Van Morrison with his own band, doing R&B the traditional way, exactly as he wanted. Amit says every song is great.

items.title: My Friend Sancho
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's own novel, which he dismisses as slight ('a bad novel I don't talk about much') while granting that its premise was strong; it comes up in his story about Nihalani and Marathi cinema.

items.title: My Top 10 Tips for Aspiring YouTubers
items.creator: Ali Abdaal
items.why: Advice Amit takes seriously because it comes from someone who has done it: make two videos a week for two years and don't look at the numbers, the antidote to quitting while you're still bad.

items.title: Narendra Shenoy and Mr Narendra Shenoy (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 250)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Naren Shenoy
items.why: A conversation with Amit's friend Naren Shenoy, with a charming arranged-marriage story; Amit plans to research the caste and class roots of cuisine with him.

items.title: Natasha Badhwar Lives the Examined Life (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 301)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Natasha Badhwar
items.why: Natasha Badhwar, who homeschools her children, on parenting, writing and how to educate your kids; Amit calls it his 'perfect episode' for its balance and a generous guest.

items.title: National Highway 420 (and the EV of Aggressive Batting)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's column applying expected value to cricket: aggressive batting pays, and teams batting first were systematically underestimating the par score.

items.title: Naushad Forbes Wants to Fix India (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 282)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Naushad Forbes
items.why: A business leader who backed reform when there was almost no public support, showing that reformers inside government needed outsiders to sell the ideas.

items.title: Nehru's Debates (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 262)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Tripurdaman Singh and Adeel Hussain
items.why: Tripurdaman Singh and Adeel Hussain on the clashes that shaped India's early constitutional politics: a 'sleeper hit' that shows Nehru and Patel respecting each other while disagreeing, against both caricatures of their relationship.

items.title: Nehru: The Debates that Defined India
items.creator: Tripurdaman Singh and Adeel Hussain
items.why: Nehru's debates with Jinnah, Syama Prasad Mookerjee and Patel show fine minds disagreeing in good faith over power and rights, a spirit of 'assume goodwill', lost in today's discourse, that Amit finds deeply inspiring.

items.title: Not What They Had in Mind
items.creator: Arnold Kling
items.why: Arnold Kling's book-length case that the 2008 crisis was a failure of the state, driven by overreach rather than free markets.

items.title: Nothing is Indian! Everything is Indian! (Everything is Everything, Ep 12)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: One of the show's most popular episodes: almost everything we consider quintessentially Indian, from food to clothes to languages, came from elsewhere and blended together, so getting nationalistic about it is ridiculous.

items.title: Nuclear Power Can Save the World
items.creator: Joshua S. Goldstein, Staffan A. Qvist and Steven Pinker
items.why: The data behind the hosts' case for nuclear power: sixty years of nuclear deaths, Chernobyl included, roughly equal one month of coal-related deaths, and 60 years of American nuclear waste could fit in a single Walmart.

items.title: Paris, Texas
items.creator: Wim Wenders
items.why: Amit's favourite Wim Wenders film, 'such a masterpiece', and his reminder that great art comes young too.

items.title: Poker and Stock Markets (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 47)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Mohit Satyanand
items.why: Mohit Satyanand on the cognitive biases poker and investing share, and on poker-style probabilistic thinking applied to markets.

items.title: Politics and the English Language
items.creator: George Orwell
items.why: Orwell's primer on clear writing, which shows the link runs both ways: writing clearly forces you to think clearly, and jargon is where muddled thinking hides.

items.title: Premature Imitation and India's Flailing State
items.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan and Alexander Tabarrok
items.why: A 'great paper' on why India copies the forms of advanced-economy policy from Britain, the US or Sweden too early and ends up with a flailing state, building on Lant Pritchett's idea of isomorphic mimicry.

items.title: Prices, Fast and Slow
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's piece, which Amit calls wonderful, on what happens when the state messes with prices.

items.title: Public Opinion
items.creator: Walter Lippmann
items.why: Lippmann's century-old masterpiece on how the media shapes what we believe and what to watch out for, which no technological change has made obsolete; Amit says everyone should read it.

items.title: Pune Public Policy Festival
items.why: A festival (and the show's sponsor) that brings young professionals together with bureaucrats, economists and thinkers to debate trade-offs such as environment versus growth and technology versus privacy; Amit likes that it pulls policy discussion back to Pune, once called the Oxford of the East.

items.title: Remnants of a Separation
items.creator: Aanchal Malhotra
items.why: Aanchal Malhotra's book on Partition, built from the memories of families who lived through it; preparing to interview her taught Amit how memory reshapes itself every time it is recalled.

items.title: Rent Control (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 14)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Alex Tabarrok
items.why: Alex Tabarrok's short primer on the unseen consequences of rent control, with the vivid case of rent-controlled New York looking like a bombed-out city.

items.title: Restaurant Regulations (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 18)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Madhu Menon
items.why: Madhu Menon on how restaurant regulation in India works as an opportunity for rent-seeking: an overreaching state makes honest business impossible and bribes unavoidable.

items.title: Rethinking innovation policy in India: Amplifying spillovers through contracting-out
items.creator: RA Mashelkar, Ajay Shah and Susan Thomas
items.why: A clear, rigorous paper arguing that the state should 'buy' rather than 'make' innovation by contracting R&D out, with a concrete 20-year blueprint. Amit says the logic makes a lot of sense once you read it, even if you share his doubts about the 'why'.

items.title: RODE Wireless PRO
items.creator: RODE
items.why: Microphones that record 32-bit float audio, which Amit calls miraculous: like RAW for photographs, it captures everything, so sound never clips and levels can be fixed afterwards.

items.title: Rohini Nilekani Pays It Forward (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 317)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Rohini Nilekani
items.why: Rohini Nilekani's framework of society, state and markets as separate pillars, which Amit critiques: he sees markets as a mechanism through which society meets its own needs by voluntary cooperation.

items.title: Romantic Outlaws
items.creator: Charlotte Gordon
items.why: A joint biography of Mary Wollstonecraft and her daughter Mary Shelley, beautiful and inspiring lives that show how hostile their world was to women: animals gained legal protection twenty years before the first law limiting violence against women.

items.title: Rules, Not Discretion (Everything is Everything, Ep 92)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Why a good society is built on rules rather than discretionary power, which can't anchor long-term investment, and why experts should stay sceptical of their own expertise.

items.title: Russia, Ukraine, Foreign Policy (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 268)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Pranay Kotasthane and Nitin Pai
items.why: Pranay Kotasthane and Nitin Pai on Europe's disastrous reliance on Russian pipelines instead of diversifying supply, and their fear, later borne out, that the gas dependence could be used as a weapon.

items.title: Salil Tripathi and the Gujaratis (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 409)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Salil Tripathi
items.why: Salil Tripathi tells the Havel and Mandela stories that Amit uses to show how power changes people, including Havel's moral clarity in power.

items.title: Sara Rai Inhales Literature (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 255)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Sara Rai
items.why: Sara Rai's strikingly detailed childhood memories, and her explanation that 'we had nothing else to do, so we looked at things', which inspired Amit's argument that unfilled time sharpens attention.

items.title: Sell the Tiger to Save It
items.creator: Barun Mitra
items.why: Barun Mitra's argument, against the reflex to ban everything, that legalising the tiger trade would give people a reason to breed tigers as they breed cows and chickens, and so save the species.

items.title: Separation of Powers (Everything is Everything, Ep 91)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Why fusing legislative, executive and judicial powers, as Indian regulators do, is so dangerous. With the other state episodes, Amit says it forms a fundamental framework for thinking about the Indian state.

items.title: Servant of the People
items.creator: Volodymyr Zelenskyy
items.why: The TV show in which Zelenskyy played Ukraine's president before becoming it for real: the improbable starting point of the most unlikely accidental-politician story.

items.title: Shedding Light on the Russia-Ukraine War
items.creator: Rounak Hande, Ayush Patnaik, Ajay Shah and Susan Thomas
items.why: Ajay's co-authored paper that uses carefully corrected nighttime lights to read Russia's economy while official data is withheld: roughly flat from 2019 to 2025, with damage along its borders and a 245 km eastward shift in its centre of mass. The data is freely available to play with.

items.title: Shephali Bhatt Is Searching for the Incredible (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 391)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Shephali Bhatt
items.why: Journalist Shephali Bhatt on finding her sense of purpose through individuals in newsrooms that treated journalists as a cost centre, which Amit finds very moving. Her reporting that over a lakh Indian creators earn one to ten lakh rupees a month counters the survivor-bias worry.

items.title: Sixteen Stormy Days
items.creator: Tripurdaman Singh
items.why: The definitive account of India's First Amendment, which, unlike America's, was a blow against free speech: the Lok Sabha debates show Nehru taking illiberal positions to silence his rivals, a great statesman undone by hubris. Amit says everyone should read it.

items.title: Solutions When the Solution is the Problem: Arraying the Disarray in Development
items.creator: Lant Pritchett and Michael Woolcock
items.why: Pritchett and Woolcock ask whether an intervention is easy or hard to implement, a question Ajay calls a breakthrough that Indian policy debate rarely asks: interventions with many transactions or much discretion for frontline staff are harder to deliver. Kelkar and Shah later added stakes and secrecy to the test.

items.title: Songs of Surrender
items.creator: U2
items.why: U2 rethink songs they wrote as kids from a more grown-up place, changing arrangements and lyrics instead of staying frozen in the famous versions. Ajay likes that some young listeners will start here and only later go back to The Joshua Tree.

items.title: South India Would Like to Have a Word (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 320)
items.creator: Amit Varma with RS Nilakantan
items.why: RS Nilakantan on how differently South India's needs look from the North's, though the North's priorities drive national policy, and on the North-South disparities behind that.

items.title: Sowmya Dhanaraj Is Making a Difference (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 380)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Sowmya Dhanaraj
items.why: One of Amit's ten favourite episodes: economist Sowmya Dhanaraj, whose parents were factory workers and whose mother sold tea on the Coimbatore highway, questions received wisdom from lived Indian reality rather than imported frameworks.

items.title: Startup Archive
items.why: An Instagram account of founder and investor advice clips, the source of most of the material for the hosts' episodes on starting a business; Amit counts many of these founders among today's finest thinkers.

items.title: Subhashish Bhadra on Our Dysfunctional State (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 333)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Subhashish Bhadra
items.why: Subhashish Bhadra on India's overreaching state, built to rule rather than to serve: the longer conversation behind his book Caged Tiger.

items.title: Suyash Rai Embraces India's Complexity (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 307)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Suyash Rai
items.why: A way into the mind of Suyash Rai, whom Amit regards as a great thinker, deeply influenced by Alasdair MacIntyre, on dharma, India's complexity and the limits of the state.

items.title: Ten Years Gone
items.creator: Led Zeppelin
items.why: Ajay's pick for the greatest Led Zeppelin song that is not widely known.

items.title: The Age of Hybrid Warfare (Everything is Everything, Ep 84)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Why, in modern conflict, you may not know whether you have been attacked or by whom, and why covert, opportunistic attacks such as crippling another country's payroll system are the strategy of rogue nations and backfire in the long run.

items.title: The Anti-Defection Law (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 13)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Barun Mitra
items.why: Barun Mitra on how a well-meant law to stop horse-trading turned MPs into votes that follow the whip, one of the things Amit sees getting in the way of Indian democracy.

items.title: The Art and Science of Economic Policy (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 154)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
items.why: A long conversation with Vijay Kelkar and Ajay about their book In Service of the Republic and its framework for economic policy.

items.title: The Ascent of Man
items.creator: Jacob Bronowski
items.why: Bronowski's history of scientific thought, the written companion to the TV series that shaped Ajay from childhood and fed his stories of scientific outlaws. Ajay thinks every literate adult should read it.

items.title: The Baptist, the Bootlegger and the Dead Man Walking
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's written account of the Lal Bihari saga, which applies the bootleggers-and-Baptists framework.

items.title: The Bookshop Romeo
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's column with the Milan Kundera bookshop example: a high-reward, near-zero-cost move is massively plus-EV, a portable illustration of expected value in everyday life.

items.title: The Calculus of Consent
items.creator: James M. Buchanan and Gordon Tullock
items.why: The founding text of public choice theory, which frames a constitution as the 'rules of the game' that should ideally rest on consensus. Amit calls it a masterpiece: not an easy read, but foundational for anyone who wants to understand the field.

items.title: The Candlemakers' Petition
items.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
items.why: Bastiat's satire takes protectionist logic seriously until it reaches absurdity; once you've laughed at it, you can't take 'save local businesses' rhetoric at face value. Amit calls it one of the greatest pieces of satire ever written.

items.title: The Case for Nuclear Electricity (Everything is Everything, Ep 78)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The case for nuclear power as a path out of fossil fuels: Amit calls it the safest form of energy known and an obvious answer to climate change, pointing to France, which at 71% nuclear emits a tenth of the world average CO2 per kilowatt hour.

items.title: The case for trade barriers against Chinese imports
items.creator: Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
items.why: The written case behind the hosts' most uncomfortable disagreement: why a committed free trader like Ajay worries about a systemically important, rule-breaking revisionist power. Read it next to Amit's argument that even unilateral free trade benefits both sides.

items.title: The Cathedral and the Bazaar
items.creator: Eric S. Raymond
items.why: Raymond's account of why Unix and open source work: the teeming, arguing bazaar of unpaid volunteers beats a few great people building a cathedral. Ajay calls it critical reading for every advocate of technology monopolies.

items.title: The Changing Forms of Creativity (Everything is Everything, Ep 72)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: How form shapes content: the venue shapes the music, from percussion in the open air to none in echoing gothic churches to alternative rock in CBGB's crowded room. The hosts use it as the frame for how constraints and methods shape creative work.

items.title: The Communist Manifesto
items.creator: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels
items.why: Ajay rejects its prescriptions but finds whole chunks 'absolutely brilliant' on how capitalism and globalisation would tear up the feudal order. Read its closing programme for action and you'll be astonished how much of it exists in modern India.

items.title: The Constitution of Liberty
items.creator: Friedrich Hayek
items.why: Hayek's case for freedom, the book Margaret Thatcher used to declare her government's creed.

items.title: The Design of Everyday Things
items.creator: Don Norman
items.why: Norman shows that everything around us looks and works the way it does for reasons we have stopped noticing, and that nothing is beautiful unless it is also beautifully functional, a lesson for engineering too.

items.title: The Economic Consequences of the Peace
items.creator: John Maynard Keynes
items.why: Keynes's vivid record of how globalised the pre-war world was and what war destroyed. His point that reparations demands were extreme partly because nobody knew national wealth helped create the demand for something like GDP.

items.title: The Elements of Style
items.creator: William Strunk Jr. and E.B. White
items.why: The classic statement of clarity and brevity, values Bell Labs carried into programming; Ajay says 'the simple Strunk and White' should be universal knowledge for everyone doing research.

items.title: The Elusive Quest for Growth
items.creator: William Easterly
items.why: Easterly knocks out the faddish ideas that have damaged development and leaves you asking what your theory of growth really is. Amit calls Easterly's books essential reading on where philanthropists and economists go wrong.

items.title: The Evolution of Cooperation
items.creator: Robert Axelrod
items.why: Axelrod uses game theory to show why we evolved to cooperate, and formalises the best response to being wronged: strike back once, but not forever, so some punishment is optimal but grudges are not.

items.title: The Evolution of Human Sexuality
items.creator: Donald Symons
items.why: Symons used natural selection to explain why men and women are wired differently: a formative book for Amit that set off a flood of later work, its arguments later confirmed with data by A Billion Wicked Thoughts.

items.title: The Ferment of Our Founders (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 272)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Kapila
items.why: Shruti Kapila on the ferment of India's founders, the source of her line that Hindutva is 'a theory of violence in search of a history'.

items.title: The Free Press
items.creator: Bari Weiss
items.why: Bari Weiss's publication, evidence that one person starting a newsletter can build a very large business on platforms where creators own their audience, without a mass-media gatekeeper.

items.title: The Functions of the Executive
items.creator: Chester Barnard
items.why: Chester Barnard's book opened Ajay's thinking on organisational behaviour and on what goes wrong in large, complex organisations, firms and governments alike. Lant Pritchett recommended it to him alongside Seeing Like a State.

items.title: The God Delusion
items.creator: Richard Dawkins
items.why: Dawkins's case against organised religion and dogma, which Amit thinks deserves to be taken seriously even though his own atheism is gentler.

items.title: The Good Boatman
items.creator: Rajmohan Gandhi
items.why: Thematic essays on Gandhi's life, from women to caste, that synthesise a vast amount of material: 'a powerful book of ideas' for engaging with his contradictions, and Amit's model of a synoptic book.

items.title: The Importance of Finance (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 125)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
items.why: The very first episode Amit and Ajay recorded together, on why finance matters.

items.title: The Incredible Insights of Bastiat and Hayek (Everything is Everything, Ep 6)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Where the hosts first laid out how prices carry information and incentives that change the behaviour of consumers and producers, and how tariffs redistribute wealth from the poor to the rich.

items.title: The India Uncut Newsletter
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's newsletter, where he thinks through ideas like virtuous and vicious cycles before they reach the show.

items.title: The India-Pakistan Conflict (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 111)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Srinath Raghavan
items.why: Srinath Raghavan on India-Pakistan relations and, in great detail, the history of the Kashmir problem; Amit cites it for the view that the nuclear shadow doesn't make conventional war go away.

items.title: The Indian Armed Forces (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 175)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Lt Gen Prakash Menon
items.why: An earlier deep conversation about the Indian Army with Lt Gen Prakash Menon, who gives the army's side on Kashmir: what is it supposed to do if Pakistan sends its people in?

items.title: The Indian State Is the Greatest Enemy of the Indian Farmer
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's short piece arguing that state overreach, such as state-backed APMC monopolies that squeeze both farmers and consumers, is at the root of farmers' misery.

items.title: The Indianness of Indian Food (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 95)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Vikram Doctor
items.why: Vikram Doctor, whom Amit calls the world's best food writer, on how Indian cuisine is built from imported ingredients such as the potato, the chilli and the guava.

items.title: The Innovator's Dilemma
items.creator: Clayton Christensen
items.why: Why dominant companies like Kodak can have the know-how to adapt yet fail, trapped by their own processes, priorities and incentives, while disruption comes from small upstarts.

items.title: The lesson from this IPL: Front-load your innings
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's original argument that T20 teams should drop the pinch-consolidate-slog grammar inherited from ODIs: send the hitters in first, keep attacking for all twenty overs and hold the anchor back for emergencies.

items.title: The Liberal Nationalism of Nitin Pai (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 318)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Nitin Pai
items.why: A long-form debate in which Nitin Pai, whom both hosts admire, defends 'liberal nationalism' and Amit argues against it, on the tension between defending a nation's borders and serving its people. Amit admits he might be wrong and leaves listeners to judge.

items.title: The Life and Times of Gurcharan Das (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 425)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Gurcharan Das
items.why: Gurcharan Das's first-hand stories of selling reform and of corporate nimbleness; the conversation led Amit to reread Sisyphus as a story about finding meaning in the act itself rather than futility.

items.title: The Life and Times of Mrinal Pande (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 263)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Mrinal Pande
items.why: A first-hand portrait of a legendary Hindi writer who wrote within the constraints of running a household. Her uninterrupted first answer of more than an hour, covering almost thirty years of her life, is Amit's showcase for why a host must not interrupt.

items.title: The Lives of Others
items.creator: Florian Henckel von Donnersmarck
items.why: A debut film about surveillance in divided Germany, about watching and being watched and how that changes both sides; Amit calls it a masterpiece and one of the finest debut films he has seen.

items.title: The Loneliness of the Indian Man (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 303)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Nikhil Taneja
items.why: More than seven hours with Nikhil Taneja on the male side of the gender divide: half the country can't talk to the other half. Amit suggests pairing it with the episode on the loneliness of the Indian woman.

items.title: The Mahatma and the Poet
items.creator: Mahatma Gandhi and Rabindranath Tagore
items.why: The Gandhi-Tagore debate laid out in full, two great minds disagreeing well: Tagore more reasoned and right about the dangers of nationalism, yet seeing something special in Gandhi's force of will. Amit and Ajay share Tagore's view that nationalism is simply bad.

items.title: The Matunga Racket
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: A concrete case of how criminalising consenting adults turns a victimless 'crime' into a tool for police extortion.

items.title: The Narrow Corridor
items.creator: Daron Acemoglu and James A. Robinson
items.why: Acemoglu and Robinson argue that liberty and prosperity depend on a rare balance between state power and a society that pushes back, and that countries can easily fall out of that corridor.

items.title: The Nighttime Lights of Russia (Everything is Everything, Ep 116)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: How satellite night-lights let Indian researchers see into the Russian economy in ways traditional statistics never could, part of the show's series on measurement.

items.title: The Notebook Trilogy
items.creator: Agota Kristof
items.why: Agota Kristof fled Hungary, learned French as an adult and wrote these novels in it, stripping prose and narrative to the bone with enormous power. Amit holds it up as the benchmark for mastering a language learned late: every word doing a job.

items.title: The Paper Menagerie and Other Stories
items.creator: Ken Liu
items.why: Ken Liu's collection, whose title story Amit calls a masterpiece of 'decluttered language' (nothing in it doesn't belong) that will leave you weeping; he sends it to his writing students, and the rest moved him to tears at individual sentences.

items.title: The policy posture as an incomplete contract
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay explains why no law truly pre-commits the state, since any law can be amended tomorrow: reforms stick only when an intellectual community, a credible team and honest communication stand behind them.

items.title: The Push Man and Other Stories
items.creator: Yoshihiro Tatsumi
items.why: Gekiga at its best: dark urban stories that stare into the depths of the human soul and go where manga doesn't, in the vein Goya opened up centuries earlier.

items.title: The Road
items.creator: Cormac McCarthy
items.why: A father and son walk through a post-apocalyptic landscape: Ajay says it takes you deep inside what it means to be a father and a son, and it is his image of the barbarism that would follow if civilisation's material base disappeared.

items.title: The Road to Serfdom
items.creator: Friedrich Hayek
items.why: Hayek's classic argument for freedom against state planning: central planning and its authoritarianism lead to serfdom. Amit calls it brilliant.

items.title: The Role of Monetary Policy
items.creator: Milton Friedman
items.why: The paper Ajay sees as the turning point of 20th-century macroeconomics in ideas and policy: it treats people as optimisers, introduces the natural rate of unemployment and confines monetary policy to keeping prices stable, because inflation adds noise to price signals.

items.title: The Rooted Cosmopolitanism of Sugata Srinivasaraju (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 277)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Sugata Srinivasaraju
items.why: Five and a half hours on Sugata Srinivasaraju's life, the milieu he grew up in and how he watched his city transform, offering an ideal Amit calls 'a treasure': being both rooted and cosmopolitan.

items.title: The Royal Game
items.creator: Stefan Zweig
items.why: Zweig's moving novella about a prisoner in solitary confinement who plays chess against himself until he can beat a world champion. Amit uses it to argue that humans need conversation with other minds to improve.

items.title: The Skeptical Environmentalist
items.creator: Bjørn Lomborg
items.why: Lomborg traces how great Western cities like London, once as filthy and unhealthy as any Indian city today, cleaned up as they got richer. Amit's takeaway: growth helps sustainability.

items.title: The State of Our Farmers (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 86)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Gunvant Patil
items.why: A Hindi-language conversation with Gunvant Patil on the condition of Indian farmers, which Amit calls 'a masterpiece of illumination': farmers stating free-market ideas drawn from lived experience.

items.title: The Story of Art
items.creator: E.H. Gombrich
items.why: Gombrich explains the context and stories behind works of art, painting by painting, so even people who respond to art only viscerally can understand it. Amit calls it a story of the human mind too, and suggests reading 'a page a day'.

items.title: The Theory of Moral Sentiments
items.creator: Adam Smith
items.why: Smith's often-overlooked philosophical masterpiece, which coined the 'man of system', the planner who treats people like chess pieces: the best warning against Maoist-style grand designs.

items.title: The Three Languages of Politics
items.creator: Arnold Kling
items.why: A slim book you can read in an hour on why political discourse is broken: progressives argue from equality, conservatives from tradition and libertarians from freedom, so they talk past each other. It teaches you to grant the other side's first principles and argue on their terms, which is how minds actually change.

items.title: The Vintage Book of Indian Writing 1947–1997
items.creator: Salman Rushdie and Elizabeth West (editors)
items.why: An anthology that opens with Nehru's 'Tryst with Destiny', which Ajay calls one of the transcendental pieces of Indian writing and evidence that great leaders can convey complex ideas.

items.title: The White Man's Burden
items.creator: William Easterly
items.why: Easterly on why the West's efforts to aid the rest have done so much ill and so little good: essential reading on how incentives distort development work, by a clear writer and great thinker.

items.title: The Wire
items.why: A show that ignores the habits of traditional cinema (no hook, no background score, fifteen or sixteen major characters, a story unfolding slowly over seasons) and proved that TV can do what a novel does.

items.title: This Be The Verse
items.creator: Philip Larkin
items.why: A great poem whose image of sediment deepening like a coastal shelf Amit uses for how knowledge builds up in layers across generations, and can be washed away.

items.title: Thought and Choice in Chess
items.creator: Adriaan de Groot
items.why: De Groot's finding that grandmasters look no further ahead than novices but excel at pattern recognition, which underpins Amit's account of why the Soviet school dominated chess.

items.title: Three Great Leaps by Firms (Everything is Everything, Ep 22)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' first episode purely about firms: three companies that surprised them by how they changed, and why firms, where modern production happens, are where knowledge must flow.

items.title: Three Hundred Ramayanas
items.creator: A.K. Ramanujan
items.why: Ramanujan's essay shows the Ramayana constantly retold across times and places, each version (tribal ones completely different) adapting the epic to the society that told it.

items.title: Time Out of Mind
items.creator: Bob Dylan
items.why: Amit's favourite Dylan album, a prime example of late-career mastery.

items.title: To Kill a Mockingbird
items.creator: Harper Lee
items.why: Ajay read it growing up as a masterpiece about a parent and child facing bigotry he assumed was in the past; now he finds it a hundred times more relevant. It anchors his plea to look for the good in each other instead of resenting each other.

items.title: Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus
items.creator: Ludwig Wittgenstein
items.why: Wittgenstein's great book, whose line 'whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent' Amit loves and uses to argue that any one language is inadequate.

items.title: Traffic
items.creator: Tom Vanderbilt
items.why: Vanderbilt documents that a large share of accidents happen close to home, when familiar ground makes drivers switch off, which is exactly what happened to Ajay on a hike.

items.title: Triumph of the City
items.creator: Edward Glaeser
items.why: Glaeser explains that cities are great because they pack clever people close together, while admitting dense cities can be terrible (crime, slums, public health), which makes good governance the real challenge.

items.title: Two great investment strategies
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's older piece on investing, a caution that stories of great fund managers are mostly survivorship bias and that track records can mislead.

items.title: Unboxing Bengaluru
items.creator: Malini Goyal and Prashanth Prakash
items.why: A book on Bangalore with a line Amit loves: its software is 5G but its hardware 2G, a failure of governance. Its Tinder data and interviews also show how dating differs across Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore.

items.title: Underrated, Overrated, Complicated (Everything is Everything, Ep 85)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' underrated-overrated-complicated episode, including round one of their debate on Twitter (Ajay: a cesspool; Amit: a gift if you curate your feed) and the setup for Amit's story of early failure with Sonictown.

items.title: Varun Grover Is in the House (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 292)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Varun Grover
items.why: Amit's conversation with Varun Grover, who shares his idea of home as whatever surrounds you wherever you are comfortable: your books, your room, the vibe.

items.title: Volodymyr Zelenskyy playing the piano with, um, you know
items.creator: Volodymyr Zelenskyy
items.why: A clip from Zelenskyy's comedy days that shows how improbable his journey from comedian to wartime leader was, and makes Amit's point that making a fool of yourself on stage night after night takes courage too.

items.title: Watching the Wheels
items.creator: John Lennon
items.why: A song both hosts love and the runner-up name for the podcast: contemplative and humble, the universe trundling along while we watch, curious and amused.

items.title: We Are All Gamblers
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's argument that every life choice, from marriage to jobs to stocks, is a bet weighed on probabilities, so 'gambler' shouldn't be an insult and singling out gambling for stigma makes little sense.

items.title: We Love Vaccines! We Love Freedom! (Everything is Everything, Ep 27)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The third part of the state series, applying its toolkit to vaccines: COVID vaccine makers were paid far less than the value they created, and letting prices rise would allocate vaccines better and fund research for the next pandemic.

items.title: What Cricket Can Learn From Poker
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's foundational case for applying expected value and probabilistic thinking to cricket, with football data showing how far other sports had already moved.

items.title: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?
items.creator: Thomas Nagel
items.why: Nagel's essay arguing that we can understand intellectually how a bat navigates by echolocation but can never imagine being one. Amit contrasts it with stories, through which we do manage to imagine other people's lives.

items.title: What is Populism?
items.creator: Jan-Werner Müller
items.why: The book that taught Amit most of what he knows about populism: it replaces the naive 'populism = popular' with a precise checklist for spotting populists anywhere. He says everyone should read it.

items.title: What is the cost of one-rank-one-pension?
items.creator: Renuka Sane and Ajay Shah
items.why: Renuka Sane and Ajay put a cost on the OROP scheme that the hosts blame for crowding out military modernisation, and published all their code and assumptions so readers can rerun the numbers.

items.title: What Our Genes and Phones Tell Us (Everything is Everything, Ep 117)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Part of the show's series on measurement: how new data, such as borrowers' phone top-up habits, is replacing the bank manager's personal judgement. A later episode was split off from it because there was too much material.

items.title: What Really Happened?
items.creator: Lawrence H. White
items.why: Larry White's essay on how easy money, bad government incentives and quasi-government entities caused the 2008 crisis, usually called a market failure.

items.title: What These Labels Mean (Everything is Everything, Ep 107)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: One of Amit's favourite episodes: what labels like liberal and conservative really mean, why nationalism differs from patriotism, and the hosts' own conservatism of changing the world carefully, one step at a time, because of unintended consequences.

items.title: When Ideas Have Sex
items.creator: Matt Ridley
items.why: Ridley's talk on why ideas must collide and recombine freely for the best ones to emerge and for society to progress; the hosts apply it to contracting research out to universities and firms.

items.title: Where Has All the Education Gone?
items.creator: Lant Pritchett
items.why: Pritchett's cross-country analysis finding that expanding schooling produced essentially zero growth, which Ajay calls one of the most important papers in development economics. It taught him to apply the same scepticism to infrastructure.

items.title: Where Have All the Leaders Gone?
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's public-choice answer to why the freedom struggle attracted people of principle while today's centralised state attracts careerists chasing power and money.

items.title: Where Indian Regulation Went Wrong (Everything is Everything, Ep 99)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's diagnosis of India's statutory regulators as a new central planning system that has to be fixed upstream, at the level of organisational design, and of why financial regulators will never work perfectly.

items.title: Wherever I Lay My Hat (That's My Home)
items.creator: Marvin Gaye (Paul Young's cover)
items.why: A song Amit calls a masterpiece, especially in Paul Young's cover, which captures his idea of a portable home you carry with you (though he has lost every hat he's owned).

items.title: Who Lends to the Indian State?
items.creator: Aneesha Chitgupi, Ajay Shah, Manish K. Singh, Susan Thomas and Harsh Vardhan
items.why: XKDR Forum's paper, the first to measure India's financial repression: 95% of the Indian state's borrowing is coerced out of the financial system, which makes its debt look cheaper than it really is.

items.title: Why Both Modi and Trump are Textbook Populists
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit applies Müller's framework to two contemporary leaders and shows how slogan-sized stories crowd out complex truths.

items.title: Why I Am a Free Speech Absolutist (Everything is Everything, Ep 88)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Amit's case for free speech: why the Indian Constitution doesn't really protect it, why Nehru's First Amendment was a mistake to be understood in context, and why legitimacy needs an open marketplace of ideas.

items.title: Writings and Speeches of Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar
items.creator: B.R. Ambedkar
items.why: More than sixty volumes of Ambedkar's writings and speeches, free online and 'amazing to read'. They show the arc of his thinking, including how he became much more pro-capitalist by the early 1950s, and how prolific writing went hand in hand with great thinking.

items.title: XKDR Forum
items.creator: XKDR Forum
items.why: Ajay's research organisation, which builds a body of work in areas like law and economics so that the policy ideas are ready when the problem and the politics line up; its working papers and YouTube channel are where he points people who ask him to teach.

items.title: Yes Minister (The Complete Yes Minister)
items.creator: Jonathan Lynn and Antony Jay
items.why: Among the loveliest and funniest books Ajay has read, with real insight into politics and the difficulty of change; its satire of reflexive policymaking ('we must do something, this is something') explains why price caps are the default political response.

items.title: Yuganta
items.creator: Irawati Karve
items.why: One of Amit's favourite books: a brilliant, sometimes disquieting sociological reading of the Mahabharata and the role of women in it, candid about its misogyny, and an analysis of a society we still live in.

items.title: On Tyranny
items.creator: Timothy Snyder and Nora Krug
items.why: An illustrated version for readers who need pictures. Ajay says you should give one to 'every WhatsApp uncle in your life.'

items.title: UNIX: A History and a Memoir
items.creator: Brian Kernighan
items.why: A brief history of the early years of Unix and Bell Labs, and the source of several origin stories Ajay tells, including Thompson's forged application and his recruitment.

items.title: "Black and grey" lists
items.creator: FATF
items.why: Shows the pressure behind FATF. Ajay explains that countries were offered a choice: join the financial surveillance regime or face more friction in the world.

items.title: $800,000 to Zero - The FASCINATING History of DaVinci Resolve
items.creator: Learn Color Grading
items.why: Amit calls it a great video on how a once-unaffordable professional tool became free.

items.title: 'Action produces information' — Brian Armstrong
items.creator: Brian Armstrong
items.why: Every action teaches you something. Armstrong's foggy-mountain image: wait for the fog to clear and you stay at the bottom forever.

items.title: 'An Act of War': Inside America's Silicon Blockade Against China
items.creator: Alex W Palmer
items.why: It shows how far the US now reaches: goods made and shipped entirely outside America, with no US components, can still count as American goods if American technology or software was used to make them.

items.title: 'Better to be loved by a few than liked by many'
items.creator: Paul Graham
items.why: Deep engagement builds trust, real community and better discourse. Chasing mass appeal leads to mediocrity.

items.title: 'Stop the war.' 44 Top Russian Players Publish Open Letter To Putin
items.creator: Sam Copeland
items.why: Amit sees these players as the true patriots: they stood up for their country by opposing its state.

items.title: 100BeatlesX30
items.creator: The Pocket Gods
items.why: A large batch of 30-second Beatles covers, another response to the same streaming rule.

items.creator: George Orwell
items.why: Amit says it will teach you so much about politics and calls it a masterpiece that feels like 'the future written in the past.'

items.title: 2,374 IAF Crashes. 1,305 Pilots Killed
items.creator: Ajai Shukla and Devesh Kapur
items.why: It puts numbers on the human cost of ageing aircraft and failed planning.

items.title: A 75-litre backpack (Ajay uses the Volt 75), and a women's-fit pack for women
items.why: Any old backpack works for a day hike. For big trips, 75 litres fits a sleeping bag and clothes, and he says people often buy too small or too big. He strongly encourages women to hike, for the freedom and resilience it builds, and notes women's backpacks are cut differently.

items.title: A Bridge Too Far
items.creator: Cornelius Ryan
items.why: It immortalises the failed Arnhem bridges operation, a brilliant airborne plan that collapsed because the main forces never reached the paratroopers.

items.title: A brief history of globalization
items.creator: Peter Vanham
items.why: A concise overview of how trade reshaped what the world eats: imagine Italian cuisine without tomatoes, or Irish history without the potato.

items.title: A Business History of India
items.creator: Tirthankar Roy
items.why: It tells the story of India's evolution through the lens of firms and markets. Ajay urges even a businessperson who has never read a book to pick it up. What struck him most was how little has changed, and he came away with new respect for the people of a hundred and a hundred and fifty years ago.

items.title: A Commentary on the UNIX Operating System
items.creator: John Lions
items.why: It is how universities worldwide learned how an operating system is actually written, which made Unix their common language.

items.title: A Conflict of Visions
items.creator: Thomas Sowell
items.why: Explains how ideologies take shape and come into being. Amit's broader advice is to read all of Sowell's books.

items.title: A Deregulatory Moment
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's written take on the current opening for reforming India's regulatory state.

items.title: A Dominant Character
items.creator: Samanth Subramanian
items.why: Amit calls it a great book on Haldane, the scientist who spent his last years in India.

items.title: A Few Thoughts on Limericks
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: For readers who want to understand the craft, including the ideal 9-9-6-6-9 syllable count.

items.title: A First Course in Probability
items.creator: Sheldon Ross
items.why: The classic probability textbook behind the episode's expected-value reasoning, for anyone who wants the rigorous maths beneath the intuitions.

items.title: A Godless Congregation
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Further reading from Amit's own writing on atheism over the years.

items.title: A History of Global Health: Interventions into the Lives of Other Peoples
items.creator: Randall M. Packard
items.why: It is one of the great books in public health, a field Ajay says is practically absent in India. India has healthcare, plus doctors trying to make health policy without having read this book. Amit adds that public health and healthcare are completely different things.

items.title: A History of Hinduism (Everything is Everything, Ep 76)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Their earlier episode built on Manu Pillai's account of Hinduism as an assimilative, almost 'open source' tradition.

items.title: A Life in Indian Politics (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 149)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Jayaprakash Narayan
items.why: Jayaprakash Narayan tells how India almost adopted proportional representation, until Sonia Gandhi said no.

items.title: A Movable Feast
items.creator: Ernest Hemingway
items.why: Source of Hemingway's one-true-sentence advice, which Amit reads as writing something authentic to the moment.

items.title: A petty money dispute holds market to ransom
items.creator: Jayanth R Varma
items.why: Ajay calls it a 'great blog article' on an episode that shows Percy Mistry's lesson in practice: a financial centre can never let a payment fail, whatever the reason.

items.title: A Poetry Handbook
items.creator: Mary Oliver
