items.why: It covers the mechanics of language, not just of poetry. Amit says you will fall in love with language all over again, and he turns to poetry in his moments of deepest emotion.

items.title: A Prehistory of Hinduism
items.creator: Manu Devadevan
items.why: Argues that worshipping Shiva or Vishnu was simply part of everyday life and not a marker of identity.

items.title: A router that runs an open-source version of Unix
items.why: You can tinker with the software that runs your own network hardware.

items.title: A rowing machine (the Concept2 is the most common)
items.creator: Concept2
items.why: If you are lazy and will commit to only one exercise, make it rowing. It is cardio and works something like 80–85% of the body's muscles.

items.title: A Short Film About Killing
items.creator: Krzysztof Kieślowski
items.why: Amit names it alongside A Short Film About Love, and calls both of them masterpieces.

items.title: A Short Film About Love
items.creator: Krzysztof Kieślowski
items.why: Amit calls it a masterpiece. Its bicycle-in-the-courtyard scene is the example he uses to teach his writing students show-don't-tell.

items.title: A Small-Sized Mystery
items.creator: Jane Hirshfield
items.why: A companion piece to the episode's point that much about human beings remains a mystery.

items.title: A sustainable and scalable approach in Indian pension reform
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Further reading from the period when the reform community was active and making the case for the NPS design.

items.title: A Tale Of Two Bandits: Naxals And The Indian State
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: It applies Mancur Olson's roving-versus-stationary-bandit frame to India's Naxal areas. In many of them both the state and the Naxalites behaved like roving bandits, and in some it was the Naxals who settled in and provided services.

items.title: A Tryst With Destiny
items.creator: Jawaharlal Nehru
items.why: Ajay urges listeners to step out of the cliché and read it with fresh eyes, as transcendental writing.

items.title: A Venture Capitalist Looks at the World (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 213)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Sajith Pai
items.why: Pai argues the Indian market is far smaller than its 1.4 billion headcount suggests.

items.title: A weekly pill case
items.why: He fills it once a week and then follows it without thinking. A glance shows whether he took the lunch dose, so he no longer misses doses or second-guesses himself.

items.title: Aadha Gaon
items.creator: Rahi Masoom Raza
items.why: A villager's answer — Mecca for prayer, his village for home — captures rootedness and belonging in a single line.

items.title: Abandon the Old in Tokyo
items.creator: Yoshihiro Tatsumi
items.why: More bleak, unforgettable gekiga with endings you have to read for yourself.

items.title: Abbé Faria: The Hypnotic Story of A Goan Son
items.creator: Carol Lobo
items.why: Background on the Goan prodigy who became one of the fathers of hypnotism.

items.title: Accidental Politicians (Everything is Everything, Ep 108)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: In that episode Ajay talked about his admiration for Nehru, the background to his point about separating the art from the artist.

items.title: Activism and wonkery are the yin and yang
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: It argues that street and social-media activism is useful but useless without careful conceptual work about how a complex system actually fits together.

items.title: Adam Smith – A Primer
items.creator: Eamonn Butler
items.why: An accessible entry point to one of the thinkers Amit most often gets asked how to read.

items.title: Adaptive Political Economy: Toward a New Paradigm
items.creator: Yuen Yuen Ang
items.why: He calls it a fantastic paper by a great scholar who reached the same diagnosis on her own.

items.title: Aella on Twitter
items.creator: Aella
items.why: Aella is an openly happy sex worker who is also 'incredible at data' and runs large-scale surveys. She is a living counter to the assumption that sex work is always coerced.

items.title: Affirmative Action Around the World: An Empirical Study
items.creator: Thomas Sowell
items.why: It asks whether such policies actually helped the people they were meant to help. Amit believes growth helps far more.

items.title: After the Gold Rush
items.creator: Neil Young
items.why: Included in the episode's show notes. The hosts don't say why on air.

items.title: After Virtue
items.creator: Alasdair MacIntyre
items.why: Amit loved it so much he woke with its argument in his head and read it over breakfast instead of prepping. That is his living example of the joy idea books can give.

items.title: agadmator's Chess Channel
items.creator: agadmator
items.why: He plays through classic games and talks about them, which Amit finds wonderful.

items.title: Ahimsa: 100 Reflections on the Harappan Civilization
items.creator: Devdutt Pattanaik
items.why: Offers a frame Amit loves: Harappan cities prioritised traders over raiders, and ahimsa is voluntary exchange between consenting adults.

items.title: Ajay Shah on how LLMs will impact us
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: The longer written version of his view: LLMs are useful word-prediction tools that need a master's oversight, not intelligence.

items.title: Ajay Shah on state capacity, governance and institutions (Episode 18 of Jack of All Knowledge)
items.creator: Ajay Shah (guest)
items.why: This is where Ajay first told the story of turning down Kirit Parikh's apprenticeship offer.

items.title: Ajay Shah's conversation with Rahul Ahluwalia
items.creator: Rahul Ahluwalia
items.why: Amit calls it a lovely chat and the companion to this episode's subject.

items.title: Ajay Shah's paper on why the Indian FRBM failed
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: The LLMs couldn't, which by his own law proved it was worth writing.

items.title: Ajay Shah's writings for mass media
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: This is another of the outlets that give his ideas a broad audience so he can protect his time for deep work.

items.title: Alan Turing's life and story
items.why: Ajay says studying Turing's life 'will reshape your moral calculus' by showing what state coercion over private matters actually costs. Amit adds that Turing's story stands for that of homosexuals through most of human history.

items.title: Ali Abdaal's advice: don't look at the numbers for two years
items.creator: Ali Abdaal
items.why: Ignoring early metrics stops creators from dumbing themselves down to chase validation before they have improved.

items.title: Ali Abdaal's YouTube channel
items.creator: Ali Abdaal
items.why: Useful for figuring out tools, mental models and frameworks. Abdaal started small and grew big, so he has lived his own productivity advice.

items.title: Alice Evans Studies the Great Gender Divergence (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 297)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Alice Evans
items.why: Explores how maintaining endogamy requires controlling female sexuality, which drives female seclusion.

items.title: Alice Munro's short stories
items.creator: Alice Munro
items.why: He separates art from artist and says he will continue loving her work while withholding judgment on her as a person.

items.title: AliExpress
items.why: 'Gentle reader, if you have not used AliExpress, you should.' It is part of the cheap bounty that makes experimenting with gadgets affordable.

items.title: Alone in the City
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: It is where Amit first tied the search for a home in the city to the damage rent control does.

items.title: AlphaDev discovers faster sorting algorithms
items.creator: DeepMind
items.why: It shows machines finding better code for something as fundamental as sorting, which then feeds back into stronger machines.

items.title: Altman on burnout
items.creator: Sam Altman
items.why: Hard work doesn't burn you out, because momentum is energising. Amit thinks burnout comes more from worry, procrastination and overthinking.

items.title: Altman on hiring
items.creator: Sam Altman
items.why: Hire for values first, aptitude second, skill third.

items.title: Altman on long-term thinking
items.creator: Sam Altman
items.why: 'A long term commitment is the only arbitrage opportunity left in the market' when everyone else chases the next quarter.

items.title: Amit Varma on Public Choice Theory (mashup of The Seen and the Unseen and The Pragati Podcast)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: An audio introduction to the field Amit says explains why state failure is ubiquitous.

items.title: Amit's column on the benefits of reading books
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Sets out his argument that books multiply the dots we join to picture the world, letting us live many lives.

items.title: Amit's MAMI live-tweet threads (2018 and 2019)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: They are a ready-made list of strong world cinema from those years, for viewers who want to start watching more films.

items.title: Amitava Kumar Finds the Breath of Life (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 265)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: The origin of Amit's recurring 'Where is your Gangauli?' question about home.

items.title: Amused to Death
items.creator: Roger Waters
items.why: Ajay says Roger Waters read Neil Postman's book and then wrote the album, so it is a musical companion to Postman's argument.

items.title: Amusing Ourselves to Death
items.creator: Neil Postman
items.why: It completes his reading list on the media, which fits an episode about sensationalism, fragmented attention and media as entertainment.

items.title: An Adman Reflects on Society & the Self (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 199)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Here advertising legend Ambi Paramaeswaran said that far more than half of ad spend is wasted and that online advertising is a scandal.

items.title: An American Tail
items.creator: Don Bluth
items.why: He used it to mock the idea of a lost golden age of plenty in India's past, and to argue that philosophies like Jainism arose despite scarcity, not because of abundance.

items.title: An annotated reading list on the Indian bankruptcy reform
items.creator: The Leap Journal blog
items.why: A guided route into the literature for anyone who wants to go deeper than this episode.

items.title: An Area of Darkness
items.creator: VS Naipaul
items.why: Supports Amit's argument that Gandhi's influences were unusual for an Indian leader of his time.

items.title: An Economic Theory of Democracy
items.creator: Anthony Downs
items.why: Amit first learned about rational ignorance from this book: the idea that voters sensibly don't spend scarce attention on a vote that almost never decides anything.

items.title: An Essay on the Principle of Population
items.creator: Thomas Robert Malthus
items.why: Read it to see where the idea began: Malthus claimed people grow exponentially while resources grow arithmetically, so mass starvation was inevitable.

items.title: An important change of course by policy in Indian Covid-19 vaccination
items.creator: Amrita Agarwal and Ajay Shah
items.why: Background reading on the Indian COVID vaccine policy debate, which the hosts used as a real-world case of their argument.

items.title: An Indian view on dollar domination
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Expands on why anger at the power of the advanced economies won't produce a workable alternative, and why India should simply play by the rules of the game.

items.title: An Interview with Mike Kofman
items.creator: Lawrence Freedman
items.why: Kofman captures what surprised everyone: the occupation was always expected to fail, but almost nobody expected the invasion itself to fail.

items.title: An Ode to Perun (and Orry)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: It is a written version of Amit's admiration for Perun.

items.title: Analysing India's KYC Framework through the Privacy Lens
items.creator: Vrinda Bhandari, Rishab Bailey and Trishee Goyal
items.why: Looks at Indian KYC through the privacy lens that Ajay argues should be the starting point.

items.title: Analysing India's KYC Framework: Can We Do Things Better?
items.creator: Rishab Bailey, Trishee Goyal, Renuka Sane and Ridhi Varma
items.why: Asks the constructive question the episode ends on: what would a better KYC framework look like?

items.title: Anarchy, State, and Utopia
items.creator: Robert Nozick
items.why: He calls it a 'great book' and recommends it as the place to engage seriously with the question of anarchy versus the state.

items.title: Anatomy of a Folly
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: It is the longer version of his argument about how great films balance simplifying a story with honouring complexity.

items.title: Anchor
items.why: Free hosting for your first episodes, which you can start recording on a mobile phone.

items.title: Andrew Doyle's tweet on Kemi Badenoch's grilling
items.creator: Andrew Doyle
items.why: Amit likes Doyle a lot and calls him a great free-speech thinker. The clip shows how a show gets turned into a political cudgel.

items.title: Angus Maddison's world GDP charts
items.creator: Angus Maddison
items.why: They show world GDP shooting up around 1800 and economic freedom tracking prosperity country by country, including India after 1991 and China after Deng.

items.title: Animal Farm
items.creator: George Orwell
items.why: Amit calls both novels masterpieces that teach you a great deal about politics and the world.

items.title: Annihilation of Caste
items.creator: B.R. Ambedkar
items.why: Amit calls it Ambedkar's 'great masterpiece of a book'. It is an early challenge to class-only thinking that puts caste at the centre.

items.title: Anora
items.why: He says the last 20 to 25 minutes are 'so masterful'. Its win shows that great films now take the Oscar, where a couple of decades ago the award often went to mainstream pap.

items.title: Anthony Bourdain on procrastination
items.creator: Anthony Bourdain
items.why: It describes Amit's own daily struggle with the lazy self who wants to play online chess and binge YouTube.

items.title: Anupam Manur's piece on the Bangalore water crisis
items.creator: Anupam Manur
items.why: Amit urges everyone to read it because it is so counterintuitive. Pricing water helps the poor, since the current system effectively redistributes from the poor to the rich who use far more water.

items.title: Applied Economics
items.creator: Thomas Sowell
items.why: Part of Amit's advice to read everything Sowell has written.

items.title: Arati Kumar-Rao Took a One-Way Ticket (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 383)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: It looks at people's lived connection with the land they inhabit, which sits in contrast to the political maps taught in geography class.

items.title: Aravind Srinivas speaks of Larry Page
items.creator: Aravind Srinivas
items.why: It tells the Larry Page and Excite story, and how it stopped Srinivas from blaming his own mother's search phrasing. Never blame the user.

items.title: Ardh Satya
items.creator: Govind Nihalani
items.why: It shows the director's stature, which makes it striking that he couldn't get an independent film funded.

items.title: Are all calories created equal? Your gut microbes don't think so.
items.creator: Anahad O'Connor
items.why: A readable newspaper account (Washington Post) of the gut-microbiome calorie findings.

items.title: Are fleeting orders by high frequency traders a source of market abuse?
items.creator: Nidhi Aggarwal and Chirag Anand
items.why: One of Ajay's chosen favourites; it appeared on the Leap Blog.

items.title: Army and Nation
items.creator: Steven I Wilkinson
items.why: It is a history of how the Indian Army evolved, including the debates in the 40s, 50s and 60s over what role it should play in society. Amit says it gave him a really nuanced understanding of the subject.

items.title: Arrival
items.creator: Denis Villeneuve
items.why: It brought a level of integrity and thought Amit hadn't expected from a mainstream studio film. He loved it even while his friend found it slow.

items.title: Arshia Sattar and the Complex Search for Dharma (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 315)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Arshia Sattar
items.why: Background for the episode's argument that the epics are open-source rivers rather than fixed texts.

items.title: Art of Podcasting: Brasstacks (notes PDF)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Covers the technical details of starting a podcast that he couldn't get through on camera.

items.title: Arun Shourie's books
items.creator: Arun Shourie
items.why: Ajay says Shourie 'does not get enough recognition'. He worked out many ideas credited to Western scholars first, and laid bare the venality of the socialist state.

items.title: Arvind Kejriwal's interview by Sudhir Chaudhary
items.creator: Sudhir Chaudhary
items.why: Amit calls it an interesting interview in which Kejriwal is called out on his hypocrisy.

items.title: As Tears Go By
items.creator: The Rolling Stones
items.why: A playful musical aside at the start of the episode.

items.title: Ash Joglekar's tweet on solitary hobbies
items.creator: Ash Joglekar
items.why: Reading, long-distance running and science give you a refuge from personal and world tragedies. Amit adds that they also create the solitude needed for self-reflection.

items.title: Ashwin interviewed by ChessBase
items.creator: ChessBase
items.why: More on the unsung innovator behind a now-famous broadcast feature.

items.title: Ask Me ANYTHING! (Everything is Everything, Ep 50)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The companion to this episode, recorded at the halfway mark.

items.title: Aspects of the Novel
items.creator: E. M. Forster
items.why: It gives a great insight into a great novelist's mind.

items.title: Atlantic City (from Nebraska)
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: Amit calls it a masterpiece and Nebraska 'such a great stripped down album'. It shows Springsteen's willingness to keep changing direction.

items.title: Atomic Chess and Fog of War
items.why: Your usual heuristics, instincts and even pattern recognition stop working, so you have to work out how to play from first principles. That gives you a fresh intellectual thrill on a level playing field.

items.title: ATR2100x microphone
items.creator: Audio-Technica
items.why: It is a dynamic mic, so it picks up only what is close to it, which suits a home setup better than a studio condenser mic. It costs about ₹7,000 and has both USB and regular connections, so you can plug it into a laptop and also use it for Zoom calls.

items.title: Aubrey
items.creator: Bread
items.why: He wants to bring attention back to a forgotten band's song.

items.title: Autumn Passage to the Himalaya
items.creator: Harish Kapadia
items.why: Ajay calls it a lovely book and essential if you take an interest in the Himalayas.

items.title: awk
items.why: Its pattern-and-action model lets you do serious data processing in one line. That is the point where a command-line user becomes a programmer.

items.title: Backstreets
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: Greil Marcus wrote that it 'begins with music so stately, so heartbreaking that it might be the prelude to a rock and roll version of the Iliad'. Amit says Marcus put into words what he had always felt. The song is intimate and epic, and sometimes he wishes the piano went on forever.

items.title: Bad
items.creator: U2
items.why: One of two songs from that album he calls 'absolutely great'.

items.title: Bad Science
items.creator: Ben Goldacre
items.why: A great book on seeing through medical claims with scientific evidence.

items.title: Basic facts about the map (NYT interactive)
items.creator: The New York Times
items.why: A visual primer on the counteroffensive's geography.

items.title: Beat a Drum
items.creator: R.E.M.
items.why: It is the source of the episode's central image of people as unfinished works in progress.

items.title: Beautiful Boy
items.creator: John Lennon
items.why: The source of the line that captures how life happens to us regardless of our plans. The McCartney video is a moving extra.

items.title: Beauty and the Beast
items.creator: Walt Disney
items.why: Its scene of the male character flipping through Belle's book, complaining it has no pictures, and Belle replying that some people can use their imagination.

items.title: Beggars in Spain (Sleepless series)
items.creator: Nancy Kress
items.why: He calls it a phenomenal science fiction book. Its premise is a world with two kinds of humans: those who need to sleep and those who don't.

items.title: Behave
items.creator: Robert Sapolsky
items.why: Amit calls it one of Sapolsky's masterpieces and a brilliant book.

items.title: Ben Wolff's X thread on Ritz-Carlton
items.creator: Ben Wolff
items.why: It collects the stories of employees using $2,000 of discretion, which illustrate how incentives and trust create ownership.

items.title: Beta Tumse Na Ho Payega (Gangs of Wasseypur Part 2)
items.why: Amit's Bollywood illustration of the gap between HQ and the field.

items.title: Beware of Quacks. Alternative Medicine is Injurious to Health
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's own piece on why traditional and alternative medicine deserve deep skepticism.

items.title: Bezos interviewed by Lex Fridman
items.creator: Lex Fridman
items.why: Here Bezos explains 'disagree and commit': argue, then fully own the decision without any 'I told you so' later.

items.title: Bezos on Akio Morita
items.creator: Jeff Bezos
items.why: Morita's mission, 'make Japan known for quality again', is a model of a purpose bigger than the product.

items.title: Bezos on business plans
items.creator: Jeff Bezos
items.why: Plans fall apart on contact with reality, but writing them clarifies your thinking and pushes you to look ahead.

items.title: Bezos on professional pride
items.creator: Jeff Bezos
items.why: 99% of your work will never be seen, so take pride in it anyway.

items.title: Bezos on truth-telling
items.creator: Jeff Bezos
items.why: Humans evolved to get along, not to tell the truth, so companies must deliberately build mechanisms and a culture of truth-telling.

items.title: Bezos on Work-Life Harmony
items.creator: Jeff Bezos
items.why: Bezos rejects 'work-life balance' for 'work-life harmony': go where the energy is.

items.title: Bhatiali Dhun
items.creator: Jaya Bose and Himangshu Biswas
items.why: He first thought it was nostalgia, but after all these years decided 'it's not mere nostalgia, it's something truly cool'.

items.title: Bill Gates & David Letterman being skeptical about the internet
items.why: A famous clip in which Letterman treats the internet as a mere curiosity while talking to Gates.

items.title: Bill Gates and Warren Buffet on the best advice they got
items.creator: Bill Gates and Warren Buffett
items.why: Both name focus as their most important quality. It's the source of the story of Buffett's nearly blank calendar.

items.title: Bimal Patel's forthcoming book
items.creator: Bimal Patel
items.why: Patel is India's pre-eminent urban thinker and understands town planning like almost nobody else in India. Ajay says to run, not walk, when it comes out, and Amit calls him one of the great thinkers of modern India.

items.title: Bimal Patel's talk at the Emerging Markets Conference
items.creator: Bimal Patel
items.why: Patel lays out one unifying theme for urban planning: around 40% of land should go to streets and parks, with a mechanism for money to flow back into urban infrastructure. Ajay wants manufacturing built into that kind of planning.

items.title: Birds Aren't Real? How a Conspiracy Takes Flight
items.creator: Peter McIndoe
items.why: A delightful first-hand account of how a deliberately invented conspiracy theory gets people to believe it.

items.title: Blade Runner
items.creator: Ridley Scott
items.why: Amit calls it a masterpiece and notes that Ridley Scott was one of Nolan's inspirations.

items.title: Blankets
items.creator: Craig Thompson
items.why: One of the graphic novels Amit calls a masterpiece. He says he may someday do a full list of the comics he loves.

items.title: Blood on the Tracks
items.creator: Bob Dylan
items.why: One of his two specific favourites, from different phases of Dylan's life.

items.title: Blue I, II and III
items.creator: Joan Miró
items.why: Very minimal, yet incredibly powerful in person. They show Miró confidently stripping his art down despite the critics.

items.title: Bob Dylan's own recordings (e.g. Lay Lady Lay)
items.creator: Bob Dylan
items.why: Dylan's voice is authentic to his music, and some songs only he can sing; Amit and the crew sang Lay Lady Lay to prove it needs his nasal twang. Amit also loves the covers, such as Springsteen's Chimes of Freedom and The Byrds' versions. He wrote a piece defending Dylan's Nobel as rightly given, though he warns against America-England-centric 'greatest ever' hyperbole.

items.title: Bollywood Masala and a French Art Film
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: It is where he first explored virtuous and vicious cycles, prompted by Nomsita's remark that she is happy when she does things well and does things well when she is happy.

items.title: Boltzmann's tombstone in Vienna
items.why: Boltzmann's grave bears his entropy equation, S = k ln W, a fitting pilgrimage to an outlaw who died just before the world caught up with him.

items.title: Books by William A Niskanen
items.creator: William A Niskanen
items.why: Amit says Niskanen has great books on the incentives of bureaucrats.

items.title: Born a Muslim
items.creator: Ghazala Wahab
items.why: He points to her sentence about her grandfather shelling pine nuts all day to reward the children as a model of showing rather than telling.

items.title: Born to Run (acoustic live version)
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: The wall-of-sound album version didn't suit his taste at the time. Springsteen alone with guitar and mouth organ was an eye-opener that showed him a different way to understand the song.

items.title: Born to Run (autobiography)
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: Beautiful writing that takes you right into the man's mind. Amit says everyone should read it to understand artistic process, for example the passage on how Springsteen poured his whole life into the song Born to Run.

items.title: Breaking Out
items.creator: Padma Desai
items.why: The story of a remarkable economist and a strong woman who often goes uncredited. Amit says everyone should read it.

items.title: Breaking Through
items.creator: Isher Judge Ahluwalia
items.why: A beautiful book about a Hindi-medium girl who became a fine economist. Amit regrets not reading it, and not recording with her, before she died.

items.title: Brian Chesky on co-founders
items.creator: Brian Chesky
items.why: You'll spend more time with your co-founder than your spouse, and 'winning an argument is not as important as preserving the relationship'. Amit sees this as key to his partnership with Ajay.

items.title: Brian Chesky on Graham's advice
items.creator: Brian Chesky
items.why: Chesky took Graham's words to heart at early Airbnb, including personally photographing a host's home.

items.title: Brighter Than a Thousand Suns
items.creator: Robert Jungk
items.why: It is the book that got Ajay deep into the Oppenheimer story and shaped how he thought about the world while growing up.

items.title: Brilliant Disguise
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: It begins by asking whether the lover is wearing a mask and ends by turning the gaze on himself ('I damn sure don't trust myself'). Amit finds it stunning. The video is pure simplicity, the camera moving closer and closer.

items.title: Brown Eyed Girl
items.creator: Van Morrison
items.why: It is a playful bridge from transistors on chips to the transistor radio. Amit himself calls it a cheesy early pop song and points listeners to the two albums instead.

items.title: Bruce Springsteen: All the Songs
items.creator: Philippe Margotin and Jean-Michel Guesdon
items.why: It tells the story behind every single Springsteen song, and Amit pairs it with the memoir as two wonderful books.

items.title: Building a Second Brain
items.creator: Tiago Forte
items.why: The brain is a messy, impressionistic tool for retaining knowledge. Forte's idea of using technology as a second brain addresses the fact that we lose most of what we take in.

items.title: Building State Capability
items.creator: Matt Andrews, Lant Pritchett and co-authors
items.why: It does careful measurement of state capability and finds that Indian state capability got worse during the 1991-2011 boom.

items.title: Building the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India
items.creator: MS Sahoo and Ravi Narain
items.why: Ajay calls it a milestone in India's journey: a real plan for building an organisation that will wield coercive power, even though it was largely ignored in practice.

items.title: Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid
items.creator: George Roy Hill
items.why: A light pick after an hour on banks and creditors. The recording cuts off before he says more.

items.title: Buying Maggi noodles and Kit Kats in every country you visit
items.why: 'It's great fun.' You taste first-hand how firms tailor one product to local preferences.

items.title: Caesar and Cleopatra
items.creator: George Bernard Shaw
items.why: Source of the line about the barbarian who mistakes his tribe's customs for the law of nature. It sums up the episode's case against ethnocentrism.

items.title: Calyampudi Radhakrishna Rao: A brief biography
items.why: For readers who want more on the man Ajay calls the finest product of the Bengal Renaissance.

items.title: Can men and women be just friends?
items.creator: The Economist
items.why: It explains the Facebook index and proposes naming it after When Harry Met Sally.

items.title: Carnage and Culture
items.creator: Victor Davis Hanson
items.why: Ajay calls it 'a very disturbing book' and doesn't agree with all of it, but thinks everybody should read it.

items.title: Cathedral
items.creator: Raymond Carver
items.why: He calls it a masterpiece that 'just kinda blows me away', and says it is free to read online.

items.title: Cauldron, Sword and Victory: The Rise of the Sikhs
items.creator: Sarbpreet Singh
items.why: Amit calls it a 'magnificent' and 'excellent' book. He says it tells the complicated history of the Sikh rebellions against Mughal Punjab very well.

items.title: CDC Adult Immunization Schedule (vaccine list and schedule by age)
items.creator: US CDC
items.why: Ajay calls adult vaccination 'just a free lunch': prevention is better than cure. Ajay thinks the FDA is too conservative and slow, so its approval is a high bar, and its testing is a global public good. Countries like India and Bangladesh should import these vaccines.

items.title: Chandrahas Choudhury's Country of Literature (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 288)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: A living example that email can still carry long, narrative, memory-filled letters if the writer takes the trouble.

items.title: Charlie Munger's wisdom
items.creator: Charlie Munger
items.why: Munger has always been a source of great wisdom on how to think.

items.title: Charter 77
items.creator: Václav Havel and co-signatories
items.why: It is the document behind Havel's line to a hesitant signatory: 'you have already taken a side, just not the one that you think you have.'

items.title: Chernobyl
items.creator: HBO
items.why: It is a textbook account of how a big oppressive state fails, which shows the disaster was about the political system rather than nuclear physics.

items.title: Chess.com report on Gukesh's win, with analysis of Game 14 by Rafael Leitao
items.creator: Rafael Leitao
items.why: Lets you see for yourself how the position drifted (bishop to a8, king two squares closer) before 55. Rf2.

items.title: Chicago PD
items.why: He says it started off middling and became really good in later seasons. It also shows the safeguards at work: a wiretap or search needs a judge and a high bar of evidence, and the person who wants to raid is not the person who grants permission.

items.title: chickenhappyhour on Instagram (and Amit's favourite chicken video)
items.why: Amit finds them 'mind blowing' and watches his favourite on loop. Ironically, it's the very distraction he says books must beat.

items.title: Child Labor in the Global Economy
items.creator: Eric V Edmonds and Nina Pavcnik
items.why: Calls it another great study supporting the case that prosperity, not bans, ends child labour.

items.title: China's Future
items.creator: David Shambaugh
items.why: His pick if you read just one book on China. It is short and compact. Written in 2016, against the pro-China intellectuals of the time, it understood everything that would happen from 2016 to 2023. Hindsight has been very kind to it.

items.title: China's Gilded Age
items.creator: Yuen Yuen Ang
items.why: Amit calls both of Ang's books critical for understanding China's recent decades without falling into simplistic narratives.

items.title: Chintaman and I
items.creator: Durgabai Deshmukh
items.why: He loves its opening lines, in which Chintaman proposes by carving Sanskrit shlokas into a eucalyptus tree. It is a window into an unusual couple.

items.title: Chip War
items.creator: Chris Miller
items.why: It explains the semiconductor wars, the core battlefield of the US–China tech conflict discussed in the episode.

items.title: Chocolate by Manam
items.creator: Manam Chocolate
items.why: A Hyderabad company making expensive, really good chocolate. Not sponsored, just something they love.

items.title: Chris Horner's YouTube channel
items.creator: Chris Horner
items.why: After every stage of a major race, Horner breaks down what happened and calls teams 'knuckleheads' for wasted energy or pointless breakaways. Along the way he teaches real tactical and strategic thinking, and Amit says it makes you a better thinker.

items.title: Christopher Hitchens's writing
items.creator: Christopher Hitchens
items.why: Amit says he adored Hitchens and misses him. He calls his writing amazing and incredible. He admires how Hitchens, once a communist, turned away from 'that religion' and became a fearless voice against all kinds of conventional thinking.

items.title: Cicada
items.creator: Shaun Tan
items.why: Amit calls Shaun Tan a great illustrator, writer and artist and the book 'marvelous'. He deliberately says nothing about its contents, only asks you to read it.

items.title: Citizens Jain
items.creator: Ken Auletta
items.why: It is the source of the line that captures how a big media company defines its own purpose.

items.title: Civilisation
items.creator: Kenneth Clark
items.why: A foundational book for him when he was young.

items.title: Classical Liberalism – A Primer
items.creator: Eamonn Butler
items.why: People often ask Amit what to read to understand individual freedom and classical liberalism. He argues that the ideas we absorb by osmosis when young feel virtuous but are often socialist and deeply illiberal. He calls Butler one of the finest liberal minds in the world, and says Butler gets to the heart of each subject and breaks it down beautifully: 'These books are an education, and it is a miracle that they are free.'

items.title: Climate change for practical people
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: It sets out Ajay's view that the world will not hold back carbon dioxide emissions, so adaptation, including people moving away from badly affected regions, becomes essential.

items.title: Code 2.0
items.creator: Lawrence Lessig
items.why: The first book he thinks of on the power of law and how every word matters. Lessig argues that law works like code and shapes how the rest of the machinery runs, which fits the episode's theme of living 'in the shadow of the law'.

items.title: Collected Poems
items.creator: Mark Strand
items.why: Strand is his favourite poet of all time. The hardback collection includes Strand's last book, Almost Invisible, a masterpiece of one-paragraph prose poems. Amit says reading it would be like knowing a part of him.

items.title: Collison on beauty
items.creator: Patrick Collison
items.why: People like beautiful things. Beauty and simplicity go together and are worth aiming for even when hard to quantify.

items.title: Collison on choosing cofounders
items.creator: Patrick Collison
items.why: Starting a company with someone you're close to is a feature, not a bug.

items.title: Communism
items.creator: Richard Pipes
items.why: A slim volume on what actually happened under communism, linking ideas to actions to consequences. Amit suggests it as a way into Pipes's other books and into historians like Robert Conquest.

items.title: Comparative Advantage explained
items.creator: Econlib
items.why: A clear explainer of why trade benefits both sides even when one is better at everything.

items.title: Concerns About Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference (FIMI): An Indian Perspective
items.creator: University of Navarra and XKDR Forum
items.why: It collects global evidence and fragments of hard information about foreign actors around Indian elections. Ajay's point is that India cannot assume hybrid warfare only happens elsewhere.

items.title: Conflict
items.creator: David Petraeus and Andrew Roberts
items.why: A book on the recent history and evolution of warfare that Amit enjoyed a few months ago and found full of things he didn't know. He had wanted to use it as the base for a 'history of war' episode before Ajay steered them to the future.

items.title: Conflict in Ukraine: A timeline (2014 – present)
items.creator: Nigel Walker (House of Commons Library)
items.why: A chronology of the conflict since Crimea in 2014.

items.title: Consciousness Explained
items.creator: Daniel Dennett
items.why: It helped him apply evolutionary thinking to the mysteries of the mind and human nature.

items.title: Constraints & Creativity (Everything is Everything, Ep 90)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Early computing was done under severe limits, such as landing Apollo on the moon with 64 KB of RAM. Those limits produced deep insight worth studying.

items.title: Conversations with Tyler
items.creator: Tyler Cowen
items.why: Cowen asks great prepared questions, which Amit says someone like him couldn't even come up with, and moves through them crisply. It works beautifully and shows there is no single right way to interview.

items.title: Cooking the world's oldest known curry
items.creator: Soity Banerjee
items.why: As Amit recalls it, the only ingredient we would recognise today is baingan, which shows how little of our food is native.

items.title: Counterinsurgency Warfare: Theory and Practice
items.creator: David Galula
items.why: Its central point is that fighting insurgents is completely different from conventional war, captured in the fly-versus-lion metaphor and the principle that you must keep the people on your side.

items.title: Court
items.creator: Chaitanya Tamhane
items.why: Another debut film Amit places at the very top.

items.title: Covid-19 in the tropics: How will high heat and humidity shape the outcomes?
items.creator: Suja Thomas
items.why: It illustrates a uniquely Indian question: how COVID spreads in hot, humid conditions in open, fan-ventilated homes. Nobody abroad has an incentive to study this.

items.title: Creative destruction (column on the demise of STD booths)
items.creator: Ila Patnaik
items.why: A clear real-world case of creative destruction: an industry employing millions disappeared, and India's dynamic market economy absorbed the people.

items.title: Crime Victimisation in India
items.creator: Edited by Ajay Shah et al
items.why: Source of the survey question about what time parents think their teenage daughter should be home, which he treats as a measure of women's empowerment.

items.title: Critic Declares Springsteen Future of Rock and Roll
items.creator: Mass Moments
items.why: The background to the night that started the Landau-Springsteen partnership.

items.title: Crowds and Power
items.creator: Elias Canetti
items.why: Useful for understanding how anger gets mobilised into an 'us vs them' route to power.

items.title: CRRao.jl
items.creator: Sourish Das / XKDR Forum
items.why: It gives one consistent interface across many estimators and is uncompromisingly Bayesian, removing the extra effort Bayesian computation usually requires.

items.title: Cycling monument (Wikipedia)
items.why: A quick reference for the races and terrains discussed in the episode.

items.title: Dancing in the Dark
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: A masterpiece with levels: depressive lyrics ('tired and bored with myself') set to an upbeat tune. It shows Springsteen turning a commercial demand into real art.

items.title: Daniel Hannan's tweet on the left and compassion
items.creator: Daniel Hannan
items.why: It argues that the left's defining trait is not compassion but the conviction that compassion is unique to their side, which leads to a grotesque misreading of the other side.

items.title: Danish Husain and the Multiverse of Culture (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 359)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Danish Husain
items.why: Where Amit learned that Danish shared his admiration for Vicky's acting.

items.title: Darkness at Noon
items.creator: Arthur Koestler
items.why: It goes inside the minds of Soviet leaders confessing at show trials. Ajay says it changed the world, including the 1946 French election. He urges reading both Daphne Hardy's original translation and the 2015 translation of the rediscovered German manuscript.

items.title: Darkness on the Edge of Town
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: 'Just beautiful, simple language, and everyone relates.' It is specific to his life, yet anyone anywhere can see themselves in it.

items.title: Darwin's Dangerous Idea
items.creator: Daniel Dennett
items.why: One of the core books the hosts learned evolution from, by the thinker who framed it as an idea that dissolves simple preconceptions.

items.title: Data localisation in India: Questioning the means and ends
items.creator: Rishab Bailey and Smriti Parsheera
items.why: Further reading on state control over data in India.

items.title: DaVinci Resolve
items.why: The free version alone gives you state-of-the-art editing and the best colour grading, from software that once cost $800,000.

items.title: Dead Poets Society
items.creator: Peter Weir
items.why: He saw it at seventeen or eighteen, and just thinking about it, especially the last scene, makes him well up. He recommends it as a deeply inspiring film about seizing the day (carpe diem).

items.title: Decathlon
items.why: After a lifetime of hunting for the right equipment, he calls Decathlon's arrival a breakthrough: good gear, readily available and affordable.

items.title: DeepStateMap (live Ukraine war map)
items.creator: DeepStateMap
items.why: The geography and logistics of the front only make sense when you can see them.

items.title: Defending the Undefendable
items.creator: Walter Block
items.why: Block, an Austrian economist, defends ideas considered beyond the pale, much as Amit has just defended sweatshops and legal prostitution. You don't have to agree, but it makes you think in different ways instead of swallowing a tribe's dogma.

items.title: Der Edelstein
items.creator: Ulrich Boner
items.why: A visual starting point for the story of how printing and distribution shaped writing.

items.title: Determined
items.creator: Robert Sapolsky
items.why: Amit calls it one of Sapolsky's masterpieces and a brilliant book.

items.title: Devdutt Pattanaik and the Stories That Shape Us (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 404)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Devdutt Pattanaik
items.why: A deep immersion in Indian mythology. Devdutt's books are among the first things Amit recommends at the end.

items.title: Development Projects Observed
items.creator: Albert O. Hirschman
items.why: Part of the hosts' development reading list. It is not discussed in the conversation itself.

items.title: Devils and Dust
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: Springsteen said it wrote itself after a lifetime of craft; Ajay calls it 'one of those sweet and perfect songs'. It is his example of late-career mastery.

items.title: Dhano Dhanne
items.creator: Jaya Varma and the Chandigarh Choir
items.why: A personal bonus, 'because hey, why not?'

items.title: Dharmesh on imperfectionism
items.creator: Dharmesh
items.why: Amit calls it almost the mantra of his life, the same thing he tells his writing students.

items.title: Dhruv Rathee's YouTube channel
items.creator: Dhruv Rathee
items.why: Amit sets aside the question of quality, but says his numbers show huge demand for the filtering and sense-making that mainstream media should be providing.

items.title: Did Frederick The Great Introduce The Potato To Germany?
items.creator: Matt Robinson
items.why: Lets you dig into a story Ajay himself flags as possibly apocryphal.

items.title: Did the Indian Capital Controls Work as a Tool of Macroeconomic Policy?
items.creator: Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
items.why: A closer look at India's capital controls, part of the state machinery Ajay criticises for its anti-foreign stance.

items.title: Did the Indian GDP just jump up by a basis point?
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: It makes the case that free navigation creates a huge consumer surplus for every user, large enough to ask whether it showed up in GDP.

items.title: Digital public infrastructure and public value
items.creator: David Eaves, Mariana Mazzucato and Beatriz Vasconcellos
items.why: Another perspective on DPI, useful for setting against the episode's critique.

items.title: Diluting the role of the IIT JEE
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: It shows Ajay has been arguing for years against the JEE as the be-all and end-all.

items.title: Discovering faster matrix multiplication algorithms with reinforcement learning
items.creator: Alhussein Fawzi and others
items.why: It produced the first improvements in about 50 years to one of computing's most basic operations, by turning algorithm design into a game.

items.title: Do Not Go Gentle Into That Good Night
items.creator: Dylan Thomas
items.why: He uses it as the contrast to his own stance: not raging against the world, but a quiet, confident, curious engagement with it.

items.title: Do prestigious science journals attract bad science?
items.creator: Julia Belluz
items.why: Background for Ajay's argument that top-journal papers are often weaker because researchers pour their energy into gaming the system rather than into the knowledge.

items.title: Does the currency regime shape unhedged currency exposure
items.creator: Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
items.why: One of Ajay's chosen favourite papers involving himself.

items.title: Doing applied statistics research in Julia
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: A follow-up for anyone interested in the case for doing data analysis in Julia.

items.title: Domestic Violence and Intra-Household Resource Allocation in Rural India: An Exercise in Participatory Econometrics
items.creator: Vijayendra Rao
items.why: It shows what combining qualitative and quantitative work reveals: links between violence and family power, sterilisation, alcoholism and dowry. It is also a case study of how journal incentives fragment research.

items.title: Don't Follow the Money
items.creator: Peter R Neumann
items.why: Fits his argument that tracking money has not disrupted terrorist plots and has only fouled up finance.

items.title: Don't Punish Victimless Crimes (Everything is Everything, Ep 73)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: It covers why banning drinking doesn't solve the problem but creates an underground run by bootleggers.

items.title: Down to Earth
items.creator: Sharad Joshi
items.why: Joshi was a great thinker and politician who also took the role of public intellectual seriously and worked hard to get his thinking out. If you want to understand agriculture from the view of a farmer who lived it and led a great farmers' movement, this is the book to read.

items.title: Drew Houston on focus
items.creator: Drew Houston
items.why: Houston describes how Dropbox dropped its video-sharing work to focus on one thing.

items.title: Dwarkesh Patel's tweet on why LLMs haven't made discoveries
items.creator: Dwarkesh Patel
items.why: Amit calls it a great question, one Dwarkesh said nobody had answered satisfactorily, and it sharpens the human-vs-AI novelty debate.

items.title: Dylan O'Sullivan's tweet quoting Matt Kahn: 'People can only meet you as deeply as they've met themselves.'
items.creator: Dylan O'Sullivan
items.why: You understand others only as far as you understand yourself. Ajay adds that a good conversation takes a rich, mature mind.

items.title: Dylan O'Sullivan's tweet quoting Schopenhauer on the art of not reading
items.creator: Dylan O'Sullivan
items.why: To read good books you have to skip bad ones, starting with whatever the crowd is excited about this week, because life is short.

items.title: E-Yantra
items.creator: Kavi Arya
items.why: It replaces exam questions with creative challenges like 'build me a robot that does X'. Cheap sourced parts let students all over India take part. There are no marks or certificates, so the only reason to do it is the pleasure of doing it and the thirst for knowledge.

items.title: Earwitness to Place
items.creator: Bernie Krause (interviewed by Erin Robinsong)
items.why: The source for how habitat shapes birdsong and how a soundscape revealed species loss during a drought.

items.title: Eat a Peach
items.creator: The Allman Brothers Band
items.why: Amit singles out two tracks, 'Little Martha' and 'Blue Sky', both featuring Duane Allman: 'Absolutely love his guitaring, great feel, great vibe, just incredible.'

items.title: Economic freedom in agriculture
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's written case for the episode's conclusion that what is wrong is a lack of freedom, with the state blocking voluntary bargains.

items.title: Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren
items.creator: John Maynard Keynes
items.why: One of the smartest people in history tried hard to predict future productivity, and much of it didn't work out. That makes it a useful lesson in how hard forecasting is. Amit adds that putting yourself out like this takes intellectual bravery.

items.title: Economic Sophisms
items.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
items.why: Bastiat could boil complex ideas down to stories anyone understands, showing how absurd protectionism and the 'more work equals more prosperity' fallacy are.

items.title: Economies of Scale, Economies of Scope
items.creator: Venkatesh Rao
items.why: Explains the two textbook growth paths (doing more of the same, or moving into adjacencies) against which Sun, Google and Amazon look so audacious.

items.title: Edited volume of papers on the Indian bankruptcy reform
items.creator: Susan Thomas (editor)
items.why: A collection of serious research on how the reform was designed and how it has worked, which is the kind of knowledge ecosystem he says the field needs.

items.title: Educational Outreach, IIT Bombay (CDEEP)
items.creator: D. B. Phatak and others at IIT Bombay
items.why: It records IIT Bombay's engineering teaching on video and takes it to hundreds of thousands of students across India. For Ajay this separates the knowledge from the credential.

items.title: Egregious Indian protectionism against trade in services
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: It applies the services-trade argument to India's own barriers.

items.title: Eichmann in Jerusalem: A Report on the Banality of Evil
items.creator: Hannah Arendt
items.why: It is a warning that ordinary people can commit extraordinary cruelty, and that neither religion nor rationality protects against it.

items.title: Einstein's Letter to President Roosevelt
items.creator: Albert Einstein
items.why: It is the letter that, after Szilard reached Einstein, persuaded Roosevelt to start the bomb project before Hitler could get there.

items.title: El Amor de Mi Vida
items.creator: Warren Zevon
items.why: Lines like 'I only wish it had been us, but I'm happy for your happiness' show true love as wanting the other person to be happy, not owning them. Amit finds them deeply moving.

items.title: Eleanor Rigby
items.creator: The Beatles
items.why: A beautiful song that, for Ajay, captures how he thinks about most government IT systems.

items.title: Elon Musk on First-Principles Thinking
items.creator: Elon Musk
items.why: It is a concrete example of pricing materials from scratch, which took battery costs from $600 to $80 per kWh against expert consensus.

items.title: Emergent Ventures India
items.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan
items.why: No monthly or yearly targets, no blame for failure. It deliberately funds the freaks and mavericks that conventional VC and private equity miss.

items.title: Emil Sutovsky about the organisation of the event
items.creator: Emil Sutovsky
items.why: The FIDE CEO's own view; Amit praises his conduct throughout as gentlemanly.

items.title: Enlightenment Now
items.creator: Steven Pinker
items.why: Shows vividly why chasing equality can mean making everyone poorer.

items.title: Entry and Exit in Agriculture (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 1)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Pavan Srinath and Karthik Shashidhar
items.why: His guests argued that small farmers are forced to master two skills, farming and entrepreneurship, when they might prefer to specialise in one, and that tiny holdings make scale impossible.

items.title: Envisioning an India-US free trade agreement
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: It records a striking consensus on the American side that a deep free trade agreement with India is one of the few politically feasible things in the US. Ajay thinks the argument matters even more now that tariff fights have begun.

items.title: Episode 170 of A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
items.why: Amit calls it a great podcast episode on Astral Weeks that he had listened to, for anyone who wants the full story behind the album.

items.title: Epitaph on Sir Isaac Newton
items.creator: Alexander Pope
items.why: It sums up in one couplet the myth of the sudden lone genius, which the rest of the chapter complicates.

items.title: Eric Schmidt on five-year plans
items.creator: Eric Schmidt
items.why: An economy can't be centrally planned but a company can. A five-year plan forces you to imagine the world ahead and where you'll need to pivot.

items.title: Eric Topol's writing on medicine
items.creator: Eric Topol
items.why: To understand cutting-edge medicine, Amit would read Topol on Twitter, in his articles or in his books rather than the Times of India.

items.title: Eric Weinstein Won't Toe the Line (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 330)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Eric Weinstein
items.why: It is the longer version of the debate this episode ends on: with far more potential artists alive than ever before, why don't we see more great art?

items.title: Ernest Hemingway, The Art of Fiction No. 21 (Paris Review interview)
items.creator: George Plimpton
items.why: Hemingway's remedy for being stuck: sit down, write one true sentence, then one more.

items.title: Essays
items.creator: Lydia Davis
items.why: Davis writing about her own craft and literature, 'and much more besides'.

items.title: Essays in Biography
items.creator: John Maynard Keynes
items.why: Read it as a model of beautiful writing and sharp insight into people, from an economist Ajay argues with but deeply admires.

items.title: Essays in Persuasion
items.creator: John Maynard Keynes
items.why: Ajay disagrees with nearly all of Keynes's economics, but sees him as a master writer who knew the world. 'Everybody should dream of writing like that.'

items.title: Eurosport cycling coverage (with Dan Lloyd, Orla Chennaoui and Adam Blythe)
items.why: Amit recommends Eurosport because the commentary, especially from Dan Lloyd, Orla Chennaoui and Adam Blythe, was one of his great joys of watching cycling. He thinks they're on Eurosport this time.

items.title: eventstudies (open-source R package)
items.creator: XKDR Forum
items.why: An event study could measure whether a six shifts expected runs or wicket probability over the next few balls. Ajay invites anyone who wants to write that paper to talk to him.

items.title: Every Breath You Take
items.creator: The Police
items.why: Its refrain, 'I'll be watching you', fits a state that watches every transaction. Ajay suggests listeners email it to the civil servants in their lives.

items.title: Everybody Lies
items.creator: Seth Stephens-Davidowitz
items.why: Amit calls it phenomenal because of its central idea: people are most honest when searching anonymously, so search data reveals human nature in a way surveys can't. Its findings range from sexless marriages to parents' gender bias.

items.title: Everything is Everything episode on the creator economy
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Expands on the creator lessons from the finale: authenticity, intimacy, and the death of old gatekeepers.

items.title: Exploring Digital Public Goods
items.why: A resource on the digital public goods idea whose terminology the episode questions.

items.title: Export Versus FDI with Heterogeneous Firms
items.creator: Elhanan Helpman, Mark J Melitz and Stephen R Yeaple
items.why: It addresses the exporting-versus-FDI question at the heart of the episode. Ajay argues the two are complementary, not a menu of choices.

items.title: Exporting & firm performance: Evidence from India
items.creator: Apoorva Gupta, Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
items.why: Indian evidence on the episode's central link between exporting and how well firms perform.

items.title: ExpressVPN (or any good VPN)
items.why: It is the practical way he has found to access coverage. He uses ExpressVPN, but any good VPN will do.

items.title: Ezra Klein interviewed by David Perell
items.creator: Ezra Klein and David Perell
items.why: Ajay says it 'goes to the core' of why we read. The payoff is the hours of grappling with an author, not a summary.

items.title: Facts Don't Matter, Stories Do
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: It argues that Trump won a following by offering simple stories: jobs shipped overseas, immigrants taking jobs. These are simplistic and wrong, but they appear to explain the world. Amit reached Müller's 'simplistic narratives' point on his own.

items.title: Fair coins tend to land on the same side they started
items.creator: František Bartoš et al.
items.why: The empirical basis for the finding that a coin tossed heads-up lands heads about 51% of the time, showing structure hidden inside apparent randomness.

items.title: False Alarm
items.creator: Bjørn Lomborg
items.why: Amit says the alarmist predictions of past decades, including Al Gore's ten-year forecasts, turned out wrong. He thinks Lomborg's books let you check the data yourself and discount the exaggeration.

items.title: Falsifiability
items.creator: Karl Popper
items.why: He finds it a lovely organising principle. A theory deserves consideration when it makes predictions that could be proven wrong, and that helps us sort our beliefs by how much confidence they deserve.

items.title: Famous Last Questions
items.creator: Sanjana Ramachandran
items.why: A longer treatment of modern Indian dating.

items.title: Farmers, Technology and Freedom of Choice: A Tale of Two Satyagrahas
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: The written version of the BT cotton satyagraha and what followed, including the adoption figures he cites.

items.title: Fascism in Baroda
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Part of the archive of real Indian free-speech battles behind this episode's arguments.

items.title: Fast Car (live at the Nelson Mandela Tribute Concert, 1988)
items.creator: Tracy Chapman
items.why: It has been Amit's all-time favourite song since the late 80s and still moves him deeply. This performance made Chapman famous and is his main example of the surface area of serendipity.

items.title: Fateful Choices
items.creator: Ian Kershaw
items.why: It shows how Churchill and Roosevelt worked to bring America into the Second World War on the Allied side. It was a close call: as late as August 1941, about half the House of Representatives still opposed it. Ajay finds it timely for understanding America today.

items.title: Father and Son
items.creator: Cat Stevens
items.why: Ajay once found it a little clichéd, but twenty years on he thinks it's a really great song, so don't worry that it's too famous. The same singer voices both the father and the son.

items.title: Father, Son & Co: My Life at IBM and Beyond
items.creator: Thomas J Watson Jr
items.why: A purely family-business book, about Designs One and Two rather than the modern firm, and beautifully written. It covers how Watson Jr took over a feudal company and bet it on OS/360. Ajay read it when he was young and says it gave him great insight into the challenges of running a family business.

items.title: Fierce Attachments
items.creator: Vivian Gornick
items.why: Gornick's constant tussle with her mother shows two people who understand each other completely and yet not at all. It is a lesson in the complexity of human relationships and why we shouldn't jump to judgment.

items.title: Fight of the Century: Keynes vs. Hayek (Economics Rap Battle Round Two)
items.why: Round two of the same playful take on the great debate.

items.title: Fighting Against Censorship
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Background reading on the Indian censorship regime the episode critiques.

items.title: Final Draft
items.why: The specialised tool for writing screenplays. Useful, though he sees such apps as pocket calculators that could become far more.

items.title: Finding Love in Modern India (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 401)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Sanjana Ramachandran
items.why: A detailed look at how hard dating apps are, and how they are hard in different ways for men and women.

items.title: Flying Spaghetti Monster
items.creator: Bobby Henderson
items.why: Amit's favourite example of the benign, tongue-in-cheek way to protest religion, by showing how absurd it is to demand special treatment for beliefs.

items.title: Fogbank (Wikipedia)
items.why: Background on the classified US nuclear aerogel whose recipe was lost and had to be reinvented at great cost.

items.title: Follow-Up: A New Ending in Tale of Young Woman From Rural India
items.creator: Ellen Barry
items.why: It continues the story of one of the young women from the original Tirupur piece.

items.title: For this Brave New World of cricket, we have IPL and England to thank
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Celebrates England as the first team to realise ODI cricket had been played too conservatively for three decades.

items.title: For Whom the Bell Tolls
items.creator: Ernest Hemingway
items.why: He calls it one of the great books of the world. Move its story to a purely urban setting and 'the oomph is lost', which shows how much wild landscapes add to a story and to life.

items.title: Foreign Currency Borrowing by Indian Firms: Towards a New Policy Framework
items.creator: Ila Patnaik, Ajay Shah and Nirvikar Singh
items.why: Connects to his steel-mill argument that Indian firms need cheaper foreign debt to compete globally.

items.title: Foreign Investors under Stress: Evidence from India
items.creator: Ila Patnaik, Ajay Shah and Nirvikar Singh
items.why: Examines how foreign investors behave in India under stress, relevant to the foreign-capital thread.

items.title: Forests, Trees, and Intellectual Roots (review of Seeing Like a State)
items.creator: Brad DeLong
items.why: An economist's engagement with the book, and the place where Ajay could have discovered it first.

items.title: Forthcoming book on taxation
items.creator: Vijay Kelkar, Arvind Modi and Ajay Shah
items.why: Amit is 'fully convinced it's gonna be great', and it's another piece of lasting stock.

items.title: Fortress and Frontier in American Health Care
items.creator: Robert Graboyes
items.why: It gave Amit 'a new framework to think about the world'. Healthcare regulation is a high-walled fortress, while tech is an open frontier where anyone can try things. Amit notes its case is nuanced, not a call to scrap the FDA.

items.title: Foundation for Economic Development (YouTube channel)
items.creator: Rahul Ahluwalia
items.why: 'Rahul's a great guy... please do check out his channel as well. Support free thinkers.'

items.title: Foundational bankruptcy and credit-risk research (papers at ifrogs.org and XKDR Forum's firms-finance work)
items.why: The research base behind the Indian bankruptcy reform. Ajay argues reform only works when a body of data and research like this exists.

items.title: Four Thousand Weeks
items.creator: Oliver Burkeman
items.why: It makes you reckon with how little time a life actually holds, which works as a spur to act now rather than keep preparing.

items.title: Free Banking in Britain: Theory, Experience and Debate 1800-1845
items.creator: Lawrence H. White
items.why: It is the historical case study behind the claim that competing private currencies worked well in practice.

items.title: Freedoms Delayed
items.creator: Timur Kuran
items.why: It follows the same institutional story into its political consequences and is rich in history.

items.title: FreeStyle Libre Glucose Monitoring System (Reader & Sensor)
items.creator: Abbott Labs
items.why: It is the CGM that made this whole journey possible. Ajay's tips: insert it and wait a full 24 hours before initialising for better accuracy, and expect it to differ from finger-prick readings because it tracks the average of the last 5-15 minutes. Amit's tips: calibrate with prick tests for a couple of days, and buy it directly, since services like Ultrahuman use the same sensor. Ajay also asks Abbott to open the API so readings can flow into a Google Sheet.

items.title: Frog and Toad on spring
items.creator: Arnold Lobel (via the Frog and Toad Bot)
items.why: A gentle reminder for anyone in dark times to zoom out, and to act.

items.title: From bark to weed: The history of artemisinin
items.creator: Claude Faurant
items.why: The history behind how an ancient Chinese remedy became the main modern treatment for malaria.

items.title: From Cairo to Delhi With Max Rodenbeck (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 281)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Rodenbeck's answer, that his home is the Cairo of his childhood which no longer exists, is a poignant take on home as a vanished place.

items.title: From domestic to global asset pricing
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Part of his kit on what changes when Indian firms and capital become integrated with the world.

items.title: Fun Home
items.creator: Alison Bechdel
items.why: Amit calls her 2006 memoir a masterpiece. It shows that comics can be a profound art form that competes with the best of literature.

items.title: Fund Schooling, Not Schools
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: The core voucher idea: public money should follow the child to whatever school the parent chooses.

items.title: Furrows in a Field
items.creator: Sugata Srinivasaraju
items.why: Amit calls it a great book, even though their five-and-a-half-hour conversation never got to it.

items.title: Futures Markets in Agriculture (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 12)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Karthik Shashidhar
items.why: Amit once thought futures were arcane finance that didn't concern ordinary people. This conversation showed him they can be a powerful tool for removing a farmer's uncertainty.

items.title: Gambling on Development
items.creator: Stefan Dercon
items.why: Part of the hosts' reading list on why some countries develop and most fail. It is not discussed in the conversation itself.

items.title: Game Changer
items.creator: Matthew Sadler and Natasha Regan
items.why: It shows which human heuristics AlphaZero's play forces us to rethink, such as material versus initiative and play down the flanks, and Amit says it will make you a better player. He also singles out Garry Kasparov's introduction, a beautiful short essay on the evolution of computer chess that 'everyone should read'.

items.title: Gandhi Before India
items.creator: Ramachandra Guha
items.why: Amit finds the South Africa years, when Gandhi was still forming, especially interesting, and calls Guha a phenomenal historian.

items.title: Gandhi: The Years That Changed the World
items.creator: Ramachandra Guha
items.why: With the first volume, it gives the full arc. Amit calls both books 'just superb.'

items.title: Garry Tan on acting small
items.creator: Garry Tan
items.why: Small companies shouldn't imitate big-company polish. Smallness lets you get close to every customer.

items.title: Genesis of Rgvedic Retroflexion
items.creator: Madhav Deshpande
items.why: A 1976 essay that 'pretty much blew everyone away' by showing that the Rig Veda's language was influenced by what was spoken here before.

items.title: Genetic Engineering (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 165)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Shambhavi Naik
items.why: Amit calls it an excellent episode with Shambhavi Naik of Takshashila. It covers the science of gene editing and the ethical questions it raises.

items.title: Geniuses and economic development
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Ties to the idea that India's small but, in absolute numbers, huge pool of very capable people matters for development.

items.title: Getting Things Done
items.creator: David Allen
items.why: Named as the classic of the productivity-tools-and-procedures tradition, which Ajay questions as too managerial.

items.title: Ghost World
items.creator: Daniel Clowes
items.why: Another graphic novel Amit calls a masterpiece.

items.title: GOAT
items.creator: Tyler Cowen
items.why: It is a delight to read and pulls together the lives and ideas of the economists the hosts love. Ajay calls it the ideal starting point if you haven't met Friedman, Hayek and Keynes before.

items.title: Goechala trek
items.why: Of all his Himalayan treks, he rates it one of the best of his life. Reaching Goechala 1 with Kanchenjunga in front of him was one of his life's great moments.

items.title: Going from strong as in scary to strong as in capable
items.creator: Suyash Rai and Ajay Shah
items.why: It sets out the distinction Ajay makes in the episode: India should want strength meaning competence, not strength meaning the power to jail anyone or pass any law overnight.

items.title: Gokhale: The Indian Moderates and the British Raj
items.creator: B.R. Nanda
items.why: A window into Gokhale and the radical intellectual culture of late-nineteenth-century Pune.

items.title: Google Autocomplete experiments (incognito window, optionally with a VPN)
items.creator: Google
items.why: In an incognito window autocomplete isn't biased by your history, and a VPN shows other countries' results. You don't need special access to Google's data to learn something.

items.title: Google Gemini (paid)
items.creator: Google
items.why: It gave five good suggestions 'like what a master editor would do', and he signed up for $20 a month that day. He treats LLMs as good language processors, not AGI.

items.title: Google Guys: The Playboy Interview
items.creator: Playboy (interview with Larry Page and Sergey Brin)
items.why: Shows that Playboy ran serious long-form journalism alongside its fiction.

items.title: Google Maps
items.creator: Google
items.why: He calls it 'a madly great map.' It is free to users and routes you on foot, by car or by public transport through any city. Ajay himself regularly contributes corrections and missing places.

items.title: Google Scholar
items.creator: Google
items.why: It is his first stop for any search, ahead of Google. Spending time with original papers, even ones you can't fully follow, teaches you their rhythm. He credits this habit for being able to read papers across many disciplines.

items.title: Google Scholar's citations list
items.why: Open any paper, click its citation count, and you see every later paper that engaged with it, both critics and follow-ups. It's a way to go down real rabbit holes.

items.title: Google Trends
items.creator: Google
items.why: You can save a search as a fixed URL and rerun it to see what the world is paying attention to over time.

items.title: Google's AlphaZero Destroys Stockfish In 100-Game Match
items.creator: Mike Klein
items.why: The contemporary report on the match that made AlphaZero famous.

items.title: Gorakhgad and Kothaligad day hikes
items.why: They are an easy first step: a backpack, two litres of water, five apples and some route-finding. Enough people use them that you'll meet someone to set you right.

items.title: GothamChess
items.creator: Levy Rozman
items.why: He builds human drama into the analysis and makes you feel you understand chess like an expert. He communicates the passion and magic of the board, not just the moves.

items.title: Grand Tamasha
items.creator: Milan Vaishnav
items.why: Vaishnav is a fine thinker, and the podcast is a good way to follow Indian politics.

items.title: Grand Tour (cycling) (Wikipedia)
items.why: Background on the format behind most of the episode's stories.

items.title: Great leaders choose prosperity over pride
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: The core stance for negotiating with Trump: national interest over ego.

items.title: Great Soul
items.creator: Joseph Lelyveld
items.why: Lelyveld, a fine writer who has written widely for the New Yorker, hinted at a homosexual relationship, partly because the two called each other 'upper house' and 'lower house.' That was shocking enough to get the book banned. Guha doesn't accept the theory, but Amit loves the book.

items.title: Green Eggs and Ham
items.creator: Dr Seuss
items.why: It shows a tight constraint producing something joyful, and it supports his advice that writers don't need a big vocabulary.

items.title: Greg Isenberg on greatness
items.creator: Greg Isenberg
items.why: It prompted a discussion of when to stay in your comfort zone and when to leave it.

items.title: Growing Up (live)
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: Before the song, Springsteen talked for what seemed like half an hour, and it was brilliant. It is proof that he never played 'cover versions of himself' and every show was new.

items.title: Gukesh interviewed at length by Sagar Shah after the World Championship
items.creator: Sagar Shah
items.why: Source for Gukesh saying he was about to play Rb3, and for his plan to make every game long because Ding looked tired.

items.title: Gukesh stating his ambition to Sagar Shah at age 11
items.creator: Sagar Shah
items.why: An 11-year-old Gukesh says he wants to be the youngest world champion, and now he is.

items.title: Gurpriya Sidhu's tweet: 'Be like a coach or a comrade in your professional relationships. Be like a gardener in your personal ones.'
items.creator: Gurpriya Sidhu
items.why: Work relationships have a function, while personal ones mean accepting people as they are. The tweet led to the gardener-versus-architect discussion of firms and novels.

items.title: Gurwinder Bhogal Examines Human Nature (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 331)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Gurwinder Bhogal
items.why: The source of the idea that we shape ourselves on the reflections of us we see in other people's eyes.

items.title: Gurwinder Bhogal on our shrinking future
items.creator: Gurwinder Bhogal
items.why: Amit reads it as a call to action and calls Gurwinder a fount of wisdom.

items.title: Gurwinder Bhogal quoting Christ Williamson on hiding your true self
items.creator: Gurwinder Bhogal
items.why: It links search data, where people's hidden selves show up, to a point about why being authentic matters for being loved.

items.title: Gurwinder Bhogal's Substack
items.creator: Gurwinder Bhogal
items.why: Bhogal built his reputation on Twitter megathreads that combine existing knowledge into original insights and see the world very sharply.

items.title: Gurwinder Bhogal's tweet on grappling with complex issues
items.creator: Gurwinder Bhogal
items.why: It diagnoses tribal thinking on questions that really are complex. Ajay objected that some debates, such as nationalism and militarism, are closed for him.

items.title: Gurwinder Bhogal's tweet on what AI does to us
items.creator: Gurwinder Bhogal
items.why: It sharpens the case for using AI as a tool rather than a crutch.

items.title: Gurwinder Bhogal's tweet on whiners
items.creator: Gurwinder Bhogal
items.why: Amit has made cutting out negativity close to a life mission. Ajay added that people should encourage new ideas at birth.

items.title: Gyan Prakash on the Emergency (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 103)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Gyan Prakash
items.why: It frames the Emergency as part of the Indian state's centralising DNA, inherited from the colonial state.

items.title: Halfway From Coal, Halfway to Diamond (Everything is Everything, Ep 1)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The starting point of the Kuran connection and the hosts' earlier discussion of his ideas.

items.title: Hans Niemann interviewed in 2022 about his alleged cheating
items.why: Niemann admits his past online cheating as a teenager and insists it is behind him, which is his side of the story.

items.title: Harishchandragad and Ratangad
items.why: He calls it world class and says he has never seen anything more beautiful. He also warns it is now overrun by boorish young men with alcohol.

items.title: Hateship, Friendship, Courtship, Loveship, Marriage
items.creator: Alice Munro
items.why: Amit calls both collections masterpieces and suggests them as a break from the state, economics and politics, because he believes every good work of fiction speaks to the reader personally.

items.title: Havel: A Life
items.creator: Michael Zantovsky
items.why: Amit calls it a great biography and finds a 'stirring' portrait of Havel's self-education in it.

items.title: Heaven's Gaits
items.creator: Adam Gopnik
items.why: Amit enjoys its lines ('our backs and arches, like querulous cabinet ministers, at first complain and then resign'). He also likes its argument that walking as a pastime depended on technologies such as gaslight, the rule of law, the Walkman and sneakers.

items.title: Hikaru Nakamura on Gukesh's game against Wei Yi
items.creator: Hikaru Nakamura
items.why: Even commentators who rarely give credit called the endgame miraculous.

items.title: Hikaru Nakamura's channel
items.creator: Hikaru Nakamura
items.why: He plays bullet game after game for five or six hours while explaining his thinking, which is fantastic and instructive. Amit thinks streaming may even have revitalised Nakamura's own love for chess before his strong showings in the last two Candidates.

items.title: Hiking in the Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve
items.why: He calls it one of the world's most glorious hiking regions and tells listeners who have never hiked to 'run, not walk' there.

items.title: Hind Swaraj
items.creator: Mohandas Gandhi
items.why: Part of our history, and the best evidence for Amit's argument that Gandhi was incoherent on most things but right about nonviolent resistance.

items.title: Homeopathic Faith
items.creator: Amit Varma
