items.why: It is an example of the critical eye that Ajay says academics must now turn on themselves.

items.title: Horizon
items.creator: Barry Lopez
items.why: Lopez is one of the great travel writers and a beautiful, introspective writer. Amit says a journey becomes truly beautiful when it is also a journey inside you.

items.title: Host-diet-gut microbiome interactions influence human energy balance
items.creator: Karen D Corbin et al.
items.why: It compared diets with identical calories and found that complex carbs feed the gut microbiome, which consumes some of the energy. The result is roughly a 200-calorie-a-day 'discount', evidence that a calorie is not a calorie.

items.title: Housefull Economics on Pragati
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: It explains economic concepts through films. Amit asks listeners whether they'd like a regular segment like it on the show.

items.title: How 32-bit Float Recording Works on the Wireless PRO
items.why: For anyone curious about the technology Ajay admits he 'only dimly' understands.

items.title: How Amazon grew an awkward side project into AWS, a behemoth that's now 4 times bigger than its original shopping business
items.creator: Geoff Colvin
items.why: Further reading on how a bookshop's internal infrastructure turned into the cloud computing business.

items.title: How Amul became utterly butterly delicious and salty
items.creator: Vikram Doctor
items.why: Tells the full history of how Amul's first, too-perfect butter flopped in Bombay before it won the market.

items.title: How Bing Crosby Made Silicon Valley Possible
items.creator: Ted Gioia
items.why: Shows how a new technology produced a new style of singing: soft, close-up and intimate, as with Bing Crosby and Frank Sinatra.

items.title: How Fiction Works
items.creator: James Wood
items.why: Useful for readers, not just writers. It explains voice and how the modern novel evolved, including Flaubert's role. Amit promises it 'will transform the way you read a book'.

items.title: How Frameworks (howframeworks.com)
items.creator: Sudhir Sarnobat
items.why: It offers frameworks to grow a business, turn it around or take it to the next level. Amit says these come from a lifetime of experience in Indian conditions, not consultant talk or bookish theory. Amit doesn't run a business and still spent hours going down the rabbit hole, because the frameworks also apply to how individuals live. The code 'seen unseen' gets listeners a discount; Amit takes no commission.

items.title: How Innovation Works: And Why It Flourishes in Freedom
items.creator: Matt Ridley
items.why: Ridley shows innovation as a bottom-up process emerging from within society. Amit thinks Ridley would share much of his skepticism about top-down innovation policy, so it is a good counterweight to the paper.

items.title: How Life Imitates Chess
items.creator: Garry Kasparov
items.why: Amit considers Kasparov a great mind, and hopes he succeeds in 'the larger game that he is playing'.

items.title: How Much Does Free Education Cost?
items.creator: Centre for Civil Society
items.why: A Delhi survey of households earning under Rs 5,000 a month found the same thing: a large share send their kids to budget private schools.

items.title: How Much Wealth Do You Need to Retire? (Everything is Everything, Ep 110)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Pointer to the preceding episode in the series.

items.title: How Should One Read a Book?
items.creator: Virginia Woolf
items.why: Amit calls it a great essay on exactly this episode's question.

items.title: How The Desperate Norwegian Salmon Industry Created A Sushi Staple
items.creator: Jess Jiang
items.why: The full account of how Norway's salmon glut turned into the world's default sushi.

items.title: How the vaccine story will play out
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Further reading from Ajay on the economics of COVID vaccines, written while the pandemic was unfolding.

items.title: How the War Was Won
items.creator: Phillips Payson O'Brien
items.why: A recent book offering new insights on the grunt on the ground versus the high economic strategy of the Second World War. Ajay has studied the subject all his life and still found it full of new knowledge.

items.title: How This Nobel Has Redefined Literature
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: It argues that the Nobel honoured the prize more than the man, and that literature is words and storytelling, not just books. This is the premise of the episode.

items.title: How to correctly draw the perimeter for government software systems (Big Ideas, Episode 20)
items.why: It expands on the idea that the state should open up an API and let private players like ClearTrip and MakeMyTrip build on it.

items.title: How to Enhance Performance & Learning by Applying a Growth Mindset
items.creator: Huberman Lab Podcast
items.why: Amit calls it a great episode of a podcast that is excellent on the whole. An accessible way into the growth-mindset research.

items.title: How To Know a Person
items.creator: David Brooks
items.why: It echoes what Amit learned from long-form podcasting: the power of long conversations, of learning to listen, of genuine interest in others, of intentionally building friendships. Brooks himself changed late in life; Oprah remarked on how much he'd changed when he returned to her show years later. Amit also commends Brooks's columns and other books for making us think about our own lives.

items.title: How to make digital payments work
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's own case for how India's payments field should work, in line with his argument for open entry.

items.title: How to Miss By a Mile: An Alternative Look at Uber's Potential Market Size
items.creator: Bill Gurley
items.why: Gurley argued that Uber was out to replace car ownership, not just compete with taxis. That shows why you can't size a disruptor by looking at what already exists.

items.title: How to Read a Book
items.creator: Mortimer Adler and Charles Van Doren
items.why: Lays out the four levels of reading (elementary, inspectional, analytical, synoptical). It also gives a concrete four-step method for analytical reading: classify the book, state its gist briefly, outline its parts, and define the problem the author is solving.

items.title: How to Read and Why
items.creator: Harold Bloom
items.why: Bloom explains what attitude each genre demands. Slow down for short stories and novels, memorize poems, and read a Shakespeare play, watch it, then read it again.

items.title: How to Write a Paper (Everything is Everything, Ep 62)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: It explains the IMRD structure (Introduction, Methodology, Results, Discussion), which is the key to extracting value from papers outside your field.

items.title: How to Write Well
items.creator: Tim de Lisle
items.why: Amit calls it a lovely book on writing that focuses on clarity. He uses some of its examples in his own writing course.

items.title: How Will You Measure Your Life?
items.creator: Clayton Christensen et al.
items.why: It extends the idea of judging your life by your own values rather than external success.

items.title: Huang on not wearing a watch
items.creator: Jensen Huang
items.why: 'Now is the most important time.' Give whatever you're doing your full attention.

items.title: Huang on work & suffering
items.creator: Jensen Huang
items.why: Greatness involves suffering. Huang doesn't feel joy about his company every day, but he feels love, and love drives the hard work.

items.title: Huntsville, Alabama
items.why: A cow town seeded with relocated German rocket scientists became a world R&D capital over generations. It is a living case study of how clustering talent compounds.

items.title: Hussain Haidry, Hindustani Musalmaan (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 275)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Hussain Haidry
items.why: It is a fuller conversation with the poet whose experience shows what online mobs do to the people they target.

items.title: I'm Gonna Crawl
items.creator: Led Zeppelin
items.why: Ajay considers it one of the great things Plant, Page, John Paul Jones and Bonzo ever did, made at the peak of their powers just before the band ended.

items.title: I'm on Fire
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: The approach works even on a 'non-metaphysical' subject like lust. Amit points to the image of waking with 'a sheet soaking wet and a freight train running through the middle of my head'.

items.title: I, Pencil (The Movie)
items.why: A filmed version of the pencil parable for those who prefer watching to reading.

items.title: I, Robot: The Man Behind the Google Phone
items.creator: John Markoff
items.why: Further reading on Andy Rubin, the central figure in the Android leap.

items.title: Ideas of India
items.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan
items.why: He thinks she does an incredible job.

items.title: Identifying the Real SBO: A critique of the LinkedIn and Samsung Orders
items.creator: Chirag Motwani and Ananya Badaga
items.why: Further reading on India's disclosure demands on firms, connected to his argument that firms deserve financial privacy.

items.title: Illiberal Reformers
items.creator: Thomas Leonard
items.why: It shows that some celebrated progressive labour legislation of the early 20th century was meant to keep African Americans and women out of the workforce. The already privileged were protecting themselves.

items.title: Imagined Communities
items.creator: Benedict Anderson
items.why: Possibly his favourite book on nationalism. It supplies the episode's core definition (a nation is an 'imagined political community', necessarily limited and sovereign) and the three paradoxes of nationhood.

items.title: Implications of US tariffs
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: It is Ajay's written take on what the tariffs mean, as a companion to the episode's discussion.

items.title: Impossible Germany
items.creator: Wilco
items.why: Amit calls it 'absolutely magnificent', adding: 'Nothing to do with finance, and thank God for that.'

items.title: Improving governance using large IT systems
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: It argues that IT can tame high-transaction, high-discretion components and make a hard problem manageable.

items.title: In Defence of Tanmay Bhat
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: A precursor to his defence of Ranveer: standing up for the speech rights of creators under fire.

items.title: In My Tribe
items.creator: Arnold Kling
items.why: It continues Kling's thinking, and Amit recalls a follow-up there or elsewhere that adds nuance to the three-languages framework.

items.title: In search of inclusion
items.creator: Renuka Sane and Susan Thomas
items.why: Further reading on pension systems from Renuka Sane, who Amit notes has spent recent years working on this field.

items.title: In the Beginning...Was the Command Line
items.creator: Neal Stephenson
items.why: It is not an engineering book. Stephenson 'gets the dream, he gets the philosophy' of this world and tells it in an instinctive, passionate way.

items.title: Independence Day
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: It's about fathers and sons, and Ajay sees in it the drama of small towns all over India: despair, the darkness at the edge of town, family conflict, the decision to leave, and the lost social network after you go.

items.title: India = Migration (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 128)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Chinmay Tumbe
items.why: A conversation companion to India Moving.

items.title: India Grows at Night
items.creator: Gurcharan Das
items.why: Amit calls the title great because it captures how Indians live and thrive despite a dysfunctional, extractive state, which makes the question of its legitimacy almost beside the point.

items.title: India in the Nuclear Age (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 80)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Prakash Menon
items.why: It explores the counterintuitive idea that nuclear weapons make conventional war more important, not less.

items.title: India in the Persianate Age
items.creator: Richard Eaton
items.why: A 'magnificent book' adored by the Mughal historians on Amit's show. It suggests global trade shifted power to the port cities and weakened the centralised empire.

items.title: India's Far From Free Markets (2005, Wall Street Journal)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: It is Amit's early argument that India's liberalisation was incomplete.

items.title: India's Financial Globalisation
items.creator: Ajay Shah and Ila Patnaik
items.why: Background on foreign capital as a mode of internationalisation. Ajay argues Indian firms need foreign capital to match competitors' cost of capital.

items.title: India's Founding Moment
items.creator: Madhav Khosla
items.why: Helps explain the elite, top-down mindset of the founders, who felt they had to teach the nation how to think.

items.title: India's MSME Landscape — Some Useful Frameworks (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 419)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Sudhir Sarnobat and Naren Shenoy
items.why: Ajay calls it one of the best Seen and the Unseen episodes he has experienced. It takes you inside the minds of people who know Indian business at the ground level. He compares it to the expensive, difficult fieldwork researchers would otherwise have to do.

items.title: India's Policy Responses to Big Tech
items.creator: Smriti Parsheera
items.why: Background on how Indian policy treats big tech, which matters for the Google-versus-state comparison in the episode.

items.title: India's Tryst With Pandemics (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 205)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: The deeper conversation on the history of pandemics and how they play out.

items.title: India's Water Crisis (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 60)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Vishwanath S (zenrainman)
items.why: It covers groundwater depletion in India, which is driven partly by bore wells and tube wells drawing excess water because of bad incentives.

items.title: India, Pakistan, Kashmir: We Won't Need To Fight A War If We Can Win The Peace
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: It sets out his argument that India treated Kashmir as a purely military problem and lost its people, when the job of the state is to serve its citizens rather than rule over them.

items.title: India: Cookbook
items.creator: Pushpesh Pant
items.why: Calls it a great book. It shows that food moved both ways: traders brought leavened bread, baking and noodles, and India gave Europe curry, mangoes and chutney.

items.title: Indiahikes website
items.creator: Indiahikes
items.why: Ajay has never used them as a services firm, but for almost any hike in India their page is often the best, with the story, the route and a map. From there you can move to Google Earth.

items.title: Indian Defence Strategy: Forces, Potential and Procurement Disasters
items.creator: Perun
items.why: It is detailed and accurate on the Indian defence industry, with no elementary errors, and Amit found it better informed than many people whose job is to know this.

items.title: Indian economic strategy in the new globalisation
items.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
items.why: A single, coherent roadmap for what India should do after the tariffs. This episode is built on it.

items.title: Inside the CIA Mission to Haul Plutonium Up the Himalayas
items.creator: Robert Beckhusen
items.why: Ajay calls it a beautiful Wired article. It tells the American side, including how the CIA secretly recruited elite US climbers one by one.

items.title: Insiders and Outsiders
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: It sets out his changed view that insiders shaping a system can be as valuable as outsiders criticising it.

items.title: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Reforms in India: 10 Years After the IBC (forthcoming book, 2026)
items.why: A live attempt to bring researchers back together on bankruptcy after the community scattered. This is the pipeline of papers and debate Ajay says reform depends on.

items.title: Integration of the Indian States
items.creator: VP Menon
items.why: A first-hand account from the man who executed the integration.

items.title: International Diversification Calculation spreadsheet
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: It lets you play with equity index performance, holding periods, and reward-to-risk ratios, and see how much risk smarter diversification removes. It comes with a warning: Excel is not the ideal tool, and you should not expect answers from one sheet.

items.title: Into the Wild
items.creator: Jon Krakauer
items.why: Ajay says Krakauer has 'some really good books' and this is another one.

items.title: Into Thin Air
items.creator: Jon Krakauer
items.why: It is about one summer on Everest when many bad things happened, and it shows the go/no-go call on the final summit day. Ajay says every Everest accident comes down to that judgment.

items.title: Introduction to Modern Climate Change
items.creator: Andrew E Dessler
items.why: Ajay sees climate change as one of the great crises of the modern world, alongside populism. This slim, sensible book of about 200 pages covers climate science, mitigation and adaptation. He thinks everybody should read it.

items.title: Inventing Money
items.creator: Nicholas Dunbar
items.why: Ajay thinks Dunbar's LTCM book, which came out a year later, is the better of the two.

items.title: Inverting the Pyramid
items.creator: Jonathan Wilson
items.why: It is a great book on football tactics. It helps you watch sport with deeper attention, as the chess game underneath, instead of in a shallow, tribal 'my team is winning' way.

items.title: Investment Risk in Indian Pension Sector and Role for Pension Guarantees
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: It frames pension guarantees as put options on a portfolio, which can be very expensive. That is the core of his worry about whether the UPS is affordable.

items.title: Invisible Infrastructure (Everything is Everything, Ep 82)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Advanced economies run on an invisible infrastructure of institutions and norms that makes everything work smoothly. India needs that, not just the stadium.

items.title: IPCC reports
items.creator: IPCC
items.why: Ajay usually finds reports by international bodies such as the World Bank and IMF bland, because they are written by committee. IPCC reports are different. They are written by committees of scientists with real processes for debate, they give state-of-the-art thinking, and they show where experts disagree by setting out the range of models. He says just looking at the graphics will make you think about the world in new ways.

items.title: Is Google Making Us Stupid?
items.creator: Nicholas Carr
items.why: Argues that our shallow interaction with the internet keeps us from going deep and makes us stupider, while books pull the other way. Amit thinks things have only gotten worse since.

items.title: Is Old Music Killing New Music?
items.creator: Ted Gioia
items.why: Gioia's data shows old music is outselling new music by a mile. Amit's own habits turned out to be part of a structural shift in the industry, not just ageing.

items.title: Is Your Impact Evaluation Asking Questions That Matter? A Four Part Smell Test
items.creator: Lant Pritchett
items.why: Amit calls it a great paper on how to figure out whether a policy has actually made a difference in the world.

items.title: Is–Ought Problem
items.creator: Wikipedia
items.why: Hume's point that you cannot derive an 'ought' from an 'is' guards against reading evolutionary explanations as moral justifications.

items.title: Jan Koum on charging for WhatsApp
items.creator: Jan Koum
items.why: WhatsApp charged a dollar early on to keep growth in check while it learned to please its existing users. Amit finds this really inspiring.

items.title: Jan-Krzysztof Duda interviewed by Sagar Shah
items.creator: Sagar Shah
items.why: Duda, who played 300+ practice games with Gukesh, says his help might have mattered more in a tiebreak than in the classical games.

items.title: Japanese Kit Kat Flavours: The Complete List
items.why: It shows how far one brand will go to localise for a single market.

items.title: Jayaprakash Narayan Wants to Mend Our Democracy (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 334)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Jayaprakash Narayan
items.why: It is where Amit first learned the stakes, and the conversation that led to this episode.

items.title: Jeff Bezos product & marketing
items.creator: Jeff Bezos
items.why: Bezos describes how, over his lifetime, the focus has shifted from marketing to product. Build something great and word of mouth spreads it.

items.title: Jensen Huang's fish-pond metaphor
items.creator: Jensen Huang
items.why: Huang wasn't trying to be a big fish in a small pond but to enlarge the pond, creating new markets instead of fighting over old ones.

items.title: Jerry Seinfeld on early naysayers
items.creator: Jerry Seinfeld
items.why: The source of the story about the brutal focus-group feedback on the 1989 Seinfeld pilot.

items.title: Jim Goetz on pain points
items.creator: Jim Goetz
items.why: Supports the idea of starting from a real problem rather than a hunt for a market.

items.title: Joan Didion's writing
items.creator: Joan Didion
items.why: Her line 'I don't know what I think until I write it down' sums up writing as a way of discovering your own thoughts. Amit calls the piece it comes from an amazing essay.

items.title: Johan Norberg's books and videos
items.creator: Johan Norberg
items.why: Norberg shows that Scandinavia grew rich through free markets and entrepreneurship first and added the welfare state only after becoming advanced economies. That order matters for anyone who wants to copy Sweden.

items.title: John Collison on passion
items.creator: John Collison
items.why: It blew Amit's mind. Almost everything good around us exists because someone tenaciously made it happen. He urges viewers to follow such accounts.

items.title: John Coltrane on desire
items.creator: John Coltrane
items.why: Amit's answer to people who say they lack the gear or resources to pursue what they love.

items.title: Jonathan Haidt's books on social media
items.creator: Jonathan Haidt
items.why: They lay out the research on the damage social media has done to society, especially to the mental health of young people and teenage girls. Ajay uses them to support his view that social media is a net negative.

items.title: Jonathan Haidt's episode on Brave New World
items.creator: Vasant Dhar
items.why: Haidt explains the studies linking social media to teenage depression, especially among girls.

items.title: Jonathan Ive on saying no to things you love
items.creator: Jonathan Ive
items.why: Ive recalls Jobs telling him, after Jobs returned to Apple, that you must learn to say no even to things you love and lose sleep over.

items.title: Jugalbandi: The BJP Before Modi
items.creator: Vinay Sitapati
items.why: Same enthusiasm for Sitapati's work as an interpreter of post-Independence political history.

items.title: Jungle Lore
items.creator: Jim Corbett
items.why: Completes his recommended Corbett sequence.

items.title: Jungleland
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: Stairway to Heaven starts with an alaap and builds. Jungleland runs in reverse: wall of sound, guitar solo, what Springsteen calls the world's greatest saxophone solo, a little saxophone-and-piano jazz, then the alaap at the end. Ajay thinks they nailed it. Compare the 1976 and 2012 versions.

items.title: Just (song and music video)
items.creator: Radiohead
items.why: There's so much more to Radiohead than Creep. 'Just' is also awesome, and its video is a masterpiece.

items.title: Karthik Muralidharan and the Bureaucrat's Burden (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 375)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Karthik Muralidharan
items.why: Gives Muralidharan's side of the debate, in which focusing on education was implied to be the route to development.

items.title: Karthik Muralidharan Examines the Indian State (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 290)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Karthik Muralidharan
items.why: These are where Amit first learned that India's 15 biggest states would each rank among the world's top 42 countries by population, and where they discuss India's tiny local-level spending.

items.title: Karthik Muralidharan's episodes on The Seen and the Unseen
items.creator: Amit Varma with Karthik Muralidharan
items.why: Amit calls him a brilliant economist doing amazing work who is clearly on that track.

items.title: Katadyn gravity-fed water filter
items.creator: Katadyn
items.why: You fill a six-litre bag and gravity pushes the water through a filter. He calls it a big gain that many Indian hikers are not yet using.

items.title: Kavitha Rao and Our Lady Doctors (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 235)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: The long-form conversation behind the book that introduced him to Haimabati.

items.title: Keeping India Safe (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 219)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Sushant Singh
items.why: It gives more background on Indian national security.

items.title: Kefir grain (Kefirwala)
items.why: Good for your health and fun to explore, even though its ideal 20°C fermentation temperature is hard to get in India.

items.title: Kevin Hale on marketing
items.creator: Kevin Hale
items.why: 'Marketing is a tax you pay for not making your product awesome' captures Amit's product-first philosophy.

items.title: Kevin Systrom on a bias for action
items.creator: Kevin Systrom
items.why: Systrom's biggest regret was Instagram's months-long private beta. His advice: put the product out there and refine it.

items.title: Kitaben Bahut Si (Baazigar)
items.creator: Zafar Gorakhpuri (lyricist)
items.why: Amit reads the lyrics, with mock seriousness, as an argument that bookish knowledge and credentials matter less than real, local knowledge, which is the theme of the episode.

items.title: Knowledge Lost and Knowledge Regained (Everything is Everything, Ep 63)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: It explains why being cut off from global trade and knowledge cripples a country: it is very hard to make a pencil, let alone an iPhone, on your own.

items.title: Kohrra
items.creator: Sudip Sharma
items.why: Amit calls it a marvellous series and was so impressed by Suvinder Vicky's lead performance that he wants him to play Montek.

items.title: Lady Doctors
items.creator: Kavitha Rao
items.why: He calls it a great book by an excellent writer, about 19th-century women doctors who were all remarkable, because a woman had to be remarkable even to become one.

items.title: Lancelot Pinto's tweet on respecting patients
items.creator: Lancelot Pinto
items.why: Patients know what they are going through better than anyone and are their own best advocates. Doctors should encourage them to read up instead of gaslighting them.

items.title: Las Meninas
items.creator: Diego Velázquez
items.why: Its depth, light, mirror and self-portrait of the painter make it more enigmatic than the Mona Lisa. It shaped Goya and Picasso, and seen in person it feels like you could walk into it.

items.title: Laughable Loves
items.creator: Milan Kundera
items.why: He calls it 'a great book' and 'magnificent'.

items.title: Lawrence Freedman's Substack newsletter
items.creator: Lawrence Freedman
items.why: Freedman has been writing prolifically on Substack for the past couple of years, 'and thank God for that.'

items.title: Layla
items.creator: Derek and the Dominos
items.why: Ajay insists on the original: 'Be sure to find the right version of it. Not the lame Eric Clapton unplugged version.' Amit says the unplugged version is very good too, but calls the original an absolute masterpiece.

items.title: Learning to Eat Soup with a Knife
items.creator: John Nagl
items.why: It sits in the counterinsurgency canon Amit worked through after Kaplan and Galula, which convinced him that this kind of war is mostly a political problem.

items.title: Led Zeppelin
items.creator: Led Zeppelin
items.why: His advice is to 'invest in great music.' The CD may now be worthless, but the music stays with you and shapes who you become.

items.title: Lenin's Tomb: The Last Days of the Soviet Empire
items.creator: David Remnick
items.why: It shows how a society struggles with an authoritarian state and how progress is damaged for a very long time. It is doubly interesting now because we know what Remnick didn't: Russia was headed back to hell under Putin.

items.title: Let It Be
items.creator: The Replacements
items.why: Amit calls it the best album named Let It Be, ahead of the Beatles. It's where the song Answering Machine comes from.

items.title: Letters to Chief Ministers
items.creator: Jawaharlal Nehru
items.why: They show a prime minister who wrote copiously and clearly. For Amit, that habit made Nehru a better thinker, and no modern politician of any party does it.

items.title: Letters to Olga
items.creator: Václav Havel
items.why: Amit calls it beautiful and quotes a line that sends a chill up his spine: 'If I am to be punished, let it be for who I am. If I am to be free, let it be as myself, not someone else's puppet.'

items.title: Life and labour of the people in London
items.creator: Charles Booth
items.why: A 17-year, multi-volume study that mixed surveys, interviews and observation so freely that you can't assign it to any one discipline. It is a model of the integrated social science the episode mourns.

items.title: Life Lessons (Scorsese segment of New York Stories)
items.creator: Martin Scorsese
items.why: Amit calls Scorsese's short a masterpiece whose scenes still play in his head. It inspired the name of their course. It is also where he first heard Procol Harum's 'A Whiter Shade of Pale', over a slow-motion shot of a falling cigarette: 'the magic of film editing'. Even many Scorsese fans have missed it.

items.title: Life's Grandeur: The Spread of Excellence From Plato to Darwin
items.creator: Stephen Jay Gould
items.why: He calls it brilliant on how baseball keeps adjusting its rules to keep the game balanced. That is a kind of central planning that works only because a game, unlike the real world, has bounded complexity.

items.title: Lifespan: Why We Age – and Why We Don't Have To
items.creator: David Sinclair
items.why: Amit calls it a great book on the case that we can live healthy, active lives past a hundred rather than decline into decades of dementia.

items.title: LifeStraw bottle
items.creator: LifeStraw
items.why: You can fill it with any bad water, and sucking pushes it through a filter. Ajay says the output is cleaner than any tap water in India.

items.title: Like a Rolling Stone: Bob Dylan at the Crossroads
items.creator: Greil Marcus
items.why: Amit calls Marcus a genius music writer whose phrases capture what listeners feel but can't articulate.

items.title: Lincoln
items.creator: Steven Spielberg
items.why: An eye-opener for Ajay. It skips Gettysburg and the war and stays on the legal battle to pass the 13th Amendment, and he finds it great storytelling.

items.title: Listen, The Internet Has SPACE
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: It makes the point he states on air: the old page and binding limits no longer apply, so today an author could simply put the rest online.

items.title: Live Chess Ratings (2700chess.com)
items.why: Tracks the top players' live ratings, where Arjun reached world number two.

items.title: Long As I Can See The Light
items.creator: Chris Cornell
items.why: A musical wink that fits an episode literally recorded until the daylight ran out.

items.title: Looking beyond the label 'algorithmic trading'
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Expands his argument that algorithms are human ideas carried out by code acting as a clerk, and that the hostility to algo trading comes from ignorance.

items.title: Lord of the Flies
items.creator: William Golding
items.why: Ajay spent his life worrying about 1984, but feels we have stumbled into Lord of the Flies instead. The social media dystopia is people bullying and tormenting each other, and 'you don't even need the state to make you miserable.'

items.title: Los Caprichos (especially The Dream of Reason Produces Monsters)
items.creator: Francisco Goya
items.why: They are dark, socially piercing work, and The Dream of Reason Produces Monsters is perhaps Amit's favourite single Goya work.

items.title: Lost a shock absorber
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Further reading from Ajay alongside this episode on monetary policy.

items.title: Louie
items.creator: Louis CK
items.why: Amit calls it a great show, and the bit perfectly names his pizza-plus-biryani binges.

items.title: Ludwig von Mises – A Primer
items.creator: Eamonn Butler
items.why: A short, clear, free introduction to Mises from a writer Amit rates highly.

items.title: Luke Burgis Sees the Deer at His Window (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 337)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: A fuller treatment of mimetic desire and why some wants are borrowed.

items.title: Lunapark
items.creator: Luna
items.why: He calls it a great album from a band he loved.

items.title: Luxury Beliefs are Status Symbols
items.creator: Rob Henderson
items.why: Gives the original framing: beliefs that confer status on the upper class while inflicting costs on the lower classes.

items.title: Lynk's tweet on crackheads
items.creator: Lynk
items.why: Crackheads never say they are too broke to smoke tonight. They get up and make it happen. If you want something badly enough, you find a way.

items.title: Machines of Loving Grace
items.creator: Dario Amodei
items.why: Ajay is no 'rah-rah' booster of tech paradises, but he finds this essay sensible and thoughtful about what happens as AI progresses, and says everyone should read it.

items.title: Magnus Carlsen on getting his way
items.creator: Take Take Take
items.why: Here he says there are 'no grown-ups in FIDE' and that Anand is not up for his job, the behaviour Amit calls deplorable.

items.title: Magnus Carlsen on Jeansgate
items.creator: Take Take Take
items.why: Carlsen says he refused to change 'on principle' and lashes out at FIDE.

items.title: Magnus Carlsen Ranks The Candidates Players
items.creator: Magnus Carlsen
items.why: Amit felt Carlsen broadly got it right but missed that some players, Gukesh among them, had high ceilings and high variance. It is a useful backdrop to Gukesh's run.

items.title: Magnus Carlsen's interview on Take Take Take about Freestyle Chess
items.creator: Take Take Take
items.why: Carlsen explains why he sees freestyle (Chess960) as the most alive form of chess now.

items.title: Main Aai Hoon U.P. Bihar Lootne (Shool)
items.why: A joking nod to region-specific strategy. Amit admits it's 'not quite' hyperlocal but 'a step in the right direction'.

items.title: make
items.why: Another good tool for automating your own work. Ajay tells viewers to look it up.

items.title: Make Me a Canteen for My Soul (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 304)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Sameer Seth and Yash Bhanage
items.why: About preserving food heritage through memories and stories. Amit recalls Bombay Canteen asking people to send in their grandmothers' recipes and serving them as a day's menu.

items.title: Making it Less Random
items.creator: Lapham's Quarterly
items.why: Covers how a product had to be engineered to match people's faulty intuitions about randomness.

items.title: Making Policy Fun with Khyati Pathak and Friends (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 374)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Khyati Pathak, Anupam Manur and Pranay Kotasthane
items.why: A conversation with Takshashila friends that includes Anupam Manur's case for pricing water, the same logic this episode applies to electricity.

items.title: Making Regulation in India Work Better
items.creator: KP Krishnan
items.why: A talk on fixing Indian regulation by the official who started the FSLRC project.

items.title: Making the way for nuclear energy in India
items.creator: Akshay Jaitly and Ajay Shah
items.why: Amit calls it fantastic and 'most excellent reading'. It is the full written version of the policy case made in the episode.

items.title: Malayalam and Marathi cinema
items.why: With the mainstream crumbling and the means of production available to everyone, the exciting action is in world and indie cinema, not standard commercial fare. In India, he says, you should be watching a lot of Malayalam and Marathi films.

items.title: MAMI Film Festival
items.why: It is his annual vacation: four films a day for about ten days. He counts living in Mumbai near its theatres as a lucky boost to his own surface area of serendipity, and says it reminds him how good world cinema is today.

items.title: Man's Search for Meaning
items.creator: Viktor Frankl
items.why: Frankl records that for concentration-camp inmates, literature, whether held, remembered or discussed, gave solace and a sense that the present moment is not all there is.

items.title: Man-eaters of Kumaon
items.creator: Jim Corbett
items.why: Part of the reading that made mountains and forests seem like 'the greatest thing in the world' to him. He calls Corbett's three best books 'really wonderful' and says everybody will enjoy them.

items.title: Manifold Destiny
items.creator: Sylvia Nasar and David Gruber
items.why: Further reading on Perelman, the mathematician who refused both journals and the million-dollar prize.

items.title: Manmohan Singh's PhD thesis
items.creator: Manmohan Singh
items.why: One of the first works to challenge India's 'export pessimism'. It argued that exporting depends on incentives, prices and exchange rates, not on anything peculiar to India.

items.title: Marc Andreeson on early naysayers
items.creator: Marc Andreessen
items.why: Andreeson explains how innovations we now take for granted, like the telephone, were first seen as curiosities that would never go mainstream.

items.title: Marginal Revolution University
items.creator: Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok
items.why: Amit calls it the best way to understand concepts like the price system and opportunity cost clearly. The videos are essentially recorded PowerPoints with no fancy production, and the knowledge is brilliant.

items.title: Marginlands: Indian Landscapes on the Brink
items.creator: Arati Kumar-Rao
items.why: It is a companion to the lived, land-based way of seeing geography that Amit holds up against lines on maps.

items.title: Mark Zuckerberg on Peter Thiel's advice
items.creator: Mark Zuckerberg
items.why: Zuckerberg names Thiel's line as the best advice he got: in a rapidly changing world, the biggest risk is not changing. That matters more than ever in an age of AI and automation.

items.title: Massacre in Korea
items.creator: Pablo Picasso
items.why: Critics don't rate it, but Amit calls it a masterpiece. You can see Goya's influence 'stolen' and made Picasso's own.

items.title: Matthew Walker's episode on the Huberman Lab podcast
items.creator: Andrew Huberman
items.why: In it, Walker explains the importance of sleep.

items.title: Maya C Popa's tweet quoting William Faulkner, and her Twitter feed
items.creator: Maya C Popa
items.why: Amit calls her a poet and a fine poetry editor whose feed is 'awesome'. The line spoke to him because good work requires breaking from conventional thinking.

items.title: Mayabono Biharini (from BEDROOM)
items.creator: Somlata
items.why: Rabindrasangeet breaking out of genre boundaries: Tagore's music doing what living culture should.

items.title: Mera Joota Hai Japani
items.why: He introduces it, playfully, as 'a famous song that is about the glory of globalization'.

items.title: Messy
items.creator: Tim Harford
items.why: It makes the case for embracing mess. Being pushed out of your comfort zone, and juggling several projects at once (it cites research by Howard Gruber and Sara Davis), is where creativity comes from.

items.title: Michael Pettis interviewed by Forward Guidance
items.creator: Forward Guidance (with Michael Pettis)
items.why: Pettis lives in China and, in Ajay's words, gets this stuff deeply. The interview is 'absolutely eye opening' on Chinese macroeconomics, the collapse of the China model, overproduction, and the global protectionism against China.

items.title: Michael's response to Dwarkesh Patel
items.creator: Michael
items.why: It argues that to an LLM a novel discovery is indistinguishable from an error. Amit thinks this holds a grain of truth, though AI isn't only LLMs.

items.title: Mike Moritz on Bill Gates's car radio
items.creator: Mike Moritz
items.why: Gates removed his car radio so he could think about Microsoft. It is a vivid picture of founder obsession.

items.title: Milestone
items.creator: Ivan Ayr
items.why: The film where Suvinder Vicky first impressed Danish Husain, backing up Amit's casting choice.

items.title: Miller's Pyramid
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Part of the set of columns he points readers to for depth beyond the presentation.

items.title: Milton Friedman: A Concise Guide to the Ideas and Influence of the Free-Market Economist
items.creator: Eamonn Butler
items.why: A concise introduction to Friedman's ideas for anyone curious about free-market thinking.

items.title: Missing In Action
items.creator: Pranay Kotasthane and Raghu S Jaitley
items.why: A great book on the Indian state by friends of the show, worth reading even if, like Amit, you think markets belong inside society rather than as a third pillar.

items.title: Modern Principles of Microeconomics
items.creator: Alex Tabarrok and Tyler Cowen
items.why: It contains the line 'a price is a signal wrapped in an incentive', which Amit says almost sums up Hayek's essay.

items.title: Modern Times
items.creator: Charlie Chaplin
items.why: The film captures the mental image most people carry when they hear 'economic development'. The episode then examines and questions that image.

items.title: Mohak Mangal's YouTube channel
items.creator: Mohak Mangal
items.why: Amit says he works hard and does a pretty good job of the sense-making function.

items.title: Mohit Satyanand's newsletter
items.creator: Mohit Satyanand
items.why: About three years without missing a Sunday. Amit is very proud of him.

items.title: Monetary policy is easy; Financial regulation is hard
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: It is the original statement of the episode's central worked example: two 'central bank' jobs that differ sharply in difficulty.

items.title: Monkey Cuisine
items.creator: BBC Earth
items.why: Documents non-human culture: an idea, not instinct, spreading from one female to her band and then to other bands.

items.title: More Ammo: Improving Resilience Against Extreme Surges in Demand
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: It proposes option-style defence contracts, for example 100 units a month with the right but not the obligation to go to 300. That builds surge capacity into peacetime procurement instead of scrambling once war arrives.

items.title: Morgan Brown's tweet on DeepSeek
items.creator: Morgan Brown
items.why: Its line, 'Incumbents optimize existing processes while disruptors rethink the fundamental approach', is the episode's thesis in one sentence.

items.title: Morgan Housel's tweet quoting Montesquieu on happiness
items.creator: Morgan Housel
items.why: A sharp diagnosis of envy, more relevant than ever now that social media pits our real lives against other people's curated ones.

items.title: Morgan Housel's writing on money
items.creator: Morgan Housel
items.why: He is a writer on money whom Amit considers essential reading.

items.title: Mosquitoes As Big As A Bus
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: A light companion to the episode's point that Indian problems, mosquitoes included, are intensely local.

items.title: Motivations for capital controls and their effectiveness
items.creator: Radhika Pandey, Gurnain K Pasricha, Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
items.why: Relevant to his argument that restricting firms' access to foreign capital is as silly as restricting their access to imported coal.

items.title: Murali Neelakantan Looks at the World (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 329)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Murali Neelakantan
items.why: This is where Murali explained why perjury ends a lawyer's career in England but is expected in India.

items.title: Murder in Mahim
items.creator: Jerry Pinto
items.why: He calls it a beautiful crime thriller.

items.title: Mutual funds with feet of clay
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Lays out a feedback loop: large corporate bond fund redemptions hit an illiquid bond market, prices and NAVs fall, and that triggers more redemptions.

items.title: My Hero, Oppenheimer (Everything is Everything, Ep 5)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Fuller background on Oppenheimer, the episode's prime example of a misfit who flourished once he was among peers of his calibre.

items.title: My Life and Struggle
items.creator: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan
items.why: Amit calls it a great autobiography. It shows a period when the finest minds were in jail rather than in universities, and how those encounters shaped Bacha Khan.

items.title: Nannari root (Amrutmul, Hemidesmus indicus)
items.why: It gives a novel, unique flavour with hints of cardamom and camphor that most masala-chai lovers north of Karnataka have never tried.

items.title: Narrative and Numbers
items.creator: Aswath Damodaran
items.why: Amit says it makes a profound point that goes beyond valuation, into what firms are about and the stories they tell themselves. It is also a beautiful story of intellectual humility.

items.title: Narrative Economics
items.creator: Robert Shiller
items.why: Amit's example of the growing recognition that numbers don't tell the full story and that the narratives people hold matter.

items.title: Nashville
items.creator: Robert Altman
items.why: It is one of his favourite films of all time, and he calls it 'just a masterpiece'.

items.title: National Development Delivers: And How! And How?
items.creator: Lant Pritchett
items.why: Amit says Pritchett's papers are eye-opening and seminal because they are built on hard data and look at outcomes.

items.title: Naturalistic Fallacy
items.creator: Wikipedia
items.why: G. E. Moore's fallacy of equating 'natural' with 'good' was once used by bigots against homosexuality. Something being natural makes it neither good nor bad.

items.title: Naval Ravikant on co-founder qualities
items.creator: Naval Ravikant
items.why: Look for high intelligence, high energy and high integrity, and integrity matters most by far.

items.title: Naval Ravikant on networking
items.creator: Naval Ravikant
items.why: Networking is personal marketing. Do great work and your network forms around you, which matches Amit's experience with his podcasts.

items.title: Naval Ravikant: 'The future will be almost all startups'
items.creator: Naval Ravikant
items.why: Naval predicts most companies will be small startups of four or ten people that can scale to a billion dollars, a future that rewards nimble, entrepreneurial people.

items.title: Never Mind the Bullocks, Here's the Lamborghini
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Part of Amit's decade-long, often ignored campaign arguing that T20 had fundamentally changed how the game should be played.

items.title: Never normalize anything or take the world for granted
items.why: Inflation targeting is a rare, elegant piece of good legislation, and gains like that are always under threat. Keep questioning and protect the little good that has been achieved.

items.title: New work on district courts in Kerala
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: He sees it as the first time India is getting serious process improvements in the judiciary. Contract enforcement is what complex manufacturing depends on.

items.title: New York
items.creator: Lou Reed
items.why: Where to start with Lou Reed. He calls it a masterpiece.

items.title: Newton, the Man
items.creator: John Maynard Keynes
items.why: It is the source of the 'last of the magicians' view of Newton, showing the alchemist and Bible scholar behind the rational front.

items.title: Nightfall
items.creator: Isaac Asimov
items.why: He says nothing more because anything more would be a spoiler.

items.title: NighttimeLights.jl (xKDR's nighttime lights data and code on GitHub)
items.creator: xKDR Forum
items.why: Anyone can apply the bias corrections, change parameters and experiment with the data themselves. Amit calls this the 'spirit of inquiry'.

items.title: Nina Teicholz on The Joe Rogan Experience
items.creator: Joe Rogan, Nina Teicholz
items.why: An accessible entry point to Teicholz's case for readers not ready for the book.

items.title: No Surprises
items.creator: Radiohead
items.why: He loves the original as much as the cover, which he calls 'one of those schizophrenic things in my head'.

items.title: No Surprises (Regina Spektor cover)
items.creator: Regina Spektor
items.why: He calls it a beautiful cover he absolutely loves, on a par with the original.

items.title: Nonstop Dan on Air India
items.creator: Nonstop Dan
items.why: It is a live example of a crew lying about a missing special meal instead of owning the mistake.

items.title: Not Dark Yet
items.creator: Bob Dylan
items.why: 'It's not dark yet, but it's getting there' is an ageing artist facing mortality and turning it into art.

items.title: Not Waving but Drowning
items.creator: Stevie Smith
items.why: One of Amit's favourite poems. It is about a man whose lifelong distress was mistaken for waving, which mirrors his drowning IIT aspirant.

items.title: Notion
items.why: He thinks it's a great productivity tool, though he hasn't really started using it. Roam suited his wish for a loosely organised knowledge system better.

items.title: Novels of Georges Simenon
items.creator: Georges Simenon
items.why: Amit says Simenon's work keeps returning to the idea that no person can fully communicate himself to another, which he sees as one of humanity's great problems.

items.title: November Rain
items.creator: Guns N' Roses
items.why: A 1992 song that marks where his musical sense of 'recent' had stopped.

items.title: Nowhere Near
items.creator: Yo La Tengo
items.why: He calls it a beautiful song and one of the great love songs.

items.title: Numerical Methods for Scientists and Engineers
items.creator: Richard Hamming
items.why: It is by one of Bell Labs' great figures, the man Amit quotes as saying that the purpose of computing is insight, not numbers.

items.title: Nuno Bettencourt interviewed by Rick Beato
items.creator: Rick Beato
items.why: Makes the case that AC/DC's simple wall of sound is ideal for arenas, a reminder to judge music against its circumstances.

items.title: Objects From Our Past (Everything is Everything, Ep 77)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: It was his idea, and he says it's an episode he 'absolutely' loves.

items.title: Observations on International Labor Standards and Trade
items.creator: Alan B Krueger
items.why: Calls it another great study on the economics of child labour.

items.title: Obsidian
items.why: It is easy to run locally on Linux and stores notes as plain Markdown files, so the whole Unix toolchain can work on them.

items.title: Odati
items.why: Ajay has gone with them on many of his trips and likes their work a lot.

items.title: Ode to Kirihito
items.creator: Osamu Tezuka
items.why: One of the most powerful graphic novels he has read: an odyssey into the human condition and the moral decay circumstances can bring. Tezuka wrote it after being inspired by his admirer Tatsumi's gekiga movement.

items.title: Offshore wind in Tamil Nadu: from potential to reality
items.creator: Akshay Jaitly, Charmi Mehta, Renuka Sane and Ajay Shah
items.why: The detailed case behind Ajay's claim that Tamil Nadu must build the policy capability to unlock offshore wind.

items.title: On Diversification by Firms
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Background on the conventional paths of firm expansion that the three great leaps break from.

items.title: On Fire
items.creator: Galaxie 500
items.why: He calls it a brilliant album you've got to listen to, an old love finally found.

items.title: On Inequality
items.creator: Harry Frankfurt
items.why: A slim, great book that sets out the 'doctrine of sufficiency': define what is enough to live on and get everyone there. A philosopher's case for why that matters more than equality.

items.title: On PLI: Many roads lead to a sound GST
items.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
items.why: The written version of Ajay's argument that PLI patches indirect-tax mistakes that should instead be fixed at the root.

items.title: On the Mechanics of Economic Development
items.creator: Robert E Lucas
items.why: He calls it 'a beautiful paper'. Its key line is that once you start thinking about this question, it's hard to think about anything else.

items.title: On the Natural History of Destruction
items.creator: WG Sebald
items.why: A masterpiece with many pages on Dresden. Sebald's mix of old black-and-white photographs and text inspires how Amit thinks about making video essays.

items.title: On the Rise of FinTechs: Credit Scoring Using Digital Footprints
items.creator: Tobias Berg, Valentin Burg, Ana Gombović and Manju Puri
items.why: Shows that digital footprints predict default: iPhone vs Android, email provider, typos in email addresses, and late-night shopping.

items.title: Once in a Lifetime
items.creator: Talking Heads
items.why: It completely blew him away and led him to decades of David Byrne's music.

items.title: One Bad Law Goes, but Women Remain Second-Class Citizens
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's 2018 column on the now-scrapped adultery law, which treated a wife as her husband's property, and on other IPC provisions that still do.

items.title: One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich
items.creator: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn
items.why: Ajay calls it 'answer one' to the question of whether socialism works. The satellite image of the Korean peninsula is answer two.

items.title: Only Happy When It Rains
items.creator: Garbage
items.why: A fitting rain song for the moment.

items.title: Only the Paranoid Survive
items.creator: Andy Grove
items.why: Grove describes Intel's move from a crowded memory-chip market to going all in, which is why it's useful for anyone torn between too many product lines.

items.title: OpenStreetMap (OSM)
items.why: It is the true digital public good: public domain, free to download, non-rival and non-excludable, and anyone can contribute. Indian volunteers hold OSM mapping parties.

items.title: Oppenheimer
items.creator: Christopher Nolan
items.why: Amit admires Nolan for bringing artistic, intimate sensibility to big-screen spectacle. Nolan left Warner Brothers for Universal because Warner was releasing films on HBO Max at the same time as in theatres. Ajay is anxious that the film may reduce Oppenheimer to caricature.

items.title: Oppenheimer, Nullified and Vindicated
items.creator: Kai Bird
items.why: It tells how archival digging led the US government to admit it had wronged Oppenheimer.

items.title: Opportunity, Choice and the IPL
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit is proud of it for predicting, before the fact, that the IPL would revolutionise cricket, rescue Test cricket, and create competition for talent despite the BCCI being a monopsony.

items.title: Org Mode
items.why: It does much of what Amit demoed in Roam and is very powerful. Its one gap is a shared, networked file for collaborators, so it is best for solo work.

items.title: Orienting
items.creator: Pallavi Aiyar
items.why: A travelogue that reads like a beautiful essay, by a 'spectacularly good writer'.

items.title: OSI: The Internet That Wasn't
items.creator: Andrew Russell
items.why: Background history of how a top-down networking standard lost to the bottom-up internet.

items.title: Our FSI Problem (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 11)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Alex Tabarrok
items.why: The source of Tabarrok's line that Bombay reclaims the sea when it should be reclaiming the sky. FSI limits leave enormous value unused.

items.title: Outliers
items.creator: Malcolm Gladwell
items.why: Where Amit learned the research on elite athletes being born early in the year, a vivid case of a trivial-looking distribution with real effects.

items.title: Outlive: The Science and Art of Longevity
items.creator: Peter Attia
items.why: More reading on the episode's idea that much longer, healthier lives are possible.

items.title: Pallavi Aiyar Has Seen the World (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 351)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: A long conversation with the author of Orienting.

items.title: Pandit's Mind (1951 Time magazine cover story on Nehru)
items.creator: Time magazine
items.why: A vivid portrait of how Fabian socialism and Brahminical contempt for the 'Banya' shaped Nehru's distrust of capitalism.

items.title: Pandoc
items.why: He calls it a Swiss Army knife that converts any file format to any other from the command line, and it can be wrapped into your own automated commands.

items.title: Paper Thin Hotel
items.creator: Greg Dulli
items.why: He calls it 'an absolute masterpiece'.

items.title: Parade's End
items.creator: Ford Madox Ford
items.why: The passage argues that real intimate conversation needs years of living together. Amit's response: 'Beautiful. You have a romantic soul in you.'

items.title: Paradise Lost
items.creator: John Milton
items.why: To see where Frankenstein's central question, a creature confronting its creator, comes from.

items.title: Parkinson's Law
items.creator: C Northcote Parkinson
items.why: Amit calls it a classic book of comedy that is also a public choice book. It covers how work expands to fill the time available, how officials multiply subordinates rather than rivals, and how they grow budgets and turf.

items.title: Party
items.creator: Govind Nihalani
items.why: Amit holds it up as a landmark of Nihalani's career.

items.title: Passports Were a 'Temporary' War Measure
items.creator: Speranta Dumitru
items.why: Covers the history behind his point that passports and controls on movement began as wartime measures and were never rolled back.

items.title: Pather Panchali
items.creator: Satyajit Ray
items.why: Amit puts it among the greatest debut films ever made.

items.title: Patrick Collison on Stripe's mission
items.creator: Patrick Collison
items.why: 'Increase the GDP of the internet' is another mission bigger than the company itself.

items.title: Paul
items.creator: Big Thief
items.why: A self-described old fogey whose music is 'all ancient', he is amazed to have found a song from as recently as 2016 that he absolutely loves.

items.title: Paul Graham on compressing your working life
items.creator: Paul Graham
items.why: Graham's frame: instead of working at low intensity for forty years, work at high intensity for four and give it everything.

items.title: Paul Graham on hiring
items.creator: Paul Graham
items.why: Ten random rowers make an average boat; the ten best make a much faster one.

items.title: Paul Graham on talent
items.creator: Paul Graham
items.why: A sharp answer to today's xenophobia and anti-immigrant sentiment.

items.title: Paul Graham says, Just Learn
items.creator: Paul Graham
items.why: Start by learning and gaining domain expertise, and projects worth building will emerge from it.

items.title: Pearl Jam's live and bootleg albums
items.creator: Pearl Jam
items.why: In the late '90s and early 2000s they gave Amit the same joy as Springsteen's live recordings: 'all of their live albums are just so incredible'.

items.title: Pedestrianism
items.creator: Matthew Algeo
items.why: It is a vivid case of a pastime loved for itself being turned into a competitive spectacle and turning ugly.

items.title: Penelope Fitzgerald's novels
items.creator: Penelope Fitzgerald
items.why: She wrote her first novel after 60, so 'there is time for you to be a novelist'.

items.title: Peppa Pig
items.why: Amit's tongue-in-cheek promise to introduce Ajay to 'that magic'.

items.title: Perplexity (Pro)
items.creator: Perplexity
items.why: A 'mind blowing' learning tool: it answers better than search or Wikipedia and nudges you towards the right questions and down rewarding rabbit holes.

items.title: Perseverance and Adaptation: Ukraine's Counteroffensive at Three Months
items.creator: Michael Kofman and Rob Lee (War on the Rocks)
items.why: A three-month assessment of how the counteroffensive is going.

items.title: Persuasion
items.creator: Yascha Mounk
items.why: It shows independent creators building serious publications outside mainstream media.

items.title: Perun (YouTube channel)
items.creator: Perun
items.why: Perun is a model sense-maker. He goes deep, lays out all the data and viewpoints, writes excellent show notes, claims no false certainty, and was Amit's guide to the Russia-Ukraine war.

items.title: Peter Leko and Judit Polgar on Gukesh's heart rate
items.creator: Peter Leko and Judit Polgar
items.why: A vivid example of composure under pressure made visible.

items.title: Peter Thiel on working on problems that wouldn't get solved without you
items.creator: Peter Thiel
items.why: Amit reads it as a filter for scarce time: do what wouldn't exist if you didn't do it, at any scale, not just Mars missions.

items.title: Peter Thiel says trends are overrated
items.creator: Peter Thiel
items.why: Thiel treats buzzwords in a pitch as a red flag. A genuinely new idea doesn't need a buzzword, and often no buzzword fits it.

items.title: Peyman Milanfar's tweet on reading old work
items.creator: Peyman Milanfar
items.why: Ajay agreed at once, since computer science keeps reinventing the same things badly. Amit added that understanding how a field developed gives you depth, even where the old work is now obsolete.

items.title: Peyman Milanfar's tweet quoting Max Weber: 'I am not a donkey, I don't have a field.'
items.creator: Peyman Milanfar
items.why: A one-line rebuke of academic silos, where someone can spend ten years on wheat production in 1853 Arizona and never see the bigger picture.

items.title: Picasso's Las Meninas series
items.creator: Pablo Picasso
items.why: Seen in chronological order, they show an old master playing and growing day by day. Amit advises walking them in date order, unlike the visitors he saw rushing past backwards.

items.title: Pick up a musical instrument
items.why: If you have even two percent of the willpower, do it. It changes your life and your mind, and can give you the concentration and meditation that are otherwise hard to find.

items.title: Pico Iyer's tweet quoting Rousseau on wisdom
items.creator: Pico Iyer
items.why: The episode's closing lesson in curation, which Amit immediately turned on Ajay.

items.title: PISA
items.creator: OECD
items.why: It tests a household-based random sample of 15-year-olds, not just those in school, on applying science and maths rather than rote memory. You need a rough sense of its scores to take part in any serious education debate.

items.title: Planners vs. Searchers in Foreign Aid
items.creator: William Easterly
items.why: It frames the key contrast: planners impose top-down answers, while searchers find solutions by trial, error and feedback. Amit says poverty has only ever been ended by searchers.

items.title: Planning Democracy
items.creator: Nikhil Menon
items.why: It is full of vivid portraits and strange history from India's planning era. Amit says 'everyone should buy it'.

items.title: Plato (or Why Philosophy Matters) (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 109)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: It is the source of his point that early philosophers were essentially scientists who inquired into everything, before subjects split off and got labelled.

items.title: Playboy Stories: The Best of Forty Years of Short Fiction
items.creator: Edited by Alice K. Turner
items.why: Evidence that Playboy published the world's best short-story writers. It's where Amit first read Murakami, alongside Updike, Cheever and Nabokov.

items.title: Playwright at the Centre
items.creator: Shanta Gokhale
items.why: Amit calls it a great book on the history of Marathi theatre. Their conversation never even reached the subject.

items.title: Polina Pompliano quoting Brene Brown on normalcy
items.creator: Brene Brown (via Polina Pompliano)
items.why: Amit finds it beautiful and lives it: a blocked nostril, or a walk he couldn't take before his heart attack, reminds him to value normalcy.

items.title: Political Order and Political Decay
items.creator: Francis Fukuyama
items.why: It completes Fukuyama's history of the state's evolution and helps you see the state-society relationship more clearly.

items.title: Politics (limerick)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: It captures the link between money and power in five lines.

items.title: Politics as a Vocation
items.creator: Max Weber
items.why: Ajay calls it one of the great books of the world and says everybody should read it.

items.title: Polls get elections wrong. So use Google
items.creator: Seth Stephens-Davidowitz
items.why: It shows search data beating polls: the word order 'Trump Harris debate' versus 'Harris Trump debate' tracked which candidate won each state.

items.title: Possible, Plausible and Probable: Big markets and Networking effects
items.creator: Aswath Damodaran
items.why: Damodaran openly conceded that Gurley was right and redid his valuation based on the new story. Amit holds this up as a model of intellectual honesty.

items.title: Postwar
items.creator: Tony Judt
items.why: Amit calls it a masterpiece on post-war Europe and its recovery.

items.title: Power and Discourse in Policy Diffusion: Anti-Money Laundering in Developing States
items.creator: JC Sharman
items.why: About how anti-money-laundering rules spread to developing countries, which is the theme of his 'don't take blindly from the USA' argument.

items.title: Pranay Kotasthane's post on plasma and organ sales
items.creator: Pranay Kotasthane
items.why: Pranay lays out the economic logic for allowing sales and how it works in other parts of the world. Amit thinks the topic deserves a whole episode.

items.title: Prem Throws Your Heart to the Ground
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: It leads into his question of whether urban, thing-filled living estranges us from something essential.

items.title: Price controls for vaccines?
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: It applies the episode's argument against well-meant coercion directly to vaccine pricing during COVID.

items.title: Price Theory
items.creator: Milton Friedman
items.why: Some things were done right by the old masters, and the best way to understand prices is to go back and study them.

items.title: Pritika Hingorani Wants to Fix Our Cities (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 361)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Background on the urban governance knowledge that Ajay says can carry straight over to Himalayan towns.

items.title: Privacy 3.0
items.creator: Rahul Matthan
items.why: A book-length treatment of the privacy ideas Amit draws on in this episode.

items.title: Private Education Is Good for the Poor
items.creator: James Tooley and Pauline Dixon
items.why: Their Hyderabad study found many slum dwellers chose to pay for budget private schools over free government ones.

items.title: Probal DasGupta Goes to the Himalayas With Books in His Bag (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 412)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit discussed in detail with the military historian the tension between obeying orders and using local discretion.

items.title: Professional cycling as a sport to follow
items.why: It gives all the drama and stories of sport for far less time than cricket. Even a T20 game eats hours, and the IPL eats two months of evenings.

items.title: Promenade
items.creator: U2
items.why: The second of his two picks from the album.

items.title: Public Choice Theory (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 121)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: A companion for listeners who want more on public choice theory.

items.title: Public Policy courses at Takshashila
items.creator: Takshashila Institution
items.why: Shubham, a policy-curious young Himachali who inspired the episode, came through this course.

items.title: Publish and Perish
items.creator: Agnes Callard
items.why: Callard uses an economist's tool, incentives, to explain turgid academic writing. Tenure needs publications in particular journals, and those journals reward their conventions and the fashions of the day. Amit calls Callard the best kind of intellectual because she is always engaging with people on Twitter.

items.title: Punish Rioters, Not Writers
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: The title sums up the principle Amit argues in the episode: punish the violent act, not the words.

items.title: Quizzing is Not Just a Trivial Pursuit
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: It sets out his view that good quiz questions are ones you can work out, not ones you either know or don't.

items.title: Racing in the Street
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: It starts as a young-man-and-cars song about illegal street racing. Halfway through it turns into a psychological dive into a deeply sad person. 'You never saw it coming.'

items.title: Raju Ban Gaya Gentleman
items.creator: Aziz Mirza
items.why: Amit says he just likes the title: Raju wants to be a gentleman, and Indian firms want to be global firms.

items.title: Ramki and the Ocean of Stories (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 415)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: It is the conversation behind the shared verdict that Perfect Days could only be made by an older filmmaker.

items.title: Ranbir Kapoor's dialogue from Rocket Singh: Salesman of the Year
items.why: Introduced with the line 'Bollywood has done interquartile range. Watch.'

items.title: Ranjit Hoskote is Dancing in Chains (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 363)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: The poet Ranjit Hoskote gave Amit the phrase 'dancing in chains': we all live within constraints and dance as best we can.

items.title: Rashomon
items.creator: Akira Kurosawa
items.why: The same event is told from several points of view, each credible. It shows that perception depends on the perceiver, not that only one witness is telling the truth.

items.title: Raspberry Pi 4
items.why: Ajay calls it the best bang for the buck and says it's a delight. You boot Linux on it and tinker cheaply, for example to measure outdoor temperature, water plants or drive art installations.

items.title: Ravikant on working like a lion
items.creator: Naval Ravikant
items.why: Lions rest most of the time and then sprint. It helped Amit accept his own burst-driven way of working.

items.title: Raw Umber
items.creator: Sara Rai
items.why: He calls her a brilliant writer and this a great book of essays.

items.title: RBI's proposal for a Public Credit Registry
items.creator: Prasanth Regy
items.why: A related example of a state-run database proposed for finance, relevant to the episode's worries about state legibility.

items.title: Reading Like a Writer
items.creator: Francine Prose
items.why: Teaches you to notice the author's tools, such as why one word and not another, and how sentence length builds rhythm or immersion. Amit says this enriches reading even if you never write.

items.title: Reading Lolita in Tehran
items.creator: Azar Nafisi
items.why: Nafisi's point, that liberal values are voiced most truly by dissenters in Iran, shows what gets lost when free societies take liberty for granted.

items.title: Rebel Sultans
items.creator: Manu Pillai
items.why: Elaborates on the cultural mixing of the period, such as Hindu generals serving Mughal emperors and Muslim mercenaries fighting on the other side.

items.title: Recent columns on India's response to the tariffs
items.creator: Sajjid Z Chinoy, Soham Das, TN Ninan, M Govinda Rao, Rajeswari Sengupta, Mihir S Sharma
items.why: He respects and values their work as part of 'one communal sense of knowledge' India is building on this question.

items.title: Red Dead Redemption 2
items.creator: Rockstar Games
items.why: It is a slow, peaceful game with a thick story, history it gets right, thick characters, well-written dialogue and strong acting. It puts you among some twenty people running from the law and makes you decide what's right and wrong. Vaishnav cried at the end and learned from it.

items.title: Reflections on Gandhi
items.creator: George Orwell
items.why: It shows what a beautiful writer and thinker Orwell was: sceptical of sainthood yet fair, and alert to the shrewd, able person inside Gandhi.

items.title: Reflections on the Revolution in France
items.creator: Edmund Burke
items.why: The founding text for the idea that means matter. Burke accepts the revolutionaries' ideals but warns that you cannot burn institutions to the ground and expect good outcomes.

items.title: Reforming Development Economics (Ideas of India)
items.creator: Lant Pritchett and Shruti Rajagopalan
items.why: A companion to the 'went wrong' episode, for listeners who want Pritchett's case at length.

items.title: Reforms of prosecution in the Indian criminal justice system
items.creator: Smriti Parsheera
items.why: Ajay calls it a very nice article on the problems of prosecution in India.

items.title: Regulation: A Primer
items.creator: Susan Dudley and Jerry Brito
items.why: Amit calls it a wonderful book. It is mostly about how regulation works in America, but the first and last chapters cover the general theory of regulation. It overlaps with what Ajay covered, though 'nowhere near as comprehensively'.

items.title: Republic
items.creator: Plato
items.why: Plato was clear-eyed about democracy's weaknesses long before radio, rallies, TV and social media made it easy to blast simplistic messages to the masses.

items.title: Resisting State Injustice (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 120)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: They discussed state legitimacy directly in that episode. Amit recalls throwing many counterfactuals at Brennan and coming away impressed by the power of his ideas.

items.title: Resources vs Constraints - Why T20 Teams Need to Attack More
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Sets out the core T20 argument of the episode: the same 11 resources spread over only 20 overs means teams should attack far more than they do.

items.title: Rethinking NEET, and medical education
items.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
items.why: It applies the episode's argument to medical admissions, where Ajay says the root cause is the lack of medical colleges.

items.title: Rethinking Regulation in India (talk and slides)
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: A fuller presentation of the regulatory-theory argument Ajay makes in this episode.

items.title: Rhyme and Reason
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit says this probably made him the only professional limerick writer in the world. He wrote about a hundred before they got too political for the paper.

items.title: Richard Dawkins's books, including The Selfish Gene and The Blind Watchmaker
items.creator: Richard Dawkins
items.why: He read 'the whole shebang.' Understanding natural selection deeply changed how he sees human nature.

items.title: Rick Beato's YouTube channel
items.creator: Rick Beato
items.why: A great music channel that Amit enjoys a lot and loves, though he says it isn't much about thinking on form.

items.title: Rising to the China Challenge
items.creator: Gautam Bambawale, Vijay Kelkar, Raghunath Mashelkar, Ganesh Natarajan, Ajit Ranade and Ajay Shah
items.why: It argues that India is outmatched by China's might and must build deep partnerships with other countries. Amit calls it a wonderful book.

items.title: Rob Henderson's tweet on dark triad men and dating apps
items.creator: Rob Henderson
items.why: Amit calls it fantastic. It explains how a minority of manipulative men can push everyone on dating apps toward mutual mistreatment.

items.title: Robert Caro's multi-volume biography of Lyndon Johnson
items.creator: Robert Caro
items.why: Amit admires its extraordinary rigor, joking that Caro took longer to write about Johnson's Senate years than Johnson spent in the Senate.

items.title: Robert Sapolsky's biology lectures on YouTube
items.creator: Robert Sapolsky
items.why: Sapolsky's classroom lectures are free online and, in Amit's words, absolutely masterful. Amit had never been interested in biology before, and says Sapolsky opens your mind in different ways. It is proof that great teaching is freely available.

items.title: Roger Ebert's review of New York Stories
items.creator: Roger Ebert
items.why: A companion read to the short film that named their course.

items.title: Rolling Thunder Review
items.creator: Martin Scorsese
items.why: It captures the hunger the hosts keep describing: to get to something, to do something, and to do it with the people you love.

items.title: Rollo Tomassi quoting Ronnie Coleman on the hard yards
items.creator: Ronnie Coleman (via Rollo Tomassi)
items.why: Aspiration means nothing without the work. Amit uses it to introduce thin versus thick desires.

items.title: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead
items.creator: Tom Stoppard
items.why: Stoppard takes two of Hamlet's friends, Shakespeare's minor characters, and builds a play 'a little bit about alienation' around them, which is the template for Amit's pair.

items.title: Rules Rather than Discretion: The Inconsistency of Optimal Plans
items.creator: Finn E. Kydland and Edward C. Prescott
items.why: It is a landmark of the rational expectations revolution and, Ajay notes, part of the work behind both authors' Nobel Prizes. It made economists take credibility and commitment seriously and showed that a state which ties its own hands becomes more effective.

items.title: Rumblefish
items.creator: Francis Ford Coppola
items.why: Amit loved it, and Desai convinced that small room it was a masterpiece. It is also tied to a memory Amit treasures about mentorship and good culture.

items.title: Runaway
items.creator: Alice Munro
items.why: Munro's stories are set in one province of Canada yet capture the human condition so well that readers everywhere love her. Amit calls this collection a masterpiece.

items.title: RUSI's commentary on Ukraine
items.creator: RUSI
items.why: Ongoing analysis of the war.

items.title: Saaya & the Rituals of Tamil Muslim Milk Tea
items.creator: Maazin Buhari
items.why: The source for the recipe behind his 'better masala chai'.

items.title: Sagar & Amruta meeting Gukesh in Singapore
items.creator: Sagar Shah
items.why: Gukesh hugs Sagar and then Amruta, showing how much the two mean to Indian chess.

items.title: Sagar Shah at the under-11 workshop all those years ago
items.creator: Sagar Shah
items.why: Sagar explains positions to kids on the floor, including Gukesh, Pranav and Leon Luke Mendonca, with Gukesh's dad in the background. It shows the long game in action.

items.title: Sagar Shah's interview with Ashwin Subramanian
items.creator: Sagar Shah
items.why: It backs the claim that an Indian tinkerer did it first.

items.title: Sahil Bloom on making it
items.creator: Sahil Bloom
items.why: It resonated as a warning against the complacency that prosperity breeds.

items.title: Sahil Bloom's book on the five kinds of wealth
items.creator: Sahil Bloom
items.why: A new book from a thinker Amit has come to rate highly. He expected to have read it by the time the episode aired.

items.title: Sahil Bloom's tweet: 'Preparation always beats planning.'
