items.why: This number woke up the Vajpayee cabinet. Ajay laments that it was never redone in the two decades since.

items.title: Trade liberalisation: Looking beyond the WTO
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: It supports the episode's case that the way forward is deep integration among willing countries rather than another simple multilateral round.

items.title: Trade misinvoicing: A channel for de facto capital account openness
items.creator: Abhijit Sen Gupta, Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
items.why: One of Ajay's chosen favourite papers involving himself.

items.title: Trek the Sahyadris
items.creator: Harish Kapadia
items.why: It was a turning point in his life. He read it a hundred times, and it started his lifelong hiking in the Sahyadris.

items.title: Trick or Treatment?
items.creator: Simon Singh and Edzard Erst
items.why: A science-based look at alternative medicine, which fits Amit's line: respect tradition, but always be skeptical.

items.title: Troubled: A Memoir of Foster Care, Family, and Social Class
items.creator: Rob Henderson
items.why: Highly recommended. Henderson, whom Amit calls a very fine thinker worth following, coined 'luxury beliefs', the idea behind this episode.

items.title: True Names
items.creator: Vernor Vinge
items.why: It makes you think about identity in a new way. Ajay says that after reading it you will never sign on to state projects that force everyone to have a single Aadhaar number.

items.title: Truth and Beauty
items.creator: S Chandrasekhar
items.why: A 'lovely slim book' that Ajay says everybody should read. It is about craft and the long journey of learning to do it, including Beethoven saying, just before the Ninth Symphony, that he now knew how to write music.

items.title: Tu Youyou on the Nobel Prize website
items.creator: Nobel Prize
items.why: A profile of the non-PhD researcher whose close reading of classical Chinese produced artemisinin.

items.title: Tughlaq
items.creator: Girish Karnad
items.why: A play about a ruler whose grand schemes failed, written in the mid-sixties as a veiled comment on Nehruvian socialism. Amit adds that fiction holds truths about the human condition.

items.title: Tweet quoting Anais Nin: 'We do not see things as they are. We see things as we are.'
items.creator: Anais Nin (shared by @gigi_dreamer)
items.why: A reminder that we are part of whatever we perceive, so we should take a step back before judging. It set off the episode's first argument, with Ajay pushing back in defence of objective truth.

items.title: Twilight in the Street of Storytellers
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: A record of a place he loved before he knew it had been the scene of a massacre on the scale of Jallianwala Bagh.

items.title: Two divergent measures
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: It is further reading on the uncertainty dimension of the current moment.

items.title: Tyler Cowen on the Lex Fridman Podcast
items.creator: Lex Fridman
items.why: In it Cowen picks 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' as one of the three works most important to him and explains why.

items.title: Uber Isn't Worth $17 Billion
items.creator: Aswath Damodaran
items.why: The first half of the episode's valuation parable: a careful analysis built on what turned out to be the wrong story.

items.title: Ukraine's offensive: is it failing?
items.creator: Lawrence Freedman
items.why: Takes on the disappointment that the counteroffensive hasn't produced a quick breakthrough.

items.title: Unchecked and Unbalanced
items.creator: Arnold Kling
items.why: More of Kling's sceptical analysis, which backs Amit's worry that reactive state intervention makes the next crisis worse.

items.title: Understanding Baumol's Cost Disease And Its Impact On Healthcare
items.creator: Varun Ganapathi
items.why: He calls it 'one of those great ideas in economics.' It bears directly on his point that personal services for the elderly, which only young people can provide, become unaffordable when the young are scarce.

items.title: Understanding Evolution (Everything is Everything, Ep 125)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: It lays the natural-selection groundwork that this episode's 'why' of sexuality depends on.

items.title: Understanding Media
items.creator: Marshall McLuhan
items.why: Amit calls it absolutely worth reading for anyone thinking about how media shapes us.

items.title: Unelected Power
items.creator: Paul Tucker
items.why: It covers the softer, advanced-economy version of the problem: power wielded by unelected officials, with checks and balances weakening. You could call these 'first world problems', but Ajay says thinking about them sharpens thinking about the same problems in underdeveloped countries.

items.title: Unix and the command line
items.why: After 40 years around computers, he considers it the most productive and powerful environment there is. Small tools are strung together to do any task. Unix runs under Macs, Chromebooks, Android, Kindle and Linux, and he sees it as a philosophy as much as software.

items.title: Untitled
items.creator: Leonard Cohen
items.why: It is a slave speaking, saying that any system you design without us will not work. A poetic version of why top-down designs fail.

items.title: Urban Governance in India (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 31)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan
items.why: Shruti explains why city governance is bad: power and accountability are not linked.

items.title: Utilitarianism
items.creator: Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill
items.why: He thinks it is sound on the whole and worth knowing, but critiques it with Hayek's knowledge problem: the world is too complex to know the consequences of our actions.

items.title: V-Dem
items.why: Ajay thinks V-Dem is in many ways the better measure of democracy, though more work to use.

items.title: Vaishnav Vyas's football Substack
items.creator: Vaishnav Vyas
items.why: Amit and Vaishnav bond over the thinkers of the game (like Guardiola turning 'anti-Guardiola'). The newsletter models loving sport for ideas rather than flags.

items.title: Vasant Dhar's newsletter
items.creator: Vasant Dhar
items.why: Amit believed the personal tone would really work. That voice has since grown into a finished book.

items.title: Vinayak Calling Vinayak (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 385)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Vinayak Chaturvedi
items.why: A further deep dive for anyone intrigued by the 'two Savarkars'.

items.title: Vinod Khosla is skeptical of investors
items.creator: Vinod Khosla
items.why: Khosla, a founder turned VC, says seventy percent of VCs add negative value, because textbook advice is no substitute for having lived through a founder's daily crises.

items.title: Vinod Khosla on vision & tactics
items.creator: Vinod Khosla
items.why: 'Be obstinate about your vision, but flexible about your tactics' shows how long-term vision and daily adaptation coexist.

items.title: Virtue Ethics
items.creator: Aristotle
items.why: It appeals to him because it identifies ways of behaving that make everybody better off and lead to human prosperity, without needing religion.

items.title: Visakan Veerasamy's tweet quoting Nietzsche: 'He who has a why to live for can bear with almost any how.'
items.creator: Visakan Veerasamy
items.why: It started the discussion about whether purpose brings happiness or a burden.

items.title: Vishnu Prasanna interviewed by Sagar Shah
items.creator: Sagar Shah
items.why: Gukesh's early coach explains his experiment of training Gukesh without computers until he became a GM.

items.title: Vitalik Buterin's writings on identity and political philosophy
items.creator: Vitalik Buterin
items.why: Ajay calls him a deep thinker at the global frontier of rethinking identity. Amit adds that he is 'not just some random crypto guy' but a serious thinker on politics.

items.title: Vivian Gornick's books
items.creator: Vivian Gornick
items.why: He calls Gornick 'the great memoirist' and says all of her books are recommendations.

items.title: Vlad Tenev's product philosophy
items.creator: Vlad Tenev
items.why: 'One screen, one button, one action' guards against throwing every good idea into the product.

items.title: VP Menon: The Unsung Architect of Modern India
items.creator: Narayani Basu
items.why: A 'marvelous book' that shows the dramatic human story behind a seemingly expressionless bureaucrat.

items.title: Waiting for Godot
items.creator: Samuel Beckett
items.why: The conversations between its two characters, Vladimir and Estragon, capture the alienation Amit wants for his two young Sikhs.

items.title: Waking Life
items.creator: Richard Linklater
items.why: Vaishnav feels Linklater captures the essence of life. His films taught Vaishnav how we look at people, how people look at us, and gave him a deeper self-awareness.

items.title: Walk around an IKEA and admire the company
items.why: He urges listeners not just to shop there but to admire 'the audacity of conception': how the furniture is designed and manufactured and how the stores and global marketing are built. It shows the deep capability that sits inside great firms.

items.title: Want Free Trade? May I Introduce You to the Tariff
items.creator: Robert Lighthizer
items.why: It was the best piece he found from the American right. Several people sent it to him asking how he would respond, and writing a thorough rebuttal forced him to sharpen his thinking. He says to read it for its cleanest arguments and ignore the many bad ones.

items.title: Warren Buffett on inner scorecards
items.creator: Warren Buffett
items.why: Buffett's father taught him to live by his inner scorecard of values rather than the outer scorecard of money and reputation.

items.title: Warrior Lovers
items.creator: Catherine Salmon and Donald Symons
items.why: It contrasts the male fantasy world of 'pornotopia' (lust without courtship) with the romance novel, which it reads as a chronicle of female mate choice.

items.title: Watching the Wheels (Chris Cornell version)
items.creator: Chris Cornell
items.why: Amit says Chris Cornell's is his favourite version of the song.

items.title: Watershed 1967: India's Forgotten Victory Over China
items.creator: Probal Dasgupta
items.why: It tells the little-known story of India pushing China back in 1967. Its background chapters supplied several of Amit's stories here: the CIA war game, Pakistan's 1965 guerrilla teams, Sagat Singh at Nathu La, and the Chinese loudspeaker propaganda. It also touches on Chinese backing for the Naxalites.

items.title: Ways of Seeing
items.creator: John Berger
items.why: Amit calls it a masterpiece.

items.title: We Are All Amits From Africa (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 343)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Krish Ashok and Naren Shenoy
items.why: Covers how circumstances such as rice shortages and caste lines produce distinct foods.

items.title: We Must Save Our Farmers
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: More of Amit's written case for freeing Indian agriculture.

items.title: Weapons of the Weak
items.creator: James C. Scott
items.why: It develops the view that states emerged to tax and conscript, and that many people sensibly tried to keep the state out of their lives. Ajay sees 'more than a shadow' of this in Indian society, where many people want to stay far away from the government.

items.title: What Cricket Can Learn From Economics
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Applies the economist's idea of opportunity cost to cricket. This is the lens behind the episode's claim that T20's scarcity of deliveries makes dot balls costlier and wickets cheaper.

items.title: What Economics Can Learn (Everything is Everything, Ep 75)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: It examines how economics, sociology and anthropology have walled themselves off from each other, with further silos inside each.

items.title: What happened to global food prices?
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Background on global food price movements and why Indian farmers should be free to sell abroad when world prices rise.

items.title: What I, as a development economist, have been actively "for"
items.creator: Lant Pritchett
items.why: Part of the body of work Amit wants every listener to engage with directly, not just through podcast conversations.

items.title: What is Libertarianism? (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 117)
items.creator: Amit Varma with David Boaz
items.why: A chance to hear Boaz discuss the ideas behind the book in conversation.

items.title: What is the New Chinese Currency Regime?
items.creator: Ajay Shah, Achim Zeileis and Ila Patnaik
items.why: It is Ajay's example of serious research produced by a team spread across countries.

items.title: What Should India Do? (Everything is Everything, Ep 114)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: That episode argued that dealing with America and China requires deep knowledge of them. Hitler is the cautionary tale of what happens without it.

items.title: What You Can Learn from Family Business
items.creator: Nicolas Kachaner, George Stalk Jr, and Alain Bloch
items.why: It counters the stereotype with evidence from family firms worldwide. Professionally run firms do better in good times, but family firms do less badly in bad times. Family firms are frugal, keep a high bar for capital expenditure and carry little debt. They make fewer and smaller acquisitions, are surprisingly diversified and international, and retain talent better. Ajay says he agrees with all of it.

items.title: What's Consolation for an Atheist?
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: It is where he takes on the one function of religion he can't replace, consolation in grief, and decides he won't adopt a comforting fiction.

items.title: What's Wrong With the Indian Media? (Everything is Everything, Ep 113)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Trusted information becomes more valuable, not less, in a world full of noise and misinformation.

items.title: When All Else Fails: The Ethics of Resistance to State Injustice
items.creator: Jason Brennan
items.why: It poses the policeman-versus-stranger thought experiment, which forces you to ask why we grant state agents moral cover. Amit was blown away by the clarity of Brennan's thinking and says the book will make you think about state legitimacy and morality.

items.title: When and where do great feats of architecture come about?
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Argues that grand structures are a power move to make peasants bow, and that more totalitarian regimes build more imposing ones. Good architecture comes from local conditions.

items.title: When Crime Pays
items.creator: Milan Vaishnav
items.why: A must-read on crime in Indian politics.

items.title: When Genius Failed
items.creator: Roger Lowenstein
items.why: It tells the story of the collapse of Long-Term Capital Management, a firm with several Nobel Prize-winning academics. It shows how badly finance can go wrong.

items.title: When Harry Met Sally
items.creator: Rob Reiner
items.why: Amit loves it and calls it a charming film. Its premise that men and women can't be friends gave the Facebook friendship index its nickname.

items.title: When McKinsey Comes to Town
items.creator: Walt Bogdanich and Michael Forsythe
items.why: A cautious recommendation: he finds the book 'a bit mean' and 'one-sided'. It still gives insight into the difficulties of bringing a consulting firm and a consulting approach into complex problems of public policy, which is exactly the episode's theme.

items.title: When the Chips Are Down
items.creator: Pranay Kotasthane and Abhiram Manchi
items.why: Together with Chip War, it demystifies the semiconductor wars and what is really going on beneath the headlines.

items.title: When We Were Robots in Egypt
items.creator: Jo Walton
items.why: A literary take on the machines-take-over theme he finds farcical as a forecast but beautiful as art.

items.title: When world leaders thought you shouldn't need passports or visas
items.creator: Jo Adetunji
items.why: Documents how recent and avoidable state control of human movement really is.

items.title: Where Did Development Economics Go Wrong? (Ideas of India)
items.creator: Lant Pritchett and Shruti Rajagopalan
items.why: Amit calls Pritchett's episodes with Shruti Rajagopalan 'very good'. They extend the episode's diagnosis of how the field lost its way.

items.title: Where did the Bombay Club go wrong?
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: It is background on why some industrialists choose protection over competing in a global market.

items.title: Where Your Taxes Go (India Uncut series)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: A memorable catalogue, from moustache allowances to sixty-two sandstone elephants, of what coerced money ends up paying for.

items.title: White Magic Adventure Travel
items.why: It runs a fixed calendar of treks, so you can show up alone and join others without organising your own group.

items.title: Who's Got the Guts to Go to the Moon?
items.creator: Adam Mastroianni
items.why: Argues that most research today is super safe and nobody chases moonshots. It sets out the life cycle of new ideas: a weirdo outsider proposes one, experts ignore or suppress it, and eventually it wins because it's better.

items.title: Whole-grain sourdough bread
items.why: He calls it Pareto superior to industrial yeast bread on taste and especially on health. It's fun to make, though you have to work to keep it near 20°C in India.

items.title: Why Abhijit Banerjee Had to Go Abroad to Achieve Glory
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: It sets out the episode's core claim: talent congregates, and Harvard was critical to Banerjee's development. It uses Kremer's O-Ring paper as the mechanism.

items.title: Why AI Will Save the World
items.creator: Marc Andreessen
items.why: In Amit's words, a beautiful essay that addresses all of these questions in great detail.

items.title: Why are firms short-sighted?
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: It backs Ajay's argument that a high cost of capital in India's underdeveloped financial system forces firms into short time horizons.

items.title: Why Children Labour
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Gives the full argument and evidence, including the Oxfam Bangladesh and UNICEF Nepal follow-ups.

items.title: Why Does It Always Rain On Me?
items.creator: Travis
items.why: He loves the line 'Is it because I lied when I was seventeen?'

items.title: Why Does the Pandemic Seem to Be Hitting Some Countries Harder Than Others?
items.creator: Siddhartha Mukherjee
items.why: It led to Ajay's first-hand experience of the New Yorker's fact-checking, his main example of what real editorial process involves.

items.title: Why Gig Work Matters
items.creator: Maitreesh Ghatak and Ajay Shah
items.why: It argues that gig work is a ready-made urban safety net that needs no government, and an answer to recurring populist demands for an NREGS in the cities.

items.title: Why I Loved and Left Poker
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: It explains why he left poker. In his words, it 'may tell you why you shouldn't start playing'.

items.title: Why I Write
items.creator: George Orwell
items.why: A companion piece to Amit's segment on Orwell, clear writing and the link between writing and thinking.

items.title: Why India Needs School Vouchers
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: His early case for school vouchers, the episode's main proposal for spending public money better.

items.title: Why is solving India's inflation crisis important?
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's contemporary argument for tackling inflation, written during the inflation crisis he describes in this episode.

items.title: Why Is There A Commotion?
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: One of Amit's earlier pieces listed alongside the episode's themes, for readers who want more of his writing on them.

items.title: Why Nationalism
items.creator: Yael Tamir
items.why: A serious scholarly case for nationalism. Amit disagrees, and reading it alongside his review gives both sides. The review ends by arguing that those who divide us are the true anti-nationals.

items.title: Why Nations Fail
items.creator: Daron Acemoglu and James A. Robinson
items.why: Further reading on what separates rich nations from poor ones, the episode's central question. It is not discussed in the conversation itself.

items.title: Why Read the Classics?
items.creator: Italo Calvino
items.why: Amit calls it an excellent book on the case for the classics.

items.title: Why the Future Doesn't Need Us
items.creator: Bill Joy
items.why: Joy worried about micro-machines, nanotechnology and DNA editing, and argued that everything we know about how messy software is applies to those fields too. Ajay uses it to make the case for treating gene editing with respect, neither banning it nor rushing it.

items.title: Why the RBI communication to government on the failure to meet inflation target must be placed in the public domain
items.creator: The Indian Express
items.why: It makes the case for publishing the RBI's explanation for missing its target. A public mea culpa makes failure painful, and that pain is what makes the rule credible.

items.title: Why We Fight: The Roots of War and the Paths to Peace
items.creator: Christopher Blattman
items.why: Ajay is glad an economist has 'opened the box of violence'. Taming violence, both between citizens and between state and citizens, is central to the development story, and economists usually stick to money and markets.

items.title: Wild Strawberries
items.creator: Ingmar Bergman
items.why: Amit thinks it is the best way into Bergman, who can feel inaccessible. It is a masterpiece about old age and growing old gracefully.

items.title: William Spaniel (YouTube channel)
items.creator: William Spaniel
items.why: He had some of the best understanding of the battle as it unfolded. He also writes slower, more considered books, so he covers both the first draft of history and the sense-making.

items.title: Wiring the World
items.creator: Emily Thompson
items.why: A fascinating account of ERP's global sound crusade, including the French backlash and how Indian filmmakers mastered sound and outgrew ERP.

items.title: Womaning in India With Mahima Vashisht (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 293)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Mahima Vashisht
items.why: Shows how building your own themes layer turns a pile of material into a map of the territory, and how that made a thematic conversation possible.

items.title: Women at Work (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 132)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Namita Bhandare
items.why: Background on why women's labour-force participation in India fell even as incomes rose.

items.title: Words
items.creator: Bee Gees
items.why: 'It's only words and words are all we have' captures the episode's opening point: getting the technical meaning of words right is the foundation of clear thinking.

items.title: World Energy Outlook 2023
items.creator: International Energy Agency
items.why: He admits people flee from reports as boring official platitudes, but calls this one unputdownable. Energy is 'pure drama' right now, and the report's facts, graphs and stories make that vivid. Never read a report, he says, but make an exception for this one.

items.title: Worldly Philosopher: The Odyssey of Albert O. Hirschman
items.creator: Jeremy Adelman
items.why: Hirschman was far more than an economist: a thinker and political philosopher who, in Ajay's words, 'led the world's best life'. If you want to lead a good life, this is the life to study. Ajay says he loves Hirschman as much as he loves James C. Scott.

items.title: XKDR Forum's paper on Indian courts
items.creator: XKDR Forum
items.why: It weakens the 1992 argument for giving SEBI its own in-house judging. Ajay suggests the trade-offs have changed and the arrangement should be rethought.

items.title: Yes Minister / Yes Prime Minister (TV series)
items.creator: Jonathan Lynn and Antony Jay
items.why: It supplies the perfect parody of policy reflexes, 'We must do something, this is something, therefore we must do this.'

items.title: Yes Prime Minister
items.creator: Jonathan Lynn and Antony Jay
items.why: Ajay calls both of them masterpieces.

items.title: You Should Start a Business (Everything is Everything, Ep 102)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: It sets up this episode. It covers being inward-driven, the project-to-product-to-business path, getting a few people to love your product, ignoring naysayers, and the bias for action.

items.title: Young Rural Women in India Chase Big-City Dreams
items.creator: Ellen Barry
items.why: Ajay sees firms and exports as the heart and soul of the Indian story. This piece shows the human drama in the lives of the workers behind the export numbers.

items.title: Your maid funds Unani
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: It takes apart the myth that only about 3% of Indians pay taxes. The cost of state spending falls on the poorest too.

items.title: YouTube Music (discovery playlists)
items.why: You just ask it for a playlist without having to think, and it brings you new things. Ajay has been astonished by how much newer music he has found and liked this way.

items.title: Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance
items.creator: Robert M. Pirsig
items.why: Its line 'the Zen you find in the mountain is the Zen that you take up there' captures his point: what you get from the mountains depends on the mind you bring.

items.title: Zerodha
items.why: Ajay says modern firms like Zerodha, along with global firms, do an excellent job and make operating these accounts easy. He jokes it is only '3x harder' than using Zepto.

items.title: Zombie Firms and Creative Destruction (The Seen and the Unseen, Ep 118)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
items.why: A longer treatment of the zombie-firm problem at the heart of this episode.
